The Constant Rule shows that in computing derivatives, a constant factor
may be moved "outside" the derivative. It can only be used when <math>c</math> is a constant. For
products of two functions of <math>x</math>, we have:
THEOREM 4 (Product Rule)
Suppose u and v depend on x. Then for any value of x where <math>du/dx</math> and <math>dv/dx</math>
exist,
<math display="block">\frac{d(uv)}{dv} = u\frac{dv}{dv} + v\frac{du}{dv}, \qquad d(uv) = u\,dv + v\,du.</math>
<i>PROOF</i> Let <math>y = uv</math>, and let <math>\Delta x \neq 0</math> be infinitesimal.
<math>v + \Delta v = (u + \Delta u)(v + \Delta v),</math>
<math display="block">\Delta y = (u + \Delta u)(v + \Delta v) - uv = u \,\Delta v + v \,\Delta u + \Delta u \,\Delta v,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{u \, \Delta v + v \, \Delta u + \Delta u \, \Delta v}{\Delta x} = u \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta x} + v \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} + \Delta u \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta x}.</math>
<math>\Delta u</math> is infinitesimal by the Increment Theorem, whence
<math>st\left(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\right) = st\left(u\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta x} + v\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} + \Delta u\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta x}\right)</math>
<math display="block">= u \cdot st \left( \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta x} \right) + v \cdot st \left( \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} \right) + 0 \cdot st \left( \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta x} \right).</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = u\frac{dv}{dx} + v\frac{du}{dx}.</math>
So
The Constant Rule is really the special case of the Product Rule where <math>v</math> is
a constant function of <math>x, v = c</math>. To check this we let <math>v</math> be the constant <math>c</math> and see what
the Product Rule gives us:
<math display="block">\frac{d(u \cdot c)}{dx} = u\frac{dc}{dx} + c\frac{du}{dx} = u \cdot 0 + c\frac{du}{dx} = c\frac{du}{dx}.</math>
This is the Constant Rule.
The Product Rule can also be used to find the derivative of a power of u.

THEOREM 5 (Power Rule)
Let u depend on x and let n be a positive integer. For any value of x where
<math>du/dx</math> exists,
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^n)}{dx} = nu^{n-1}\frac{du}{dx}, \qquad d(u^n) = nu^{n-1}du.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> To see what is going on we first prove the Power Rule for <math>n = 1, 2, 3, 4</math>.
<math>n = 1</math>: We have <math>u^n = u</math> and <math>u^0 = 1</math>, whence
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^n)}{dx} = \frac{du}{dx} = 1 \cdot u^0 \cdot \frac{du}{dx}.</math>
<math>n = 2</math>: We use the Product Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^2)}{dv} = \frac{d(u \cdot u)}{dv} = u \frac{du}{dv} + u \frac{du}{dv} = 2 \cdot u^1 \cdot \frac{du}{dv}.</math>
<math>n=3</math>: We write <math>u^3=u\cdot u^2</math>, use the Product Rule again, and then use the
result for <math>n = 2</math>.
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^3)}{dx} = \frac{d(u \cdot u^2)}{dx} = u \frac{d(u^2)}{dx} + u^2 \frac{du}{dx}</math>
<math display="block">= u \cdot 2u \frac{du}{du} + u^2 \frac{du}{du} = 3u^2 \frac{du}{du}.</math>
<math>n = 4</math>: Using the Product Rule and then the result for <math>n = 3</math>,
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^4)}{dx} = \frac{d(u \cdot u^3)}{dx} = u \frac{d(u^3)}{dx} + u^3 \frac{du}{dx}</math>
<math display="block">= u \cdot 3u^2 \frac{du}{dx} + u^3 \frac{du}{dx} = 4u^3 \frac{du}{dx}.</math>
We can continue this process indefinitely and prove the theorem for every
positive integer <math>n</math>. To see this, assume that we have proved the theorem for <math>m</math>.
That is, assume that
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^m)}{dx} = mu^{m-1}\frac{du}{dx}.</math>
<b>(1)</b>
We then show that it is also true for <math>m + 1</math>. Using the Product Rule and the
Equation 1,
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^{m+1})}{dx} = \frac{d(u \cdot u^m)}{dx} = u \frac{d(u^m)}{dx} + u^m \frac{du}{dx}</math>
<math display="block">= u \cdot mu^{m-1} \frac{du}{dx} + u^m \frac{du}{dx} = (m+1)u^m \frac{du}{dx}.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^{m+1})}{dx} = (m+1)u^m \frac{du}{dx}.</math>
Thus
This shows that the theorem holds for <math>m + 1</math>.
We have shown the theorem is true for 1, 2, 3, 4. Set <math>m = 4</math>; then the theorem

holds for <math>m + 1 = 5</math>. Set <math>m = 5</math>; then it holds for <math>m + 1 = 6</math>. And so on.
Hence the theorem is true for all positive integers <math>n</math>.
In the proof of the Power Rule, we used the following principle:
PRINCIPLE OF INDUCTION
Suppose a statement <math>P(n)</math> about an arbitrary integer n is true when <math>n = 1</math>.
Suppose further that for any positive integer m such that <math>P(m)</math> is true, <math>P(m + 1)</math>
is also true. Then the statement <math>P(n)</math> is true of every positive integer n.
In the previous proof, <math>P(n)</math> was the Power Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^n)}{dx} = nu^{n-1}\frac{du}{dx}.</math>
The Principle of Induction can be made plausible in the following way. Let
a positive integer n be given. Set <math>m = 1</math>; since <math>P(1)</math> is true, <math>P(2)</math> is true. Now set <math>m = 2</math>;
since <math>P(2)</math> is true, <math>P(3)</math> is true. We continue reasoning in this way for n steps and con-
clude that <math>P(n)</math> is true.
The Power Rule also holds for <math>n = 0</math> because when <math>u \neq 0, u^0 = 1</math> and
<math>d1/dx = 0.</math>
Using the Sum, Constant, and Power rules, we can compute the derivative
of a polynomial function very easily. We have
<math display="block">\frac{d(x^n)}{dx} = nx^{n-1},</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d(cx^n)}{dx} = cnx^{n-1},</math>
and thus
<math display="block">\frac{d(a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1 x + a_0)}{dx} = a_n \cdot n x^{n-1} + a_{n-1} (n-1) x^{n-2} + \dots + a_1.</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> <math>\frac{d(-3x^3)}{dx} = -3 \cdot 5x^4 = -15x^4</math>.
EXAMPLE 2 <math display="block">\frac{d(6x^4 - 2x^3 + x - 1)}{dx} = 24x^3 - 6x^2 + 1.</math>
Two useful facts can be stated as corollaries.

2.3 DERIVATIVES OF RATIONAL FUNCTIONS
<b>COROLLARY 1</b>

THEOREM 6 (Quotient Rule)
Suppose u, v depend on x. Then for any value of x where <math>du/dx</math>, <math>dv/dx</math> exist and
<math>v \neq 0</math>,
<math display="block">\frac{d(u/v)}{dx} = \frac{v \ du/dx - u \ dv/dx}{v^2}, \qquad d\left(\frac{u}{v}\right) = \frac{v \ du - u \ dv}{v^2}.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> We combine the Product Rule and the formula for <math>d(1/v)</math>. Let <math>y = u/v</math>. We
write y in the form
<math>y = \frac{1}{n} \cdot u</math>.
<math>dy = d\left(\frac{1}{v}u\right) = \frac{1}{v}du + u\,d\left(\frac{1}{v}\right)</math>
Then
<math>=\frac{1}{v}du + u(-v^{-2})dv</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{v \, du - u \, dv}{v^2}.</math>
THEOREM 7 (Power Rule for Negative Exponents)
Suppose u depends on x and n is a negative integer. Then for any value of <math>x</math>
where <math>du/dx</math> exists and <math>u \neq 0</math>, <math>d(u^n)/dx</math> exists and
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^n)}{dv} = nu^{n-1}\frac{du}{dv}, \qquad d(u^n) = nu^{n-1}du.</math>
<i>PROOF</i> Since n is negative, <math>n = -m</math> where m is positive. Let <math>y = u^n = u^{-m}</math>. Then
<math>y = 1/u^m</math>. By the Lemma and the Power Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{(u^m)^2} \cdot \frac{d(u^m)}{dx}</math>
<math display="block">= -\frac{1}{n^{2m}} \cdot mu^{m-1} \frac{du}{dx}</math>

The six rules for differentiation which we have proved in this section are so
useful that they should be memorized. We list them all together.
Rules for Differentiation
Table 2.3.1
<math display="block">(1) \quad \frac{d(bx+c)}{dx} = b.</math>
<math display="block">d(bx + c) = b \, dx.</math>
(2) <math display="block">\frac{d(u+v)}{dx} = \frac{du}{dx} + \frac{dv}{dx}.</math>
<math display="block">d(u+v)=du+dv.</math>
(3) <math>\frac{d(cu)}{dx} = c\frac{du}{dx}</math>.
<math>d(cu) = c du</math>.
(4) <math display="block">\frac{d(uv)}{dx} = u\frac{dv}{dx} + v\frac{du}{dx}.</math>
<math display="block">d(uv) = u \, dv + v \, du.</math>
<math display="block">(5) \quad \frac{d(u^n)}{dx} = nu^{n-1}\frac{du}{dx}.</math>
<math>d(u^n) = nu^{n-1} du</math> (n is any integer).
(6) <math display="block">\frac{d(u/v)}{dx} = \frac{v \, du/dx - u \, dv/dx}{v^2}. \qquad d(u/v) = \frac{v \, du - u \, dv}{v^2}.</math>

2.4 INVERSE FUNCTIONS
Two real functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are called <i>inverse functions</i> if the two equations
<math>y = f(x), \qquad x = g(y)</math>
have the same graphs in the <math>(x, y)</math> plane. That is, a point <math>(x, y)</math> is on the curve <math>y = f(x)</math>
if, and only if, it is on the curve <math>x = g(y)</math>. (In general, the graph of the equation
<math>x = g(y)</math> is different from the graph of <math>y = g(x)</math>, but is the same as the graph of
<math>y = f(x)</math>; see Figure 2.4.1.)

If we think of f as a black box operating on an input x to produce an output
<math>f(x)</math>, the inverse function g is a black box operating on the output <math>f(x)</math> to undo the
work of <math>f</math> and produce the original input <math>x</math> (see Figure 2.4.2).

Often one can tell whether a function <math>f</math> has an inverse by looking at its
graph. If there is a horizontal line <math>y = c</math> which cuts the graph at more than one point,
the function f has no inverse. (See Figure 2.4.3.) If no horizontal line cuts the graph
at more than one point, then <math>f</math> has an inverse function <math>g</math>. Using this rule, we can see
in Figure 2.4.4 that the functions <math>y = |x|</math> and <math>y = \sqrt{1 - x^2}</math> do not have inverses.

INVERSE FUNCTION RULE
Suppose f and g are inverse functions, so that the two equations
<math>y = f(x)</math> and <math>x = g(y)</math>
have the same graphs. If both derivatives <math>f'(x)</math> and <math>g'(y)</math> exist and are nonzero,
then
<math display="block">f'(x) = \frac{1}{\varrho'(v)};</math>
that is,
<math>\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{dx/dy}</math>.
<b>PROOF</b> Let <math>\Delta x</math> be a nonzero infinitesimal and let <math>\Delta y</math> be the corresponding change
in y. Then <math>\Delta y</math> is also infinitesimal because <math>f'(x)</math> exists and is nonzero because
<math>f(x)</math> has an inverse function. By the rules for standard parts,
<math>f'(x) \cdot g'(y) = st\left(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\right) \cdot st\left(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y}\right)</math>
<math display="block">= st\left(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} \cdot \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y}\right) = st(1) = 1.</math>
<math display="block">f'(x) = \frac{1}{g'(y)}.</math>

THEOREM 1
If n is a positive integer and

Remember that <math>y = x^{1/n}</math> is defined for all x if n is odd and for <math>x > 0</math> if n is
even. The derivative <math>\frac{1}{n}x^{(1/n)-1}</math> is defined for <math>x \neq 0</math> if n is odd and for <math>x > 0</math> if n is even.
If we are willing to assume that <math>dy/dx</math> exists, then we can quickly find <math>dy/dx</math>
by the Inverse Function Rule.
<math>x = y^n</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dx}{dy} = ny^{n-1},</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{dx/dy} = \frac{1}{ny^{n-1}} = \frac{1}{n}y^{1-n}</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{1}{n} (x^{1/n})^{1-n} = \frac{1}{n} x^{(1-n)/n} = \frac{1}{n} x^{(1/n)-1}.</math>
Here is a longer but complete proof which shows that <math>dy/dx</math> exists and com-
putes its value.
<b>PROOF OF THEOREM 1</b> Let <math>x \neq 0</math> and let <math>\Delta x</math> be nonzero infinitesimal. We first
show that
<math display="block">\Delta y = (x + \Delta x)^{1/n} - x^{1/n}</math>
is a nonzero infinitesimal. <math>\Delta y \neq 0</math> because <math>x + \Delta x \neq x</math>. The standard part of
<math>\Delta y</math> is
<math display="block">st(\Delta y) = st((x + \Delta x)^{1/n}) - st(x^{1/n})</math>
<math display="block">= x^{1/n} - x^{1/n} = 0.</math>

POWER RULE FOR RATIONAL EXPONENTS
Let <math>y = x^r</math> where r is a rational number. Then whenever <math>x > 0</math>,
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = rx^{r-1}.</math>

2.5 TRANSCENDENTAL FUNCTIONS
The transcendental functions include the trigonometric functions <math>\sin x</math>, <math>\cos x</math>, <math>\tan x</math>,
the exponential function <math>e^x</math>, and the natural logarithm function <math>\ln x</math>. These functions
are developed in detail in Chapters 7 and 8. This section contains a brief discussion.
1 TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS
The Greek letters <math>\theta</math> (theta) and <math>\phi</math> (phi) are often used for angles. In the calculus it is
convenient to measure angles in radians instead of degrees. An angle <math>\theta</math> in radians is
defined as the length of the arc of the angle on a circle of radius one (Figure 2.5.1).
Since a circle of radius one has circumference <math>2\pi</math>,
<math>360 \text{ degrees} = 2\pi \text{ radians}.</math>

90 degrees = <math>\pi/2</math> radians.

By connecting the dots with a smooth curve, we obtain a function <math>y = 10^x</math>,
where x varies over all real numbers instead of just the rationals. <math>10^x</math> is called the
exponential function with base 10. It is positive for all x and follows the rules
<math>10^{a+b} = 10^a \cdot 10^b, \quad 10^{a \cdot b} = (10^a)^b.</math>
The derivative of <math>10^x</math> is a constant times <math>10^x</math>, approximately
<math display="block">\frac{d(10^x)}{dx} \sim (2.303)10^x.</math>
To see this let <math>\Delta x</math> be a nonzero infinitesimal. Then
<math display="block">\frac{d(10^x)}{dx} = st \left[ \frac{10^{x + \Delta x} - 10^x}{\Delta x} \right] = st \left[ \frac{(10^{\Delta x} - 1)10^x}{\Delta x} \right] = st \left[ \frac{10^{\Delta x} - 1}{\Delta x} \right] 10^x.</math>
The number <math>st[(10^{\Delta x} - 1)/\Delta x]</math> is a constant which does not depend on x and can be
shown to be approximately 2.303.
If we start with a given positive real number b instead of 10, we obtain the
exponential function with base b, <math>y = b^x</math>. The derivative of <math>b^x</math> is equal to the constant
<math>st[(b^{\Delta x}-1)/\Delta x]</math> times <math>b^x</math>. This constant depends on b. The derivative is computed as
follows:
<math display="block">\frac{d(b^x)}{dx} = st \left[ \frac{b^{x+\Delta x} - b^x}{\Delta x} \right] = st \left[ \frac{(b^{\Delta x} - 1)b^x}{\Delta x} \right] = st \left[ \frac{b^{\Delta x} - 1}{\Delta x} \right] b^x.</math>
The most useful base for the calculus is the number e. e is defined as the real
number such that the derivative of <math>e^x</math> is <math>e^x</math> itself,

3 THE NATURAL LOGARITHM
The inverse of the exponential function <math>x = e^{y}</math> is the natural logarithm function,
written
<math>y = \ln x</math>.
Verbally, <math>\ln x</math> is the number y such that <math>e^y = x</math>. Since <math>y = \ln x</math> is the inverse function
of <math>x = e^y</math>, we have
<math>e^{\ln a} = a</math>, <math>\ln (e^a) = a</math>.
The simplest values of <math>y = \ln x</math> are
<math>ln(1/e) = -1</math>, <math>ln(1) = 0</math>, <math>ln e = 1</math>.
Figure 2.5.8 shows the graph of <math>y = \ln x</math>. It is defined only for <math>x > 0</math>.

2.6 CHAIN RULE
The Chain Rule is more general than the Inverse Function Rule and deals with the
case where <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are both functions of a third variable <math>t</math>.
<math>x = f(t), \qquad y = G(x).</math>
Suppose
Thus x depends on t, and y depends on x. But y is also a function of <math>t</math>,
<math>y = g(t)</math>,
where g is defined by the rule
<math>g(t) = G(f(t)).</math>
The function g is sometimes called the <i>composition</i> of G and f (sometimes written
<math>g = G \circ f</math>).

## PDF page 96

86
2 DIFFERENTIATION
The composition of <math>G</math> and <math>f</math> may be described in terms of black boxes.
The function <math>g = G \circ f</math> is a large black box operating on the input t to produce
<math>g(t) = G(f(t))</math>. If we look inside this black box (pictured in Figure 2.6.1), we see two
smaller black boxes, f and G. First f operates on the input t to produce <math>f(t)</math>, and then
G operates on <math>f(t)</math> to produce the final output <math>g(t) = G(f(t))</math>.
The Chain Rule expresses the derivative of g in terms of the derivatives of f
and G. It leads to the powerful method of "change of variables" in computing deriva-
tives and, later on, integrals.

CHAIN RULE
Let f, G be two real functions and define the new function g by the rule
<math>g(t) = G(f(t)).</math>
At any value of t where the derivatives <math>f'(t)</math> and <math>G'(f(t))</math> exist, <math>g'(t)</math> also exists
and has the value
<math display="block">g'(t) = G'(f(t))f'(t).</math>
<math>x = f(t),</math> <math>y = g(t),</math> <math>y = G(x).</math>
PROOF Let
Take t as the independent variable, and let <math>\Delta t \neq 0</math> be infinitesimal. Form the
corresponding increments <math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\Delta y</math>. By the Increment Theorem for
<math>x = f(t)</math>, <math>\Delta x</math> is infinitesimal. Using the Increment Theorem again but this
time for <math>y = G(x)</math>, we have
<math display="block">\Delta y = G'(x) \, \Delta x + \varepsilon \, \Delta x</math>
for some infinitesimal <math>\varepsilon</math>. Dividing by <math>\Delta t</math>,

The equation
<math>\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx} \frac{dx}{dt}</math>
with t as the independent variable is trivial. We simply cancel the <math>dx</math>'s. But when
<math>dy/dx</math> is computed with x as the independent variable while <math>dx/dt</math> is computed with t
as the independent variable, the two <math>dx</math>'s have different meanings, and the equation
is not trivial.
Similarly, the equation
<math>dy = \frac{dy}{dx} dx</math>
is trivial with x as the independent variable but not when t is the independent variable
in dy and dx, while x is independent in <math>dy/dx</math>.
The Chain Rule shows that when we change independent variables the
equations
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}, \qquad dy = \frac{dy}{dx}dx</math>
remain true.
The Inverse Function Rule can be proved from the Chain Rule as follows.
Let
<math>y = f(x), \qquad x = g(y)</math>
be inverse functions whose derivatives exist. Then
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{dy}{dy} = 1,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{dx/dy}, \qquad f'(x) = \frac{1}{g'(y)}.</math>

2.6 CHAIN RULE
<b>POWER RULE</b>
Let r be a rational number, and let u depend on x. If <math>u > 0</math> and <math>du/dx</math> exists,
then
<math display="block">\frac{d(u^r)}{dx} = ru^{r-1}\frac{du}{dx}.</math>
This is proved by letting <math>y = u^r</math> and computing <math>dy/dx</math> by the Chain Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\frac{du}{dx} = ru^{r-1}\frac{du}{dx}.</math>
The Chain Rule has two types of applications.
(1) Given <math>x = f(t)</math> and <math>y = G(x)</math>, find <math>\frac{dy}{dt}</math>. Use <math>\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx} \frac{dx}{dt}</math>.
(2) Given <math>x = f(t)</math> and <math>y = g(t)</math>, find <math>\frac{dy}{dx}</math>. Use <math>\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}</math>.
Applications of type (1) often arise when a new dependent variable <math>x</math> is
introduced to help compute <math>\frac{dy}{dt}</math>. Applications of type (2) arise when two variables
x and y both depend on a third variable t, for example, when x and y are the co-
ordinates of a moving particle and t is time.
We give three examples of type (1) and then three of type (2).
Suppose that by investing t dollars a company can produce
EXAMPLE 3
<math>x = \frac{t}{10} - 100, \quad t \ge 1000,</math>
items, and that it can sell x items for a total profit of
<math display="block">y = 5x - \frac{x^2}{100}.</math>
Find <math>\frac{dy}{dt}</math>, which is the marginal profit with respect to the amount invested.
<math display="block">\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{1}{10}, \qquad \frac{dy}{dx} = 5 - \frac{x}{50}.</math>
We have
By the Chain Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt} = \left(5 - \frac{x}{50}\right)\frac{1}{10}</math>
<math display="block">= \left(5 - \frac{\frac{r}{10} - 100}{50}\right) \frac{1}{10}</math>
<math>=0.7-\frac{t}{5000}</math>
Thus after t dollars have been invested, an additional dollar invested will
bring <math>0.7 - t/5000</math> dollars of additional profit.

2.7 HIGHER DERIVATIVES
DEFINITION
The second derivative of a real function f is the derivative of the derivative of
<math>f</math>, and is denoted by <math>f</math>". The third derivative of <math>f</math> is the derivative of the second
derivative, and is denoted by <math>f'''</math>, or <math>f^{(3)}</math>. In general, the nth derivative of <math>f</math> is
denoted by <math>f^{(n)}</math>.
If y depends on <math>x</math>, <math>y = f(x)</math>, then the second differential of y is defined to be
<math display="block">d^2y = f''(x) dx^2.</math>
In general the nth differential of y is defined by
<math>d^n y = f^{(n)}(x) dx^n</math>.
Here <math>dx^2</math> means <math>(dx)^2</math> and <math>dx^n</math> means <math>(dx)^n</math>.
We thus have the alternative notations
<math>\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = f''(x), \qquad \frac{d^ny}{dx^n} = f^{(n)}(x)</math>
for the second and nth derivatives. The notation
<math>y'' = f''(x), 	 y^{(n)} = f^{(n)}(x)</math>
is also used.
The definition of the second differential can be remembered in the following
way. By definition,
<math>dy = f'(x) dx</math>.
Now hold dx constant and formally apply the Constant Rule for differentiation,
obtaining
<math>d(dy) = f''(x) dx dx,</math>
<math display="block">d^2y = f''(x) dx^2.</math>
or
(This is not a correct use of the Constant Rule because the rule applies to a real
constant <math>c</math>, and <math>dx</math> is not a real number. It is only a mnemonic device to remember the
definition of <math>d^2v</math>, not a proof.)
The third and higher differentials can be motivated in the same way. If we
hold dx constant and formally use the Constant Rule again and again, we obtain
<math>dy = f'(x) dx</math>
<math>d^2y = f''(x) dx dx = f''(x) dx^2</math>
<math>d^3y = f'''(x) dx^2 dx = f'''(x) dx^3</math>
<math>d^4y = f^{(4)}(x) dx^3 dx = f^{(4)}(x) dx^4</math>
and so on.
The acceleration of a moving particle is defined to be the derivative of the
velocity with respect to time,
<math>a = dv/dt</math>.

2.8 IMPLICIT FUNCTIONS
2.8 IMPLICIT FUNCTIONS
We now turn to the topic of implicit differentiation. We say that y is an implicit
function of <math>x</math> if we are given an equation
<math>\sigma(x, y) = \tau(x, y)</math>
which determines y as a function of x. An example is <math>x + xy = 2y</math>. Implicit differentia-
tion is a way of finding the derivative of y without actually solving for y as a function
of x. Assume that <math>dy/dx</math> exists. The method has two steps:
Differentiate both sides of the equation <math>\sigma(x, y) = \tau(x, y)</math> to get a new equation
Step 1
<math display="block">\frac{d(\sigma(x,y))}{dx} = \frac{d(\tau(x,y))}{dx}.</math>
<b>(1)</b>
The Chain Rule is often used in this step.
Step 2 Solve the new Equation 1 for <math>dy/dx</math>. The answer will usually involve both x
and y.
In each of the examples below, we assume that <math>dy/dx</math> exists and use implicit
differentiation to find the value of <math>dy/dx</math>.
Given the equation <math>x + xy = 2y</math>, find <math>dy/dx</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b>
Step 1 <math>\frac{d(x + xy)}{dx} = \frac{d(2y)}{dx}</math>. We find each side by the Sum and Product Rules,
<math display="block">\frac{d(x+xy)}{dx} = \frac{dx + d(xy)}{dx} = \frac{dx + x \, dy + y \, dx}{dx}</math>
<math>=1+x\frac{dy}{dx}+y.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d(2y)}{dx} = 2\frac{dy}{dx}.</math>
Thus our new equation is
<math display="block">1 + x \frac{dy}{dx} + y = 2 \frac{dy}{dx}.</math>
Step 2 Solve for <math>dy/dx</math>.
<math display="block">2\frac{dy}{dx} - x\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 + y.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1+y}{2-x}.</math>
We can check our answer by solving the original equation for y and using
ordinary differentiation:
<math>x + xy = 2y</math>.
<math display="block">2y - xy = x.</math>
<math>y=\frac{x}{2-x}</math>.
.

2 DIFFERENTIATION
By the Quotient Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{(2-x)\cdot 1 - x(-1)}{(2-x)^2} = \frac{2}{(2-x)^2}.</math>
A third way to find <math>dy/dx</math> is to solve the original equation for x, find <math>dx/dy</math>,
and then use the Inverse Function Rule.
<math>x + xy = 2y</math>.
<math display="block">x = \frac{2y}{1 + y}.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{(1+y)\cdot 2 - 2y\cdot 1}{(1+y)^2} = \frac{2}{(1+y)^2}.</math>
<math>\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}(1+y)^2</math>.
To see that our three answers
<math>\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1+y}{2-x}, \qquad \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2}{(2-x)^2}, \qquad \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}(1+y)^2</math>
are all the same we substitute <math>\frac{x}{2-x}</math> for y:
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1+y}{2-x} = \frac{1+\frac{x}{2-x}}{2-x} = \frac{2}{(2-x)^2}.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}(1+y)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{x}{2-x}\right)^2 = \frac{2}{(2-x)^2}.</math>
In Example 1, we found <math>dy/dx</math> by three different methods.
(a) Implicit differentiation. We get <math>dy/dx</math> in terms of both x and y.
(b) Solve for y as a function of x and differentiate directly. This gives <math>dy/dx</math>
in terms of <math>x</math> only.
Solve for x as a function of y, find <math>dx/dy</math> directly, and use the Inverse
(c)
Function Rule. This method gives <math>dy/dx</math> in terms of y only.

Given an equation
<b>(6)</b>

between two terms which may involve the variables x and y, we differentiate both

<b>(7)</b>
We then solve Equation 7 to get <math>dy/dx</math> equal to a term which typically involves both
x and y. We can conclude that for any system of formulas which contains Equation 6
and determines y as a function of x, Equation 7 is true. Also, Equation 7 can be used
to find the slope of the tangent line at any point on the curve <math>\tau(x, y) = \sigma(x, y)</math>.

<b>FUNCTIONS</b>
3.1 HOW TO SET UP A PROBLEM
In applications, a calculus problem is often presented verbally, and it is up to you
to set up the problem in mathematical terms. The problem can usually be described
mathematically by a list of equations and inequalities. The next two sections contain
several examples that illustrate the process of setting up a problem. The examples
in this section are from algebra and geometry, and those in the next section are from
calculus.
It is sometimes hard to see how to begin on a story problem. It is helpful
to break the process up into three steps:
Step 1 Draw a diagram if possible, and label all quantities involved.
Step 2 Write the given information as a set of equations and/or inequalities.
Step 3 Solve the mathematical problem, and interpret the mathematical solution
to answer the original story problem.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> According to a treasure map, a buried treasure is located due east
of a cave and is 200 paces from a tree. The tree is 30 paces east and 40 paces
north of the cave. How far is the treasure from the cave?
The solution of this problem uses the quadratic formula, which will be
needed throughout the calculus course. We review it here.
QUADRATIC FORMULA If <math>a \neq 0</math>, then
<math display="block">ax^2 + bx + c = 0</math>
if and only if
<math display="block">x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.</math>
We solve Example 1 in three steps.
105

<math>x = 30 + \sqrt{38,400} \sim 226</math> paces. The treasure is approximately 226 paces
from the cave.

An algebraic identity that comes up frequently in calculus problems is
<math>(a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2</math>.
Sometimes it occurs in the form
<math display="block">(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}) = a - b.</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 5</b> The area of square A is twelve square units greater than the area of
square B, and the side of A is three units greater than the side of B. Find the
areas of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>.

Step 1 Let <math>a</math> be the area of <math>A</math> and <math>b</math> the area of <math>B</math>. See Figure 3.1.5.
Step 2 The sides of the squares have length <math>\sqrt{a}</math> and <math>\sqrt{b}</math> respectively. Thus
<math>a - b = 12, \quad \sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b} = 3.</math>
Step 3 We find <math>\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}</math>.
<math display="block">(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}) = a - b,</math>
<math display="block">3(\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b})=12,</math>
<math>\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} = 4</math>
Adding the equations <math>\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} = 4</math> and <math>\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b} = 3</math>, we obtain <math>2\sqrt{a} = 7</math>, <math>\sqrt{a} = \frac{7}{2}</math>, <math>a = \frac{49}{4}</math>. Subtracting the equations gives <math>2\sqrt{b} = 1</math>,
<math>\sqrt{b} = \frac{1}{2}, b = \frac{1}{4}</math>
INTERPRET THE SOLUTION The area of square A is <math>\frac{49}{4}</math> square units, and the area
of square B is <math>\frac{1}{4}</math> square units.

3.2 RELATED RATES
In a related rates problem, we are given the rate of change of one quantity and wish to
find the rate of change of another. Such problems can often be solved by implicit
differentiation.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> The point of a fountain pen is placed on an ink blotter, forming a
circle of ink whose area increases at the constant rate of 0.03 in.<sup>2</sup>/sec. Find
the rate at which the radius of the circle is changing when the circle has a
radius of <math>\frac{1}{2}</math> inch. We solve the problem in four steps.
Label all quantities involved and draw a diagram.
Step 1
<math>A = area</math> <math>r = radius of circle</math>
<math>t = time</math>
Both A and r are functions of t. The diagram is shown in Figure 3.2.1.
radius r

Step 2 Write the given information in the form of equations.
<math>dA/dt = 0.03, A = \pi r^2.</math>
The problem is to find <math>dr/dt</math> when <math>r = 1/2</math>.
Step 3 Differentiate both sides of the equation <math>A = \pi r^2</math> with respect to t.
<math>\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r \frac{dr}{dt}</math>, whence <math>0.03 = 2\pi r \frac{dr}{dt}</math>.
Step 4 Set <math>r = \frac{1}{2}</math> and solve for <math>dr/dt</math>.
<math>0.03 = 2\pi \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{dr}{dt}</math>, so <math>\frac{dr}{dt} = \frac{0.03}{\pi}</math> in./sec.

Related rates problems have the following form.
Given:
Two quantities which depend on time, say <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>.
(a)
(b) The rate of change of one of them, say <math>dx/dt</math>.
An equation showing the relationship between <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>.
(c)
(Usually this information is given in the form of a verbal description of a physical
situation and part of the problem is to express it in the form of an equation.)
The problem: Find the rate of change of y, <math>dy/dt</math>, at a certain time <math>t_0</math>. (The
time <math>t_0</math> is sometimes specified by giving the value which x, or y, has at that time.)
Related rates problems can frequently be solved in four steps as we did in the
examples.
Label all quantities in the problem and draw a picture. If the labels are
Step 1
<math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, and <math>t</math> (time), the remaining steps are as follows:
Step 2 Write an equation for the given rate of change <math>dx/dt</math>. Write another equation
for the given relation between <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>.
Differentiate both sides of the equation relating <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> with respect to <math>t</math>.
Step 3
We choose the time t as the independent variable. The result is a new
equation involving <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, <math>dx/dt</math>, and <math>dy/dt</math>.
Step 4 Set <math>t = t_0</math> and solve for <math>dy/dt</math>. It may be necessary to find the values of <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>,
and <math>dx/dt</math> at <math>t = t_0</math> first.
The hardest step is usually Step 2, because one has to start with the given
verbal description of the problem and set it up as a system of formulas. Sometimes
more than two quantities that depend on time are given. Here is an example with
three.

away at time 2:00. This is part of the problem.

<math>x = </math>position of the second car travelling east,

Step 4

We can now find the value of z at <math>t = 2</math>,
<math>z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{(-30)^2 + 40^2} = 50.</math>
Finally, we solve for <math>dz/dt</math> at <math>t=2</math>,
<math>60 \cdot (-30) + 40 \cdot 40 = 50 \frac{dz}{dt}, \qquad \frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{-1800 + 1600}{50} = -4.</math>
The negative sign shows that <math>z</math> is decreasing. Therefore at 2:00 the cars are
getting closer to each other at the rate of 4 mph.

<math>z = y/x</math>.

We conclude with another example from economics. In this example the
independent variable is the quantity <math>x</math> of a commodity. The quantity <math>x</math> which can be
sold at price <math>p</math> is called the demand function <math>D(p)</math>,
<math>x = D(p)</math>.
When a quantity <math>x</math> is sold at price <math>p</math>, the revenue is the product
<math>R = px</math>.
The additional revenue from the sale of an additional unit of the commodity is called
the marginal revenue and is given by the derivative
marginal revenue = <math>dR/dx</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 5</b> Suppose the demand for a product is equal to the inverse of the square
of the price. Find the marginal revenue when the price is $10 per unit.
Step 1 <math>p = price</math>, <math>x = demand</math>, <math>R = revenue</math>.
Step 2 <math>x = 1/p^2, R = px</math>.
<math display="block">\frac{dR}{dx} = p\frac{dx}{dx} + x\frac{dp}{dx} = p + x\frac{dp}{dx},</math>
Step 3
<math display="block">\frac{dx}{dn} = -2p^{-3},</math>
so by the Inverse Function Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{dp}{dx} = \frac{1}{dx/dp} = -\frac{1}{2p^{-3}} = -\frac{1}{2}p^{3}.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dR}{dx} = p + \left(\frac{1}{p^2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}p^3\right) = \frac{1}{2}p.</math>
Substituting,
Step 4 We are given <math>p = $10</math>. Therefore the marginal revenue is
<math>dR/dx = </math>$5.

Here is a list of formulas from plane and solid geometry which will be useful
in related rates problems. We always let <math>A = </math>area and <math>V = </math>volume.
Rectangle with sides a and b: <math>A = ab</math>, perimeter = <math>2a + 2b</math>
Triangle with base b and height h: <math>A = \frac{1}{2}bh</math>
Circle of radius r: <math>A = \pi r^2</math>, circumference = <math>2\pi r</math>
Sector (pie slice) of a circle of radius r and central angle <math>\theta</math> (measured in
radians): <math>A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta</math>
Rectangular solid with sides <math>a, b, c</math>: <math>V = abc</math>
Sphere of radius <math>r</math>: <math>V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3</math>, <math>A = 4\pi r^2</math>
Right circular cylinder, base of radius r, height of h: <math>V = \pi r^2 h</math>, <math>A = 2\pi r h</math>
Prism with base of area B and height h: <math>V = Bh</math>
Right circular cone, base of radius r, height h: <math>V = \pi r^2 h/3</math>,
<math display="block">A = \pi r \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}</math>

3.3 LIMITS
The notion of a limit is closely related to that of a derivative, but it is more general.
In this chapter f will always be a real function of one variable. Let us recall the
definition of the slope of <math>f</math> at a point <math>a</math>:
S is the slope of f at a if whenever <math>\Delta x</math> is infinitely close to but not equal to
zero, the quotient
<math display="block">\frac{f(a+\Delta x)-f(a)}{\Delta x}</math>
is infinitely close to S.
We now define the limit. <math>c</math> and <math>L</math> are real numbers.
DEFINITION
L is the <b>limit</b> of <math>f(x)</math> as x approaches c if whenever x is infinitely close to but
not equal to <math>c</math>, <math>f(x)</math> is infinitely close to <math>L</math>.
In symbols,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L</math>

if whenever <math>x \approx c</math> but <math>x \neq c</math>, <math>f(x) \approx L</math>. When there is no number L satisfying the
above definition, we say that the limit of <math>f(x)</math> as x approaches c does not exist.
Notice that the limit
<math>\lim_{x \to c} f(x)</math>
depends only on the values of <math>f(x)</math> for x infinitely close but not equal to c. The value
<math>f(c)</math> itself has no influence at all on the limit. In fact, it very often happens that
<math display="block">\lim_{x\to c} f(x)</math>
exists but <math>f(c)</math> is undefined.

microscope.
In Figure 3.3.1(b), part of the curve with <math>x \approx c</math> is outside the field of vision
of the microscope, and the limit does not exist.

THEOREM 1
The slope of <math>f</math> at a is given by the limit
<math display="block">f'(a) = \lim_{\Delta \to -0} \frac{f(a + \Delta x) - f(a)}{\Delta x}.</math>
Verbally, the slope of f at a is the limit of the ratio of the change in <math>f(x)</math> to
the change in x as the change in x approaches zero. The theorem is seen by simply
comparing the definitions of limit and slope. The slope exists exactly when the limit
exists; and when they do exist they are equal. Notice that the ratio
<math display="block">\frac{f(a+\Delta x)-f(a)}{\Delta x}</math>
is undefined when <math>\Delta x = 0</math>.
The slope of <math>f</math> at <math>a</math> is also equal to the limit
<math>f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}</math>.
This is seen by setting
<math>\Delta x = x - a</math>
<math>x = a + \Delta x</math>
Then when <math>x \approx a</math> but <math>x \neq a</math>, we have <math>\Delta x \approx 0</math> but <math>\Delta x \neq 0</math>; and
<math display="block">\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x} = \frac{f(a + \Delta x) - f(a)}{\Delta x} \approx f'(a).</math>
Sometimes a limit can be evaluated by recognizing it as a derivative and
using Theorem 1 above.

<math>F'(3) = 2 \cdot 3 = 6.</math>

THEOREM 2
A limit has value L,
<math display="block">\lim_{x\to c}f(c)=L,</math>
if and only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal to L,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x) = L.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> If <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L</math>, it follows at once from the definition that both one-sided
limits are L.
Assume that both one-sided limits are equal to L. Let <math>x \approx c</math>, but <math>x \neq c</math>.
Then either <math>x < c</math> or <math>x > c</math>. If <math>x < c</math>, then because <math>\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = L</math>, we
have <math>f(x) \approx L</math>. On the other hand if <math>x > c</math>, then <math>\lim_{x \to c^+} f(x) = L</math> gives
<math>f(x) \approx L</math>. Thus in either case <math>f(x) \approx L</math>. This shows that <math>\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L</math>.
When a limit does not exist, it is possible that neither one-sided limit exists,
that just one of them exists, or that both one-sided limits exist but have different
values.
<b>EXAMPLE 7 (Continued)</b> <math>\lim_{x\to 0^+} \sqrt{x} = 0</math>, and <math>\lim_{x\to 0^-} \sqrt{x}</math> does not exist.

3.4 CONTINUITY
Intuitively, a curve <math>y = f(x)</math> is continuous if it forms an unbroken line, that is, when-
ever <math>x_1</math> is close to <math>x_2</math>, <math>f(x_1)</math> is close to <math>f(x_2)</math>. To make this intuitive idea into a mathe-
matical definition, we substitute "infinitely close" for "close."

## PDF page 135

3.4 CONTINUITY
<b>DEFINITION</b>
f is said to be continuous at a point c if:
f is defined at c;
(i)
whenever x is infinitely close to <math>c</math>, <math>f(x)</math> is infinitely close to <math>f(c)</math>.
(ii)
If <math>f</math> is not continuous at <math>c</math> it is said to be discontinuous at <math>c</math>.
When f is continuous at c, the entire part of the curve where <math>x \approx c</math> will be
visible in an infinitesimal microscope aimed at the point <math>(c, f(c))</math>, as shown in Figure
3.4.1(a). But if f is discontinuous at c, some values of <math>f(x)</math> where <math>x \approx c</math> will either be
undefined or outside the range of vision of the microscope, as in Figure 3.4.1(b).
Continuity, like the derivative, can be expressed in terms of limits. Again the
proof is immediate from the definitions.

3 CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
As an application, we have a set of rules for combining continuous functions.
They can be proved either by the corresponding rules for limits (Table 3.3.1 in Section
3.3) or by computing standard parts.
THEOREM 2
Suppose f and g are continuous at c.
For any constant k, the function <math>k \cdot f(x)</math> is continuous at c.
(i)
(ii) <math>f(x) + g(x)</math> is continuous at c.
(iii) <math>f(x) \cdot g(x)</math> is continuous at c.
(iv) If <math>g(c) \neq 0</math>, then <math>f(x)/g(x)</math> is continuous at c.
(v) If <math>f(c)</math> is positive and n is an integer, then <math>\sqrt[n]{f(x)}</math> is continuous at c.
By repeated use of Theorem 2, we see that all of the following functions are
continuous at c.
Every polynomial function.
Every rational function <math>f(x)/g(x)</math>, where <math>f(x)</math> and <math>g(x)</math> are polynomials and
<math>g(c) \neq 0</math>.
The functions <math>f(x) = x^r</math>, r rational and x positive.
Sometimes a function <math>f(x)</math> will be undefined at a point <math>x = c</math> while the limit
<math display="block">L = \lim_{x \to c} f(x)</math>
exists. When this happens, we can make the function continuous at <math>c</math> by defining
<math>f(c) = L</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> Let <math>f(x) = \frac{x^2 + x - 2}{x - 1}</math>.
At any point <math>c \neq 1</math>, f is continuous. But <math>f(1)</math> is undefined so f is discontinuous
at 1. However,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^2 + x - 2}{x - 1} = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{(x - 1)(x + 2)}{x - 1} = 3.</math>
We can make <math>f</math> continuous at 1 by defining
<math display="block">f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^2 + x - 2}{x - 1} & \text{if } x \neq 1, \\ 3 & \text{if } x = 1. \end{cases}</math>
(See Figure 3.4.2.)
In terms of a dependent variable <math>y = f(x)</math>, the definition of continuity takes
the following form, where <math>\Delta y = f(c + \Delta x) - f(c)</math>.
y is continuous at <math>x = c</math> if:
(i) <math>y</math> is defined at <math>x = c</math>.
(ii) Whenever <math>\Delta x</math> is infinitesimal, <math>\Delta y</math> is infinitesimal.

THEOREM 3
If <math>f</math> is differentiable at <math>c</math> then <math>f</math> is continuous at <math>c</math>.
PROOF Let <math>y = f(x)</math>, and let <math>\Delta x</math> be a nonzero infinitesimal. Then <math>\Delta y/\Delta x</math> is infinitely
close to <math>f'(c)</math> and is therefore finite. Thus <math>\Delta y = \Delta x (\Delta y / \Delta x)</math> is the product
of an infinitesimal and a finite number, so <math>\Delta y</math> is infinitesimal.
For example, the transcendental functions <math>\sin x</math>, <math>\cos x</math>, <math>e^x</math> are continuous
for all x, and <math>\ln x</math> is continuous for <math>x > 0</math>. Theorem 3 can be used to show that com-
binations of these functions are continuous.

The position in three dimensional space at time t can be represented by three
functions
<math>x = f(t),</math> <math>y = g(t),</math> <math>z = h(t).</math>
All three functions, <math>f</math>, <math>g</math>, and <math>h</math> are continuous for all values of <math>t</math>. At the time <math>t</math> of a
collision, at least one and usually all three derivatives <math>dx/dt</math>, <math>dy/dt</math>, <math>dz/dt</math> will be
undefined because the speed or direction of the molecule changes abruptly. At any
other time t, when no collision is taking place, all three derivatives <math>dx/dt</math>, <math>dy/dt</math>,
<math>dz/dt</math> will exist.
The functions we shall ordinarily encounter in this book will be defined
and have a derivative at all but perhaps a finite number of points of an interval. The
graph of such a function will be a smooth curve where the derivative exists. At points
where the curve has a sharp corner (like 0 in <math>|x|</math>) or a vertical tangent line (like 0
in <math>x^{1/3}</math>), the function is continuous but not differentiable (see Figure 3.4.7). At points
where the function is undefined or there is a jump, or the value approaches infinity
or oscillates wildly, the function is discontinuous (see Figure 3.4.8).

THEOREM 4
If f is continuous at c and G is continuous at <math>f(c)</math>, then the function
<math>g(x) = G(f(x))</math>

open intervals have one of the forms
<math>(a, b), (a, \infty), (-\infty, b), (-\infty, \infty),</math>
and half-open intervals have one of the forms
<math>[a, b),</math> <math>(a, b],</math> <math>[a, \infty),</math> <math>(-\infty, b].</math>
In these intervals, a is called the <i>lower endpoint</i> and b, the <i>upper endpoint</i>. The symbol
<math>-\infty</math> indicates that there is no lower endpoint, while <math>\infty</math> indicates that there is no
upper endpoint.
DEFINITION
We say that f is continuous on an open interval I if f is continuous at every
point c in I. If in addition f has a derivative at every point of I, we say that f
is differentiable on I.
To define what is meant by a function continuous on a closed interval, we
introduce the notions of continuous from the right and continuous from the left,
using one-sided limits.
DEFINITION
f is continuous from the right at c if <math>\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) = f(c)</math>.
f is continuous from the left at c if <math>\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = f(c)</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 6 (Continued)</b> The greatest integer function <math>f(x) = [x]</math> is continuous
from the right but not from the left at each integer <math>n</math> because
<math>[n] = n,</math> <math>\lim_{x \to n^{+}} [x] = n,</math> <math>\lim_{x \to n^{-}} [x] = n - 1.</math>
It is easy to check that <math>f</math> is continuous at <math>c</math> if and only if <math>f</math> is continuous from
both the right and left at <math>c</math>.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
f is said to be continuous on the closed interval <math>[a, b]</math> if f is continuous at each
point c where <math>a < c < b</math>, continuous from the right at a, and continuous from
the left at b.

3.5 MAXIMA AND MINIMA
Let us assume throughout this section that <math>f</math> is a real function whose domain is an
interval <math>I</math>, and furthermore that <math>f</math> is continuous on <math>I</math>. A problem that often arises is
that of finding the point <math>c</math> where <math>f(c)</math> has its largest value, and also the point <math>c</math> where
<math>f(c)</math> has its smallest value. The derivative turns out to be very useful in this problem.
We begin by defining the concepts of maximum and minimum.

(i)

(ii)
called the minimum value of f.
When we look at the graph of a continuous function <math>f</math> on <math>I</math>, the maximum
will appear as the highest peak and the minimum as the lowest valley (Figure 3.5.1).

The use of the derivative in finding maxima and minima is based on the
Critical Point Theorem. It shows that the maxima and minima of a function can
only occur at certain points, called critical points. The theorem will be stated now,
and its proof is given at the end of this section.
CRITICAL POINT THEOREM
Let f have
domain I. Suppose that c is a point in I and f has
either a maximum or a minimum at c. Then one of the following three things
must happen:
(i) <math>c</math> is an endpoint of <math>I</math>,
(ii) <math>f'(c)</math> is undefined,
(iii) <math>f'(c) = 0</math>.
We shall say that c is a critical point of f if either (i), (ii), or (iii) happens. The
three types of critical points are shown in Figure 3.5.4. When I is an open interval,
(i) cannot arise since the endpoints are not elements of <math>I</math>. But when <math>I</math> is a closed

interval, the two endpoints of <math>I</math> will always be among the critical points. Geometrically
the theorem says that if f has a maximum or minimum at c, then either c is an endpoint
of the curve, or there is a sharp corner at c, or the curve has a horizontal slope at c.
Thus at a maximum there is either an endpoint, a sharp peak, or a horizontal summit.
The Critical Point Theorem has some important applications to economics.

has a maximum at one endpoint and a minimum at the other. If the maximum
is at c, then <math>f(u_1)</math> and <math>f(u_2)</math> are both less than <math>f(c)</math>; if the minimum is at c,
then <math>f(u_1)</math> and <math>f(u_2)</math> are both greater than <math>f(c)</math>. A similar proof works when
<math>c < v_1 < v_2</math>. Note: our proof used the fact that <math>f</math> has a maximum and minimum on each closed interval. That fact, called the Extreme V alue Theorem, is proved on page 164.
SECOND DERIVATIVE TEST
Suppose c is the only interior critical point of f and that <math>f'(c) = 0</math>.
(i) If <math>f''(c) < 0</math>, f has a maximum at c and nowhere else.
(ii) If <math>f''(c) > 0</math>, f has a minimum at c and nowhere else.
We omit the proof and give a simple intuitive argument instead. (See Figure
3.5.8.) Since <math>f'(c) = 0</math>, the curve is horizontal at c. If <math>f''(c)</math> is negative the slope is
decreasing. This means that the curve climbs up until it levels off at c and then falls

increasing, so the curve falls down until it reaches a minimum at c and then climbs up.
This argument makes it easy to remember which way the inequalities go in the
test.
The Second Derivative Test fails when <math>f''(c) = 0</math> and when <math>f''(c)</math> does not
exist. When the Second Derivative Test fails any of the following things can still
happen:

In most maximum and minimum problems, there is only one critical point
except for the endpoints of the interval. We develop a method for finding the maximum
and minimum in that case.
METHOD FOR FINDING MAXIMA AND MINIMA
When to use: f is continuous on its domain I, and f has exactly one interior
critical point.
Step 1 Differentiate <math>f</math>.
Step 2 Find the unique interior critical point <math>c</math> of <math>f</math>.
Step 3 Test to see whether f has a maximum or minimum at c. The Direct Test or
the Second Derivative Test may be used.
This method can be applied to an open or half-open interval as well as a
closed interval. The Second Derivative Test is more convenient because it requires
only the single computation <math>f''(c)</math>, while the Direct Test requires the three computa-
tions <math>f(u)</math>, <math>f(v)</math>, and <math>f(c)</math>. However, the Direct Test always works while the Second
Derivative Test sometimes fails.
We illustrate the use of both tests in the examples.

from the origin.

If f has more than one interior critical point, the maxima and minima
can sometimes be found by dividing the interval into two or more parts.
<b>EXAMPLE 7</b> Find the maximum and minimum of <math>f(x) = x/(x^2 + 1)</math>.
Step 1 <math>f'(x) = \frac{(x^2+1)-2x^2}{(x^2+1)^2} = \frac{1-x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}</math>.
Step 2 <math>f'(x) = 0</math>, when <math>x = -1</math> and <math>x = 1</math>. There are two interior critical points.
We divide the interval <math>(-\infty, \infty)</math> on which f is defined into the two sub-
intervals <math>(-\infty, 0]</math> and <math>[0, \infty)</math>. On each of these subintervals, f has just one
interior critical point.
Step 3 We shall use the direct test for the subinterval <math>(-\infty, 0]</math>. At the critical
point <math>-1</math>, we have <math>f(-1) = -\frac{1}{2}</math>. By direct computation, we see that
<math>f(-2) = -\frac{2}{5}</math> and <math>f(0) = 0</math>. Both of these values are greater than <math>-\frac{1}{2}</math>. This
shows that the restriction of f to the subinterval <math>(-\infty, 0]</math> has a minimum
at <math>x = -1</math>. Moreover, <math>f(x)</math> is always <math>\ge 0</math> for x in the other subinterval
<math>[0, \infty)</math>. Therefore f has a minimum at <math>-1</math> for the whole interval <math>(-\infty, \infty)</math>.
In a similar way, we can show that f has a maximum at <math>x = 1</math>.
CONCLUSION f has a minimum at <math>x = -1</math> with value <math>f(-1) = -\frac{1}{2}</math>, and a
maximum at <math>x = 1</math> with value <math>f(1) = \frac{1}{2}</math>. (See Figure 3.5.12.)
The Critical Point Theorem can often be used to show that a curve has no
maximum or minimum on an open interval <math>I = (a, b)</math>. The theorem shows that:
If <math>y = f(x)</math> has no critical points in <math>(a, b)</math>, the curve has no maximum or
minimum on <math>(a, b)</math>.
If <math>y = f(x)</math> has just one critical point <math>x = c</math> in <math>(a, b)</math> and two points <math>x_1</math> and

PROOF OF THE CRITICAL POINT THEOREM Assume that neither (i) nor (ii) holds;
that is, assume that c is not an endpoint of I and <math>f'(c)</math> exists. We must show
that (iii) is true; i.e., <math>f'(c) = 0</math>. We give the proof for the case that f has a
maximum at c. Let <math>x = c</math>, and let <math>\Delta x > 0</math> be infinitesimal. Then
<math>f(c + \Delta x) \le f(c), \qquad f(c - \Delta x) \le f(c).</math>
(See Figure 3.5.14.) Therefore
<math display="block">\frac{f(c+\Delta x)-f(c)}{\Delta x} \le 0 \le \frac{f(c-\Delta x)-f(c)}{-\Delta x}.</math>

3.6 MAXIMA AND MINIMA—APPLICATIONS
Maximum and minimum problems arise in both the physical and social sciences.
We give three examples.
A woman wishes to rent a house. If she lives x miles from her work,
EXAMPLE 1
her transportation cost will be cx dollars per year, while her rent will be
<math>25c/(x+1)</math> dollars per year. How far should she live from work to minimize
her rent and transportation expenses?
Let y be her expenses in dollars per year. Then
<math display="block">y = cx + \frac{25c}{x+1}.</math>
The problem is to find the minimum value of y in the interval <math>0 \le x < \infty</math>.
Step 1 <math>\frac{dy}{dx} = c - \frac{25c}{(x+1)^2}</math>.
Step 2 To find x such that <math>dy/dx = 0</math> we set <math>dy/dx = 0</math> and solve for x.
<math>c - \frac{25c}{(x+1)^2} = 0</math>, <math>c = \frac{25c}{(x+1)^2}</math>, <math>(x+1)^2 = 25</math>, <math>x+1 = \pm 5</math>.
Then <math>x = 4</math> or <math>x = -6</math>. We reject <math>x = -6</math> because <math>0 \le x</math>. The only interior
critical point is <math>x = 4</math>.
Step 3 We use the Direct Test.
At <math>x = 0</math>, <math>y = c \cdot 0 + 25c/(0 + 1) = 25c</math>.
At <math>x = 4</math>, <math>y = 4c + 25c/(4 + 1) = 9c</math>.
At <math>x = 9</math>, <math>y = 9c + 25c/(9 + 1) = 11.5c</math>.
CONCLUSION y has its minimum at <math>x = 4</math> miles. So the woman should live four
miles from work. (See Figure 3.6.1.)

Let <math>x</math> be the dimension of the side along the river, and <math>y</math> be the other
dimension, as in Figure 3.6.2. Call the area A.
No fencing is needed on the side of the plot bordering the river. The given
information is expressed by the following system of formulas.
<math>A = xy</math>, <math>x + 2y = 1000</math>, <math>0 \le x \le 1000</math>.
The problem is to find the values of x and y at which A is maximum. In this
problem A is expressed in terms of two variables instead of one. However,
we can select x as the independent variable, and then both y and A are
functions of x. We find an equation for A as a function of x alone by
eliminating y.
<math>x + 2y = 1000,</math> <math>y = \frac{1000 - x}{2}.</math>
<math display="block">A = xy = \frac{x(1000 - x)}{2} = 500x - \frac{1}{2}x^{2}.</math>
We then find the maximum of A in the closed interval <math>0 \le x \le 1000</math>.
Step 1 <math>dA/dx = 500 - x</math>.
Step 2 <math>dA/dx = 0</math> when <math>x = 500</math>. This is the unique interior critical point.
Step 3 We use the Second Derivative Test: <math>d^2A/dx^2 = -1</math>. Therefore A has a
maximum at the critical point <math>x = 500</math>.
<b>CONCLUSION</b> The maximum area occurs when the plot has dimensions <math>x = 500</math> ft
and <math>y = (1000 - x)/2 = 250</math>ft (Figure 3.6.3).

3.7 DERIVATIVES AND CURVE SKETCHING
If we compute n values of <math>f(x)</math>,
<math>f(x_1), f(x_2), \ldots, f(x_n),</math>
we obtain n points through which the curve <math>y = f(x)</math> passes. The first and second
derivatives tell us something about the shape of the curve in the intervals between
these points and permit a much more accurate plot of the curve. It is especially
helpful to know the signs of the first two derivatives.
When the first derivative is positive the curve is increasing from left to right,
and when the first derivative is negative the curve is decreasing from left to right.
When the first derivative is zero the curve is horizontal. These facts can be proved as a
theorem if we define exactly what is meant by increasing and decreasing (see Figures
3.7.1 and 3.7.2).

<b>DEFINITION</b>
A function f is said to be constant on an interval I if:
<math>f(x_1) = f(x_2)</math> for all <math>x_1, x_2</math> in I.
f is increasing on I if:
<math>f(x_1) < f(x_2)</math> whenever <math>x_1 < x_2</math> in I.

## PDF page 162

152
3 CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
f is decreasing on I if:
<math>f(x_1) > f(x_2)</math> whenever <math>x_1 < x_2</math> in I.
THEOREM 1
Suppose <math>f</math> is continuous on <math>I</math> and has a derivative at every interior point of <math>I</math>.
(i) If <math>f'(x) = 0</math> for all interior points x of I, then f is constant on I.
(ii) If <math>f'(x) > 0</math> for all interior points x of I, then f is increasing on I.
(iii) If <math>f'(x) < 0</math> for all interior points x of I, then f is decreasing on I.
A proof will be given in the next section.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> The curve <math>y = x^3 + x - 1</math> has derivative <math>dy/dx = 3x^2 + 1</math>. The
derivative is always positive, so the curve is always increasing (Figure 3.7.3).
х
Figure 3.7.3
Let us now turn to the second derivative. It is the rate of change of the slope
of the curve, so it has something to do with the way in which the curve is changing
direction. When the second derivative is positive, the slope is increasing, and we would
expect the curve to be concave upward, i.e., shaped like a <math>\cup</math>. When the second
derivative is negative the slope is decreasing, so the curve should be shaped like <math>\cap</math>
(see Figure 3.7.4).
A precise definition of concave upward or downward can be given by
comparing the curve with the chord (straight line segment) connecting two points on
the curve.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
Let f be defined on I. The curve <math>y = f(x)</math> is <b>concave upward</b> on I if for any two
points <math>x_1 < x_2</math> in I and any value of x between <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math>, the curve at x is
below the chord which meets the curve at <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math>.
The curve <math>y = f(x)</math> is concave downward on I if for any two points <math>x_1 < x_2</math> in I
and any value of x between <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math>, the curve at x is above the chord which
meets the curve at <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math> (see Figure 3.7.5).

Let us show with some simple examples how we can use the first and second

and maxima are all helpful.
<b>EXAMPLE</b> 1(Continued) <math>y = x^3 + x - 1</math>. We have
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 1,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6x.</math>
<math>dy/dx</math> is always positive, while <math>d^2y/dx^2 = 0</math> at <math>x = 0</math>. We make a table of
values for y and its first two derivatives at <math>x = 0</math> and at a point to the right
and left side of 0.

With the aid of Theorems 1–3, we can draw the following conclusions:
(a) <math>dy/dx > 0</math> and the curve is increasing for all x.
(b) <math>d^2y/dx^2 < 0</math> for <math>x < 0</math>; concave downward.
(c) <math>d^2y/dx^2 > 0</math> for <math>x > 0</math>; concave upward.
At the point <math>x = 0</math>, the curve changes from concave downward to concave
upward. This is called a point of inflection.

DEFINITION
Let c be an interior point of I.
f has a <b>local maximum</b> at c if <math>f(c) \ge f(x)</math> for all x in some open interval <math>(a_0, b_0)</math>
containing c.
f has a <b>local minimum</b> at c if <math>f(c) \le f(x)</math> for all x in some open interval <math>(a_0, b_0)</math>
containing c. (The interval <math>(a_0, b_0)</math> may be only a small subinterval of I.)
f has a point of inflection at c if f changes from one direction of concavity to
the other at c.
These definitions are illustrated in Figure 3.7.9.

3.8 PROPERTIES OF CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
This section develops some theory that will be needed for integration in Chapter 4.
We begin with a new concept, that of a hyperinteger. The hyperintegers are to the
integers as the hyperreal numbers are to the real numbers. The hyperintegers consist
of the ordinary finite integers, the positive infinite hyperintegers, and the negative
infinite hyperintegers. The hyperintegers have the same algebraic properties as the
integers and are spaced one apart all along the hyperreal line as in Figure 3.8.1.

The rigorous definition of the hyperintegers uses the greatest integer function
[x] introduced in Section 3.4, Example 6. Remember that for a real number x, [x]
is the greatest integer n such that <math>n \le x</math>. A real number y is itself an integer if and
only if <math>y = [x]</math> for some real x. To get the hyperintegers, we apply the function [x]
to hyperreal numbers <math>x</math> (see Figure 3.8.2).

DEFINITION
A hyperinteger is a hyperreal number y such that <math>y = [x]</math> for some hyperreal x.
When <math>x</math> varies over the hyperreal numbers, <math>[x]</math> is the greatest hyperinteger
y such that <math>y \le x</math>. Because of the Transfer Principle, every hyperreal number x is
between two hyperintegers <math>[x]</math> and <math>[x] + 1</math>,
<math>\lceil x \rceil \le x < \lceil x \rceil + 1</math>.
Also, sums, differences, and products of hyperintegers are again hyperintegers.
We are now going to use the hyperintegers. In sketching curves we divided
a closed interval [a, b] into finitely many subintervals. For theoretical purposes in
the calculus we often divide a closed interval into a finite or infinite number of equal
subintervals. This is done as follows.
Given a closed real interval [a, b], a finite partition is formed by choosing
a positive integer <math>n</math> and dividing <math>[a, b]</math> into <math>n</math> equal parts, as in Figure 3.8.3. Each
part will be a subinterval of length <math>t = (b - a)/n</math>. The <i>n</i> subintervals are
<math>[a, a + t], [a + t, a + 2t], \dots, [a + (n - 1)t, b].</math>

The endpoints
<math>a, a + t, a + 2t, \dots, a + (n - 1)t, a + nt = b</math>
are called partition points.
The real interval <math>[a, b]</math> is contained in the hyperreal interval <math>[a, b]^*</math>, which
is the set of all hyperreal numbers x such that <math>a \le x \le b</math>. An infinite partition is
applied to the hyperreal interval <math>[a, b]^*</math> rather than the real interval. To form an
infinite partition of <math>[a, b]^*</math>, choose a positive infinite hyperinteger H and divide <math>[a, b]^*</math>
into H equal parts as shown in Figure 3.8.4. Each subinterval will have the same
infinitesimal length <math>\delta = (b - a)/H</math>. The H subintervals are
<math>[a, a + \delta], [a + \delta, a + 2\delta], \dots, [a + (K - 1)\delta, a + K\delta], \dots, [a + (H - 1)\delta, b],</math>
and the partition points are
<math>a, a + \delta, a + 2\delta, \dots, a + K\delta, \dots, a + H\delta = b</math>
where <math>K</math> runs over the hyperintegers from 1 to <math>H</math>. Every hyperreal number <math>x</math> between
a and b belongs to one of the infinitesimal subintervals,
<math>a + (K - 1)\delta \le x < a + K\delta</math>.

INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM
Suppose the real function f is continuous on the closed interval <math>[a, b]</math> and <math>f(x)</math>
is positive at one endpoint and negative at the other endpoint. Then f has a
zero in the interval <math>(a, b)</math>; that is, <math>f(c) = 0</math> for some real <math>c</math> in <math>(a, b)</math>.
There are two cases illustrated in Figure 3.8.6:

In the first case, the theorem says that if a continuous curve is below the
x-axis at a and above it at b, then the curve must intersect the x-axis at
some point c between a and b. Theorem 3 in the preceding Section 3.7 on
curve sketching is simply a reformulation of the Intermediate Value
Theorem.
SKETCH OF PROOF We assume <math>f(a) < 0 < f(b)</math>. Let H be a positive infinite
hyperinteger and partition the interval <math>[a, b]^*</math> into <math>H</math> equal parts
<math>a, a + \delta, a + 2\delta, \dots, a + H\delta = b.</math>
Let <math>a + K\delta</math> be the last partition point at which <math>f(a + K\delta) < 0</math>. Thus
<math display="block">f(a + K\delta) < 0 \le f(a + (K+1)\delta).</math>
Since f is continuous, <math>f(a + K\delta)</math> is infinitely close to <math>f(a + (K + 1)\delta)</math>.
We conclude that <math>f(a + K\delta) \approx 0</math> (Figure 3.8.7). We take c to be the standard
part of <math>a + K\delta</math>, so that
<math display="block">f(c) = st(f(a + K\delta)) = 0.</math>
The function

The Intermediate Value Theorem can be used to prove Theorem 3 of
Section 3.7 on curve sketching:
Suppose g is a continuous function on an interval I, and <math>g(x) \neq 0</math> for all x
in I.
(i) If <math>g(c) > 0</math> for at least one c in I, then <math>g(x) > 0</math> for all x in I.
(ii) If <math>g(c) < 0</math> for at least one c in I, then <math>g(x) < 0</math> for all x in I.
<b>PROOF</b> (i) Let <math>g(c) > 0</math> for some c in I. If <math>g(x_1) < 0</math> for some other point <math>x_1</math> in I,
then by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a point <math>x_2</math> between <math>c</math>
and <math>x_1</math> such that <math>g(x_2) = 0</math>, contrary to hypothesis (Figure 3.8.9). Therefore
we conclude that <math>g(x) > 0</math> for all x in I.

EXTREME VALUE THEOREM
Let f be continuous on its domain, which is a closed interval <math>[a, b]</math>. Then f
has a maximum at some point in <math>[a, b]</math>, and a minimum at some point in <math>[a, b]</math>.
We have seen several examples of functions that do not have maxima
Discussion
on an open interval, such as <math>f(x) = 1/x</math> on <math>(0, \infty)</math>, or <math>g(x) = 2x</math> on <math>(0, 1)</math>.
The Extreme Value Theorem says that on a closed interval a continuous
function always has a maximum.
SKETCH OF PROOF Form an infinite partition of <math>[a, b]^*</math>,
<math>a, a + \delta, a + 2\delta, \dots, a + H\delta = b.</math>
By the Transfer Principle, there is a partition point <math>a + K\delta</math> at which
<math>f(a + K\delta)</math> has the largest value. Let c be the standard part of <math>a + K\delta</math>
(see Figure 3.8.10). Any point <math>u</math> of <math>[a, b]^*</math> lies in a subinterval, say
<math>a + L\delta \le u < a + (L+1)\delta</math>.
<math>f(a + K\delta) \ge f(a + L\delta),</math>
We have
and taking standard parts,
<math>f(c) \ge f(u)</math>.
This shows that <math>f</math> has a maximum at <math>c</math>.

ROLLE'S THEOREM
Suppose that <math>f</math> is continuous on the closed interval <math>[a, b]</math> and differentiable on
the open interval (a, b). If
<math display="block">f(a) = f(b) = 0,</math>
then there is at least one point c strictly between a and b where f has derivative
zero; i.e.,
<math>f'(c) = 0</math> for some <math>c</math> in <math>(a, b)</math>.
Geometrically, the theorem says that a differentiable curve touching the
x-axis at a and b must be horizontal for at least one point strictly between a and b.
PROOF We may assume that [a, b] is the domain of f. By the Extreme Value Theorem,
f has a maximum value M and a minimum value m in <math>[a, b]</math>. Since <math>f(a) = 0</math>,
<math>m \le 0</math> and <math>M \ge 0</math> (see Figure 3.8.11).
<math>M=0</math> and <math>m=0</math>. Then f is the constant function <math>f(x)=0</math>, and therefore
Case 1
<math>f'(c) = 0</math> for all points <math>c</math> in <math>(a, b)</math>.
Case 2 <math>M > 0</math>. Let f have a maximum at <math>c</math>, <math>f(c) = M</math>. By the Critical Point Theorem,
f has a critical point at c. c cannot be an endpoint because the value of <math>f(x)</math>
is zero at the endpoints and positive at <math>x = c</math>. By hypothesis, <math>f'(x)</math> exists at
<math>x = c</math>. It follows that c must be a critical point of the type <math>f'(c) = 0</math>.
Case 3 <math>m < 0</math>. We let f have a minimum at c. Then as in Case 2, c is in <math>(a, b)</math> and
<math display="block">f'(c) = 0.</math>

Rolle's Theorem is useful in finding the number of zeros of a differentiable
function <math>f</math>. It shows that between any two zeros of <math>f</math> there must be one or more zeros
of <math>f'</math>. It follows that if <math>f'</math> has no zeros in an interval <math>I</math>, then <math>f</math> cannot have more than
one zero in <math>I</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 6</b> How many zeros does the function <math>f(x) = x^3 + x + 1</math> have? We use
both Rolle's Theorem and the Intermediate Value Theorem.
Using Rolle's Theorem: <math>f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1</math>. For all <math>x, x^2 \ge 0</math>, and hence
<math>f'(x) \ge 1</math>. Therefore <math>f(x)</math> has at most one zero.
Using the Intermediate Value Theorem: We have <math>f(-1) = -1</math>, <math>f(0) = 1</math>.
Therefore <math>f</math> has at least one zero between <math>-1</math> and <math>0</math>.
CONCLUSION <math>f</math> has exactly one zero, and it lies between <math>-1</math> and 0 (see Figure
3.8.16).

3 CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
Our method of sketching curves in Section 3.7 depends on a consequence
of Rolle's Theorem called the Mean Value Theorem. It deals with the average slope
of a curve between two points.
DEFINITION
Let f be defined on the closed interval [a, b]. The average slope of f between a
and b is the quotient
average slope = <math>\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}</math>.
We can see in Figure 3.8.17 that the average slope of <math>f</math> between <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> is
equal to the slope of the line passing through the points <math>(a, f(a))</math> and <math>(b, f(b))</math>.
This is shown by the two-point equation for a line (Section 1.3). In particular, if
f is already a linear function <math>f(x) = mx + c</math>, then the average slope of f between
a and b is equal to the slope m of the line <math>y = f(x)</math>.

This is shown by the two-point equation for a straight line (Section 1.2). In particular,
if f is already a linear function <math>f(x) = mx + c</math>, then the average slope of f between
a and b is equal to the slope m of the straight line <math>y = f(x)</math>.
MEAN VALUE THEOREM
Assume that <math>f</math> is continuous on the closed interval <math>[a, b]</math> and has a derivative
at every point of the open interval (a, b). Then there is at least one point c in
<math>(a,b)</math> where the slope <math>f'(c)</math> is equal to the average slope of f between a and b,
<math display="block">f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}.</math>
Remark In the special case that <math>f(a) = f(b) = 0</math>, the Mean Value Theorem becomes
Rolle's Theorem:
<math display="block">f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} = \frac{0 - 0}{b - a} = 0.</math>

PROOF OF THE MEAN VALUE THEOREM Let m be the average slope, <math>m =</math>
<math>(f(b) - f(a))/(b - a)</math>. The line through the points <math>(a, f(a))</math> and <math>(b, f(b))</math> has
the equation
<math display="block">l(x) = f(a) + m(x - a).</math>
Let <math>h(x)</math> be the distance of <math>f(x)</math> above <math>l(x)</math>,
<math display="block">h(x) = f(x) - l(x).</math>
Then <math>h</math> is continuous on <math>[a, b]</math> and has the derivative
<math>h'(x) = f'(x) - l'(x) = f'(x) - m</math>
at each point in <math>(a, b)</math>. Since <math>f(x) = l(x)</math> at the endpoints a and b, we have
<math>h(a) = 0, 	 h(b) = 0.</math>
Therefore Rolle's Theorem can be applied to the function h, and there is a
point <math>c</math> in <math>(a, b)</math> such that <math>h'(c) = 0</math>. Thus
<math display="block">0 = h'(c) = f'(c) - l'(c) = f'(c) - m,</math>
<math>f'(c) = m</math>.
whence
We can give a physical interpretation of the Mean Value Theorem in terms
of velocity. Suppose a particle moves along the y-axis according to the equation
<math>y = f(t)</math>. The average velocity of the particle between times a and b is the ratio
<math>\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}</math>
of the change in position to the time elapsed. The Mean Value Theorem states that
there is a point of time <math>c</math>, <math>a < c < b</math>, when the velocity <math>f'(c)</math> of the particle is equal to
the average velocity between times <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>.
Theorems 1 and 2 in Section 3.7 on curve sketching are consequences of
the Mean Value Theorem. As an illustration, we prove part (ii) of Theorem 1:
If <math>f'(x) > 0</math> for all interior points x of I, then f is increasing on I.

3 CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
<i>PROOF</i> Let <math>x_1 < x_2</math> where <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math> are points in I. By the Mean Value Theorem
there is a point c strictly between <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math> such that
<math>f'(c) = \frac{f(x_2) - f(x_1)}{x_2 - x_1}</math>
Since c is an interior point of I, <math>f'(c) > 0</math>. Because <math>x_1 < x_2, x_2 - x_1 > 0</math>.
Thus
<math display="block">\frac{f(x_2) - f(x_1)}{x_2 - x_1} > 0, \quad f(x_2) - f(x_1) > 0, \quad f(x_2) > f(x_1).</math>
This shows that <math>f</math> is increasing on <math>I</math>.

4.1 THE DEFINITE INTEGRAL
We shall begin our study of the integral calculus in the same way in which we began
with the differential calculus—by asking a question about curves in the plane.
Suppose <math>f</math> is a real function continuous on an interval <math>I</math> and consider the
curve <math>y = f(x)</math>. Let <math>a < b</math> where a, b are two points in I, and let the curve be above the
x-axis for x between a and b; that is, <math>f(x) \ge 0</math>. We then ask: What is meant by the
area of the region bounded by the curve <math>y = f(x)</math>, the x-axis, and the lines <math>x = a</math> and
<math>x = b</math>? That is, what is meant by the area of the shaded region in Figure 4.1.1? We
call this region the region under the curve <math>y = f(x)</math> between a and b.

Figure 4.1.2
The area under any continuous curve <math>y = f(x)</math> will be given by the definite
integral, which is written
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx.</math>
Before plunging into the detailed definition of the integral, we outline the main ideas.
First, the region under the curve is divided into infinitely many vertical
strips of infinitesimal width <math>dx</math>. Next, each vertical strip is replaced by a vertical
rectangle of height <math>f(x)</math>, base <math>dx</math>, and area <math>f(x) dx</math>. The next step is to form the sum
of the areas of all these rectangles, called the infinite Riemann sum (look ahead to
Figures 4.1.3 and 4.1.11). Finally, the integral <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math> is defined as the standard
part of the infinite Riemann sum.
The infinite Riemann sum, being a sum of rectangles, has an infinitesimal
error. This error is removed by taking the standard part to form the integral.
It is often difficult to compute an infinite Riemann sum, since it is a sum of
infinitely many infinitesimal rectangles. We shall first study finite Riemann sums,
which can easily be computed on a hand calculator.
Suppose we slice the region under the curve between a and b into thin vertical
strips of equal width. If there are n slices, each slice will have width <math>\Delta x = (b - a)/n</math>.
The interval <math>[a, b]</math> will be partitioned into n subintervals
<math>[x_0, x_1], [x_1, x_2], \dots, [x_{n-1}, x_n],</math>
<math>x_0 = a, x_1 = a + \Delta x, x_2 = a + 2 \Delta x, \dots, x_n = b.</math>
where
The points <math>x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n</math> are called partition points. On each subinterval <math>[x_{k-1}, x_k]</math>,
we form the rectangle of height <math>f(x_{k-1})</math>. The kth rectangle will have area
<math>f(x_{k-1}) \cdot \Delta x</math>.
From Figure 4.1.3, we can see that the sum of the areas of all these rectangles will be
fairly close to the area under the curve. This sum is called a Riemann sum and is equal
to
<math>f(x_0) \Delta x + f(x_1) \Delta x + \cdots + f(x_{n-1}) \Delta x</math>
It is the area of the shaded region in the picture. A convenient way of writing Riemann
sums is the "<math>\Sigma</math>-notation" (<math>\Sigma</math> is the capital Greek letter sigma),
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, \Delta x = f(x_0) \, \Delta x + f(x_1) \, \Delta x + \dots + f(x_{n-1}) \, \Delta x.</math>

<math>x_n</math> will be less than or equal to b but <math>x_n + \Delta x</math> will be greater than b. Then we define
the Riemann sum to be the sum
<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^{b} f(x) \, \Delta x = f(x_0) \, \Delta x + f(x_1) \, \Delta x + \dots + f(x_{n-1}) \, \Delta x + f(x_n) (b - x_n).</math>
Thus given the function f, the interval [a, b], and the real number <math>\Delta x > 0</math>, we have
defined the Riemann sum <math>\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) \Delta x</math>. We repeat the definition more concisely.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
Let <math>a < b</math> and let <math>\Delta x</math> be a positive real number. Then the <b>Riemann sum</b>
<math>\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) \Delta x</math> is defined as the sum
<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^{b} f(x) \Delta x = f(x_0) \Delta x + f(x_1) \Delta x + \dots + f(x_{n-1}) \Delta x + f(x_n)(b - x_n)</math>
where n is the largest integer such that <math>a + n \Delta x \leq b</math>, and
<math>x_0 = a</math>, <math>x_1 = a + \Delta x</math>, <math>x_n = a + n \Delta x</math>, <math>b</math>
are the partition points.
If <math>x_n = b</math>, the last term <math>f(x_n)(b - x_n)</math> is zero. The Riemann sum <math>\sum_{n=0}^{b} f(x) \Delta x</math>
is a real function of three variables a, b, and <math>\Delta x</math>,
<math display="block">\sum_{x}^{b} f(x) \Delta x = S(a, b, \Delta x).</math>
The symbol x which appears in the expression is called a dummy variable (or bound
variable), because the value of <math>\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) \Delta x</math> does not depend on x. The dummy variable
allows us to use more compact notation, writing <math>f(x) \Delta x</math> just once instead of writing
<math>f(x_0) \Delta x, f(x_1) \Delta x, f(x_2) \Delta x</math>, and so on.
From Figure 4.1.5 it is plausible that by making <math>\Delta x</math> smaller we can get the
Riemann sum as close to the area as we wish.

Our next step is to take <math>\Delta x</math> to be infinitely small and have an infinite Riemann
sum. How can we do this? We observe that if the real numbers a and b are held fixed,
then the Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{b}^{b} f(x) \, \Delta x = S(\Delta x)</math>
is a real function of the single variable <math>\Delta x</math>. (The symbol x which appears in the
expression is a dummy variable, and the value of
<math display="block">\sum^{b} f(x) \, \Delta x</math>
depends only on <math>\Delta x</math> and not on x.) Furthermore, the term
<math display="block">\sum_{b}^{b} f(x) \, \Delta x = S(\Delta x)</math>
is defined for all real <math>\Delta x > 0</math>. Therefore by the Transfer Principle,
<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f(x) \, dx = S(dx)</math>
is defined for all hyperreal <math>dx > 0</math>. When <math>dx > 0</math> is infinitesimal, there are infinitely
many subintervals of length <math>dx</math>, and we call
<math display="block">\sum_{b}^{b} f(x) \, dx</math>
an infinite Riemann sum (Figure 4.1.11).
