We may think intuitively of the Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{b}^{b} f(x) \, dx</math>
as the infinite sum
<math>f(x_0) dx + f(x_1) dx + \cdots + f(x_{H-1}) dx + f(x_H)(b - x_H)</math>
where H is the greatest hyperinteger such that <math>a + H dx \le b</math>. (Hyperintegers are
discussed in Section 3.8.) H is positive infinite, and there are <math>H + 2</math> partition points
<math>x_0, x_1, \dots, x_H, b</math>. A typical term in this sum is the infinitely small quantity <math>f(x_K) dx</math>
where K is a hyperinteger, <math>0 \le K < H</math>, and <math>x_K = a + K dx</math>.
The infinite Riemann sum is a hyperreal number. We would next like to take
the standard part of it. But first we must show that it is a finite hyperreal number and
thus has a standard part.
THEOREM 1
Let f be a continuous function on an interval I, let <math>a < b</math> be two points in I, and
let dx be a positive infinitesimal. Then the infinite Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{b}^{b} f(x) \, dx</math>
is a finite hyperreal number.
<b>PROOF</b> Let B be a real number greater than the maximum value of <math>f</math> on <math>[a, b]</math>.

Thus the Riemann sum <math>\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) dx</math> is finite.
We are now ready to define the central concept of this chapter, the definite
integral. Recall that the derivative was defined as the standard part of the quotient
<math>\Delta y/\Delta x</math> and was written <math>dy/dx</math>. The "definite integral" will be defined as the standard
part of the infinite Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{b}^{b} f(x) dx,</math>
and is written <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math>. Thus the <math>\Delta x</math> is changed to <math>dx</math> in analogy with our differential
notation. The <math>\Sigma</math> is changed to the long thin S, i.e., <math>\int</math>, to remind us that the integral is
obtained from an infinite sum. We now state the definition carefully.
DEFINITION
Let f be a continuous function on an interval I and let <math>a < b</math> be two points in I.
Let dx be a positive infinitesimal. Then the definite integral of f from a to b with
respect to dx is defined to be the standard part of the infinite Riemann sum with
respect to dx, in symbols
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = st \left( \sum_a^b f(x) \, dx \right).</math>
<math display="block">\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) \, dx = 0,</math>
We also define
<math display="block">\int_a^a f(x) \, dx = -\int_a^b f(x) \, dx.</math>
By this definition, for each positive infinitesimal <math>dx</math> the definite integral
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{w} f(x) dx</math>
is a real function of two variables defined for all pairs (u, w) of elements of I. The
symbol x is a dummy variable since the value of
<math display="block">\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, dx</math>
does not depend on <math>x</math>.
In the notation <math>\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) dx</math> for the Riemann sum and <math>\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx</math> for the
integral, we always use matching symbols for the infinitesimal <math>dx</math> and the dummy
variable x. Thus when there are two or more variables we can tell which one is the
dummy variable in an integral. For example, <math>x^2t</math> can be integrated from 0 to 1 with
respect to either <math>x</math> or <math>t</math>. With respect to <math>x</math>,
<math display="block">\sum_{0}^{1} x^{2}t \, dx = x_{0}^{2}t \, dx + x_{1}^{2}t \, dx + \dots + x_{H-1}^{2}t \, dx</math>

With respect to t, however,
<math display="block">\sum_{t=0}^{1} x^{2}t \, dt = x^{2}t_{0} \, dt + x^{2}t_{1} \, dt + \dots + x^{2}t_{K-1} \, dt,</math>
and we shall see later that
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{1} x^{2}t \, dt = \frac{1}{2}x^{2}.</math>

4.2 FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS
In this section we shall state five basic theorems about the integral, culminating in
the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Right now we can only approximate a
definite integral by the laborious computation of a finite Riemann sum. At the end
of this section we will be in a position to easily compute exact values for many definite
integrals. The key to the method is the Fundamental Theorem. Our first theorem
shows that we are free to choose any positive infinitesimal we wish for <math>dx</math> in the
definite integral.

## PDF page 197

4.2 FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS

THEOREM 1
Given a continuous function <math>f</math> on <math>[a, b]</math> and two positive infinitesimals <math>dx</math>
and du, the definite integrals with respect to dx and du are the same,
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \int_a^b f(u) \, du.</math>
From now on when we write a definite integral <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math>, it is understood
that <math>dx</math> is a positive infinitesimal. By Theorem 1, it doesn't matter which infinitesimal.
The proof of Theorem 1 is based on the following intuitive idea. Figure 4.2.1
shows the two Riemann sums <math>\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) dx</math> and <math>\sum_{a}^{b} f(u) du</math>. We see from the figure
that the difference <math>\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) dx - \sum_{a}^{b} f(u) du</math> is a sum of rectangles of infinitesimal
height. These difference rectangles all lie between the horizontal lines <math>y = -\varepsilon</math> and
<math>y = \varepsilon</math>, where <math>\varepsilon</math> is the largest height. Thus <math>-\varepsilon(b-a) \le \sum_a^b f(x) dx - \sum_a^b f(u) du \le \varepsilon</math>
<math>\varepsilon(b-a)</math>. Taking standard parts,
<math display="block">0 \le \int_a^b f(x) \, dx - \int_a^b f(u) \, du \le 0,</math>
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \int_a^b f(u) \, du.</math>

Theorem 1 shows that whenever <math>\Delta x</math> is positive infinitesimal, the Riemann
sum is infinitely close to the definite integral,
<math display="block">\sum_{b}^{b} f(x) \, \Delta x \approx \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx.</math>
This fact can also be expressed in terms of limits. It shows that the Riemann sum
approaches the definite integral as <math>\Delta x</math> approaches 0 from above, in symbols
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0^+} \sum_a^b f(x) \, \Delta x.</math>
Given a continuous function <math>f</math> on an interval <math>I</math>, Theorem 1 shows that the
definite integral is a real function of two variables a and b,
<math display="block">A(a,b) = \int_a^b f(x) dx, \qquad a, b \text{ in } I.</math>

DEFINITION
If f is continuous and <math>f(x) \ge 0</math> on [a, b], the area of the region below the
curve <math>y = f(x)</math> from a to b is defined as the definite integral:
Area = <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math>.
The next two theorems give basic properties of the integral.
THEOREM 2 (The Rectangle Property)
Suppose <math>f</math> is continuous and has minimum value <math>m</math> and maximum value <math>M</math>
on a closed interval [a, b]. Then
<math display="block">m(b-a) \le \int_a^b f(x) \, dx \le M(b-a).</math>
That is, the area of the region under the curve is between the area of the rectangle
whose height is the minimum value of f and the area of the rectangle whose
height is the maximum value of <math>f</math> in the interval <math>[a, b]</math>.

4.2 FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS
The Extreme Value Theorem is needed to show that the minimum value m
and maximum value M exist. The rectangle of height m is called the inscribed rectangle
of the region, and the rectangle of height M is called the circumscribed rectangle.
From Figure 4.2.3, we see that the inscribed rectangle is a subset of the region under
the curve, which is in turn a subset of the circumscribed rectangle. The Rectangle
Property says that the area of the region is between the areas of the inscribed and
circumscribed rectangles.

Figure 4.2.3 The Rectangle Property
<b>PROOF</b> By Theorem 1, any positive infinitesimal may be chosen for <math>dx</math>. Let us
choose a positive infinite hyperinteger H and let <math>dx = (b - a)/H</math>. Then
<math>dx</math> evenly divides <math>b-a</math>; that is, the interval <math>[a,b]</math> is divided into H sub-
intervals of exactly the same length <math>dx</math>. Then
<math display="block">\sum_{a}^{b} m \, dx = m \cdot H \cdot dx = m(b - a),</math>
<math display="block">\sum_{a}^{b} M \, dx = M \cdot H \cdot dx = M(b - a).</math>
For each x, we have <math>m \le f(x) \le M</math>. Adding up and taking standard parts,
we obtain the required formula.
<math display="block">\sum_{x} m \, dx \le \sum_{x} f(x) \, dx \le \sum_{x} M \, dx,</math>
<math display="block">m(b-a) \le \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx \le M(b-a).</math>
One useful consequence of the Rectangle Property is that the integral of
a positive function is positive and the integral of a negative function is negative:
If <math>f(x) > 0</math> on <math>[a, b]</math>, then <math>0 < m(b - a) \le \int_a^b f(x) dx</math>.
If <math>f(x) < 0</math> on <math>[a, b]</math>, then <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx \le M(b - a) < 0</math>.
The definite integral of a negative function <math>f(x) = -g(x)</math> from a to b is
just the negative of the area of the region above the curve and below the <math>x</math> axis.
This is because
<math>f(x) dx = -g(x) dx</math>

THEOREM 3 (The Addition Property)
Suppose f is continuous on an interval I. Then for all a, b, c in I,
<math display="block">\int_a^c f(x) dx = \int_a^b f(x) dx + \int_b^c f(x) dx.</math>
This property is illustrated in Figure 4.2.5 for the case <math>a < b < c</math>. The
Addition Property holds even if the points a, b, c are in some other order on the
real line, such as <math>c < a < b</math>.

To illustrate the other cases, we prove the Addition Property when
<math>c < a < b</math>. The previous case gives
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \int_a^a f(x) \, dx + \int_a^b f(x) \, dx.</math>
Since reversing the endpoints changes the sign of the integral,
<math display="block">-\int_{c}^{c} f(x) dx = -\int_{c}^{c} f(x) dx + \int_{c}^{b} f(x) dx,</math>
and the desired formula
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{c} f(x) dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx + \int_{b}^{c} f(x) dx</math>
follows.
The definite integral of a curve can be thought of as area even if the curve
crosses the x-axis. The curve in Figure 4.2.7 is positive from a to b and negative from
b to c, crossing the x-axis at b. The integral <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math> is a positive number and the
integral <math>\int_b^c f(x) dx</math> is a negative number. By the Addition Property, the integral
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{c} f(x) dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx + \int_{a}^{c} f(x) dx</math>
is equal to the area from a to b minus the area from b to c. The definite integral
<math>\int_a^c f(x) dx</math> always gives the net area between the x-axis and the curve, counting
areas above the x-axis as positive and areas below the x-axis as negative.
The definite integral <math>\int_{u}^{v} f(t) dt</math> is a real function of two variables u and v
and does not depend on the dummy variable t. If we replace u by a constant a and v
by the variable x, we obtain a real function of one variable x, given by
<math display="block">F(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t) dt.</math>
Our fourth theorem states that this new function is continuous.

Our fifth theorem, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, shows that
the definite integral can be evaluated by means of antiderivatives. The process of
antidifferentiation is just the opposite of differentiation. To keep things simple, let I
be an open interval, and assume that all functions mentioned have domain I.
DEFINITION
Let f and F be functions with domain I. If f is the derivative of F, then F is
called an antiderivative of f.

4.2 FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS
For example, suppose a particle is moving upward along the y-axis with
velocity <math>v = f(t)</math> and position <math>y = F(t)</math> at time t. The position <math>y = F(t)</math> is an anti-
derivative of the velocity <math>v = f(t)</math>. We shall discuss antiderivatives in more detail
in the next section. We are now ready for the Fundamental Theorem.
FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS
Suppose f is continuous on its domain, which is an open interval I.
(i) For each point a in I, the definite integral of f from a to x considered as a
function of x is an antiderivative of f. That is,
<math display="block">d\left(\int_{a}^{x} f(t) dt\right) = f(x) dx.</math>
(ii) If F is any antiderivative of f, then for any two points (a, b) in I the
definite integral of f from a to b is equal to the difference <math>F(b) - F(a)</math>,
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = F(b) - F(a).</math>
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is important for two reasons. First,
it shows the relation between the two main notions of calculus: the derivative, which
corresponds to velocity, and the integral, which corresponds to area. It shows that
differentiation and integration are "inverse" processes. Second, it gives a simple
method for computing many definite integrals.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b>
(a) Find <math>\int_a^b c \, dx</math>. Since <math>cx</math> is an antiderivative of <math>c</math>,
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} c \, dx = cb - ca = c(b - a).</math>
<math>J_a</math>

<math display="block">\int_{-a}^{b} x \, dx = \frac{1}{2}b^2 - \frac{1}{2}a^2.</math>
The above example gives the same result that we got before but is much

The Fundamental Theorem can also be used to find the derivative of a
function which is defined as a definite integral with a variable limit of integration.
This can be done without actually evaluating the integral.
<b>EXAMPLE 6</b> Let <math>y = \int_{-\infty}^{2} \sqrt{1 + t^2} \, dt</math>. Then <math>y = -\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \sqrt{1 + t^2} \, dt</math>,
<math>dy = -d\left(\int_{2}^{x} \sqrt{1+t^{2}} dt\right) = -\sqrt{1+x^{2}} dx.</math>
and
<b>EXAMPLE 7</b> Let <math>y = \int_{2}^{x^2 + x} \frac{1}{t^3 + 1} dt</math>.
Let <math>u = x^2 + x</math>. Then
<math>\frac{du}{dx} = (2x + 1), \qquad y = \int_{2}^{u} \frac{1}{t^{3} + 1} dt, \qquad \frac{dy}{du} = \frac{1}{u^{3} + 1}.</math>
By the Chain Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\frac{du}{dx} = \frac{1}{u^3 + 1}(2x + 1) = \frac{2x + 1}{(x^2 + x)^3 + 1}.</math>
We conclude this section with a proof of the Fundamental Theorem of
Calculus.

4.3 INDEFINITE INTEGRALS
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus shows that every continuous function <math>f</math>
has at least one antiderivative, namely <math>F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) dt</math>. Actually, f has infinitely
many antiderivatives, but any two antiderivatives of <math>f</math> differ only by a constant. This
is an important fact about antiderivatives, which we state as a theorem.
THEOREM 1
Let f be a real function whose domain is an open interval I.
(i) If <math>F(x)</math> is an antiderivative of <math>f(x)</math>, then <math>F(x) + C</math> is an antiderivative
of <math>f(x)</math> for every real number C.
(ii) If <math>F(x)</math> and <math>G(x)</math> are two antiderivatives of <math>f(x)</math>, then <math>F(x) - G(x)</math> is
constant for all x in I. That is,
<math>G(x) = F(x) + C</math>
for some real number C.
Parts (i) and (ii) together show that if we can find one antiderivative

<math display="block">\frac{d(F(x) + C)}{dx} = \frac{d(F(x))}{dx} + \frac{dC}{dx} = f(x) + 0 = f(x).</math>
Part (ii) follows from a theorem in Section 3.7 on curve sketching. If a
function has derivative zero on I, then the function is constant on I. The
difference <math>F(x) - G(x)</math> has derivative <math>f(x) - f(x) = 0</math> and is therefore
constant. We used this fact in the proof of the Fundamental Theorem of
Calculus.
In computing integrals of f, we usually work with the family of all anti-
derivatives of f. We shall call this whole family of functions the indefinite integral of f.
The symbol for the indefinite integral is <math>\int f(x) dx</math>. If <math>F(x)</math> is one antiderivative of f,
the indefinite integral is the set of all functions of the form <math>F(x) + C_0</math>, <math>C_0</math> constant.
We express this with the equation
<math display="block">\int f(x) \, dx = F(x) + C.</math>
It is an equation between two families of functions rather than between two single
functions. C is called the constant of integration. To illustrate the notation,
<math display="block">\int 3x^2 \, dx = x^3 + C.</math>
We repeat the above definitions in concise form.

DEFINITION
Let the domain of f be an open interval I and suppose f has an antiderivative.
The family of all antiderivatives of <math>f</math> is called the <b>indefinite integral</b> of <math>f</math> and is
denoted by <math>\int f(x) dx</math>.
Given a function F, the family of all functions which differ from F only by a
constant is written <math>F(x) + C</math>. Thus if F is an antiderivative of f we write
<math display="block">\int f(x) \, dx = F(x) + C.</math>
When working with indefinite integrals, it is convenient to use differentials
and dependent variables. If we introduce the dependent variable <math>u</math> by <math>u = F(x)</math>, then
<math>du = F'(x) dx = f(x) dx</math>.
<math display="block">\int f(x) \, dx = F(x) + C</math>
Thus the equation
<math display="block">\int du = u + C.</math>
can be written in the form
The differential symbol <math>d</math> and the indefinite integral symbol <math>f</math> behave as
inverses to each other. We can start with the family of functions <math>u + C</math>, form <math>du</math>, and
then form <math>\int du = u + C</math> to get back where we started. Some of the rules for differentia-
tion given in Chapter 2 can be turned around to give a set of rules for indefinite
integration.
THEOREM 2
Let u and v be functions of x whose domains are an open interval I and suppose
du and dv exist for every x in I.
<math display="block">\int du = u + C.</math>
(i)
Constant Rule <math>\int c du = c \int du</math>.
(ii)
Sum Rule <math display="block">\int du + dv = \int du + \int dv.</math>
(iii)
Power Rule <math display="block">\int u^r du = \frac{u^{r+1}}{r+1} + C, \text{ where } r \text{ is rational, } r \neq -1,</math>
(iv)
and <math>u > 0</math> on I.
<math display="block">(v) \int \sin u \, du = -\cos u + C.</math>
(vi) <math display="block">\int \cos u \, du = \sin u + C.</math>
<math display="block">(vii) \qquad \int e^u \, du = e^u + C.</math>

Constant Rule <math display="block">\int cf(x) dx = c \int f(x) dx.</math>
<math display="block">\int (f(x) + g(x)) dx = \int f(x) dx + \int g(x) dx.</math>
Sum Rule
In the Constant and Sum Rules we are multiplying a family of functions
by a constant and adding two families of functions. If we do either of these
two things to families of functions differing only by a constant, we get another
family of functions differing only by a constant. For example,
<math>7(3x^4 + C) = 21x^4 + 7C = 21x^4 + C'</math>
is the family of all functions equal to <math>21x^4</math> plus a constant. Similarly,
<math>(3\sqrt{x}+C)+(5x-\sqrt{x}+D)=5x+2\sqrt{x}+(C+D)=5x+2\sqrt{x}+C'</math>
is the family of all functions equal to <math>5x + 2\sqrt{x}</math> plus a constant.

(i)
functions which have the same derivative as u.
(ii) We have <math>c du = d(cu)</math>, whence

(iii) <math display="block">du + dv = d(u + v),</math>
<math display="block">\int du + dv = \int d(u + v) = u + v + C = \int du + \int dv.</math>
(iv) <math>d\left(\frac{u^{r+1}}{r+1}\right) = \frac{(r+1)u^r}{r+1}du = u^r du</math>,

Rules (v)-(viii) are similar. Only the last formula, (viii), requires an explana-

and <math>u < 0</math>. When <math>u > 0</math>, <math>u = |u|</math> and
<math display="block">d(\ln|u|) = d(\ln u) = \frac{1}{2}du.</math>
When <math>u < 0</math>, <math>\ln u</math> is undefined, but <math>|u| = -u</math> and <math>\ln |u| = \ln (-u)</math>. Thus
<math display="block">d(\ln|u|) = d(\ln(-u)) = -\frac{1}{u}d(-u) = \frac{1}{u}du.</math>

Indefinite integration is much harder than differentiation, because there are
no rules for integrating the product or quotient of two functions. It often requires
guesswork. The short list of rules in Theorem 1 will help, and as this course proceeds
we shall add many more techniques for finding indefinite integrals.
<b>EXAMPLE 4</b> Show that <math display="block">\int \frac{dx}{(1+x)^{1/2}(1-x)^{3/2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1+x}{1-x}} + C.</math>
Our rules give no hint on finding this integral. However, once the answer
is given to us we can easily prove that it is correct by differentiating,
<math display="block">\frac{d\sqrt{\frac{1+x}{1-x}}}{dx} = \frac{d((1+x)^{1/2}(1-x)^{-1/2})}{dx}</math>
<math display="block">= (1+x)^{1/2}(-1)(-\frac{1}{2})(1-x)^{-3/2} + (1-x)^{-1/2}(\frac{1}{2})(1+x)^{-1/2}</math>
<math display="block">= (1+x)^{-1/2}(1-x)^{-3/2}\left[\frac{1}{2}(1+x) + \frac{1}{2}(1-x)\right]</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{1}{(1+x)^{1/2}(1-x)^{3/2}}.</math>
Here is a warning that may prevent some common mistakes.
Warning: The integral of the product of two functions is not equal to the
product of the integrals. The same goes for quotients. That is,
<math display="block">\int (uv) dx = \left( \int u dx \right) \left( \int v dx \right).</math>

The indefinite integral can be used to solve problems of the following type.
Given that a particle moves along the y-axis with velocity <math>v = f(t)</math>, and that at a
certain time <math>t = t_0</math> its position is <math>y = y_0</math>. Find the position y as a function of t.
<b>EXAMPLE 5</b> A particle moves with velocity <math>v = 1/t^2</math>, <math>t > 0</math>. At time <math>t = 2</math> it is at
position <math>y = 1</math>. Find the position y as a function of t. We compute
<math display="block">\int v \, dt = \int \frac{1}{t^2} dt = -\frac{1}{t} + C.</math>
Since <math>dy/dt = v</math>, y is one of the functions in the family <math>-1/t + C</math>. We can
find the constant C by setting <math>t = 2</math> and <math>y = 1</math>,
<math>y = -\frac{1}{t} + C</math>, <math>1 = -\frac{1}{2} + C</math>, <math>C = 1\frac{1}{2}</math>.
Then the answer is
<math display="block">y = -\frac{1}{t} + 1\frac{1}{2}.</math>
The next theorem shows that in such a problem we can always find the answer
if we are given the position of the particle at just one point of time.

4.4 INTEGRATION BY CHANGE OF VARIABLES
We have seen that the sum, constant, and power rules for differentiation can be turned
around to give the sum, constant, and power rules for integration. In this section we
shall show how to make use of the Chain Rule for differentiation in problems of
integration. The Chain Rule will lead to the important method of integration by
change of variables. The basic idea is to try to simplify the function to be integrated
by changing from one independent variable to another.
If <math>F</math> is an antiderivative of <math>f</math> and we take <math>u</math> as the independent variable, then
<math>\int f(u) du</math> is a family of functions of u,
<math display="block">\int f(u) \, du = F(u) + C.</math>
But if we take <math>x</math> as the independent variable and introduce <math>u</math> as a dependent variable
<math>u = g(x)</math>, then du and <math>\int f(u) du</math> mean the following:
<math display="block">du = g'(x) dx, \qquad \int f(u) du = \int f(g(x))g'(x) dx = H(x) + C.</math>
The notation <math>\int f(u) du</math> always stands for a family of functions of the independent
variable, which in some cases is another variable such as x. The next theorem can be
used as follows. To integrate a given function of x, properly choose a new variable
<math>u = g(x)</math> and integrate a new function with respect to u.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
Let I and J be intervals. We say that a function g maps J into I if for every
point x in <math>J</math>, <math>g(x)</math> is defined and belongs to <math>I</math> (Figure 4.4.1).

THEOREM 1 (Indefinite Integration by Change of Variables)
Suppose I and J are open intervals, f has domain I, g maps J into I, and g is
differentiable on J. Assume that when we take u as the independent variable,
<math display="block">\int f(u) \, du = F(u) + C.</math>
Then when x is the independent variable and <math>u = g(x)</math>,
<math display="block">\int f(u) du = F(g(x)) + C.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> Let <math>H(x) = F(g(x))</math>. For any x in J, the derivatives <math>g'(x)</math> and <math>F'(g(x)) = f(g(x))</math>
exist. Therefore by the Chain Rule,
<math display="block">H'(x) = F'(g(x))g'(x) = f(g(x))g'(x).</math>
It follows that
<math display="block">\int f(g(x))g'(x) dx = H(x) + C = F(g(x)) + C.</math>
So when <math>u = g(x)</math>, we have
<math display="block">f(u) du = f(g(x))g'(x) dx, \qquad \int f(u) du = F(g(x)) + C.</math>
Theorem 1 gives another proof of the general power rule
<math display="block">\int u^n du = \frac{u^{n+1}}{n-1} + C, \qquad n \neq -1,</math>
where <math>u</math> is given as a function of the independent variable <math>x</math>, from the simpler power
rule
<math display="block">\int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C, \qquad n \neq -1,</math>
where <math>x</math> is the independent variable.

We next describe the method of definite integration by change of variables. In
a definite integral
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} h(x) dx</math>
it is always understood that x is the independent variable and we are integrating
between the limits <math>x = a</math> and <math>x = b</math>. Thus when we change to a new independent

variable u, we must also change the limits of integration. The theorem below will

THEOREM 2 (Definite Integration by Change of Variables)
Suppose I and J are open intervals, f is continuous and has an antiderivative
on I, g has a continuous derivative on J, and g maps J into I. Then for any two
points a and b in <math>J</math>,
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(g(x))g'(x) \, dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) \, du.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> Let F be an antiderivative of f. Then by Theorem 1, <math>H(x) = F(g(x))</math> is an
antiderivative of <math>h(x) = f(g(x))g'(x)</math>. Since f, g, and g' are continuous, h is
continuous on J. Then by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,
<math display="block">\int_{a(a)}^{b} f(g(x))g'(x) dx = H(b) - H(a) = F(g(b)) - F(g(a)) = \int_{a(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du.</math>
Find the area under the line <math>y = 1 + 3x</math> from <math>x = 0</math> to <math>x = 1</math>. This can
<b>EXAMPLE 5</b>
be done either with or without a change of variables.
Without change of variable: <math>\int (1+3x) dx = x + 3x^2/2 + C</math>, so
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{1} (1+3x) \, dx = x + \frac{3x^{2}}{2} \bigg|_{0}^{1} = \left(1 + \frac{3 \cdot 1^{2}}{2}\right) - \left(0 + \frac{3 \cdot 0^{2}}{2}\right) = \frac{5}{2}.</math>
With change of variable: Let <math>u = 1 + 3x</math>. Then <math>du = 3 dx</math>, <math>dx = \frac{1}{3} du</math>.
When <math>x = 0</math>, <math>u = 1 + 3 \cdot 0 = 1</math>. When <math>x = 1</math>, <math>u = 1 + 3 \cdot 1 = 4</math>.
<math display="block">\int_0^1 (1+3x) \, dx = \int_1^4 u \cdot \frac{1}{3} \, du = \frac{u^2}{6} \bigg]_1^4 = \frac{16}{6} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{15}{6} = \frac{5}{2}.</math>
Example 5 shows us that <math>\int_0^1 (1+3x) dx = \int_1^4 (u/3) du</math>; that is, the areas
shown in Figure 4.4.2 are the same.

We can use integration by change of variables to derive the formula for the
area of a circle, <math>A = \pi r^2</math>, where r is the radius. It is easier to work with a semicircle
because the semicircle of radius <math>r</math> is just the region under the curve
<math display="block">y = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}, \qquad -r \le x \le r.</math>
To start with we need to give a rigorous definition of <math>\pi</math>. By definition, <math>\pi</math> is the area of
a unit circle. Thus <math>\pi</math> is twice the area of the unit semicircle, which means:
DEFINITION
<math display="block">\pi = 2\int_{-1}^{1} \sqrt{1 - x^2} \, dx.</math>
The area of a semicircle of radius <math>r</math> is the definite integral
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{r} \sqrt{r^2 - x^2} \, dx.</math>
To evaluate this integral we let <math>x = ru</math>. Then <math>dx = r du</math>. When <math>x = \pm r</math>, <math>u = \pm 1</math>. Thus
<math display="block">\int_{-\infty}^{r} \sqrt{r^2 - x^2} \, dx = \int_{-\infty}^{1} \sqrt{r^2 - (ru)^2} \, r \, du = \int_{-\infty}^{1} r^2 \sqrt{1 - u^2} \, du</math>
<math display="block">= r^2 \int_{-1}^{1} \sqrt{1 - u^2} \, du = r^2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}.</math>
Therefore the semicircle has area <math>\pi r^2/2</math> and the circle area <math>\pi r^2</math> (Figure 4.4.6).

4.5 AREA BETWEEN TWO CURVES
A region in the plane can often be represented as the region between two curves.
For example, the unit circle is the region between the curves
<math>y = -\sqrt{1 - x^2}</math>, <math>y = \sqrt{1 - x^2}</math>, <math>-1 \le x \le 1</math>
shown in Figure 4.5.1. Consider two continuous functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> on <math>[a, b]</math> such that
<math>f(x) \le g(x)</math> for all x in [a, b]. The region R, bounded by the curves
<math>y = f(x),</math> <math>y = g(x),</math> <math>x = a,</math> <math>x = b,</math>
is called the region between <math>f(x)</math> and <math>g(x)</math> from a to b. If both curves are above the
x-axis as in Figure 4.5.2, the area of the region R can be found by subtracting the
area below f from the area below g:
area of <math>R = \int_a^b g(x) dx - \int_a^b f(x) dx</math>.
It is usually easier to work with a single integral and write
area of <math>R = \int_a^b (g(x) - f(x)) dx</math>.

This problem can be solved in three ways. Each solution illustrates a different
trick which is useful in other area problems. The three corners of the region
are:
<math>(-1, -1)</math>, where <math>y = x^3</math> and <math>y = -1</math> cross.<br>
<math>(3, -1)</math>, where <math>y = 2 - x</math> and <math>y = -1</math> cross.<br>
<math>(1, 1)</math>, where <math>y = x^3</math> and <math>y = 2 - x</math> cross.
Note that <math>y = x^3</math> and <math>y = 2 - x</math> can cross at only one point because <math>x^3</math> is
always increasing and <math>2 - x</math> is always decreasing.
FIRST SOLUTION Break the region into the two parts shown in Figure 4.5.7:
<math>R_1</math> from <math>x = -1</math> to <math>x = 1</math>, and <math>R_2</math> from <math>x = 1</math> to <math>x = 3</math>. Then
area of <math>R</math> = area of <math>R_1</math> + area of <math>R_2</math>.
area of <math>R_1 = \int_{-1}^1 x^3 - (-1) dx = \frac{1}{4}x^4 + x \Big]_{-1}^1 = 2.</math>
area of <math>R_2 = \int_1^3 (2 - x) - (-1) dx = 3x - \frac{1}{2}x^2 \Big|_1^3 = 2.</math>
area of <math>R = 2 + 2 = 4</math>.

4.6 NUMERICAL INTEGRATION
In numerical integration, one computes an approximate value for the definite
integral rather than finding an exact value. In this section we shall present two
methods of numerical integration, called the Trapezoidal Rule and Simpson's Rule.
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives us a method of computing
the definite integral of a given continuous function <math>f</math> from <math>a</math> to <math>b</math>. The method is to
find, by trial and error, an antiderivative <math>F</math> of <math>f</math> and then to use the equation
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(t) dt = F(b) - F(a).</math>
When the method works, it provides an exact value for the integral. However, the
method succeeds only if the antiderivative happens to be a function that can be
described in a simple way. For many integrals one cannot find a formula for the
antiderivative, and the method fails. Such integrals can still be computed approxi-
mately using numerical integration.
The Trapezoidal Rule and Simpson's Rule can always be applied and do
not use the antiderivative. They are easy to carry out on a computer or hand calculator.
We already discussed one method of approximating the definite integral in Section 4.1,
the Riemann sum. The Trapezoidal Rule is a modified form of the Riemann sum,
which gives a much closer approximation for a given amount of effort. Simpson's
Rule is a further modification that gives still better approximations.

4.6 NUMERICAL INTEGRATION
225
Let f be a continuous function on an interval I, and let <math>a < b</math> in I. By
definition, for each positive infinitesimal <math>dx</math> the definite integral
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx</math>
is the standard part of the infinite Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) dx,</math>
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx = st \left[ \sum_{a}^{b} f(x) dx \right].</math>
In Section 4.1, examples were worked out to show that the finite Riemann sums
become very close to the definite integral when <math>\Delta x</math> is small; that is, the finite Riemann
sums approximate the definite integral. In Section 4.2, we saw that the definite
integral is the limit of the finite Riemann sums as <math>\Delta x \rightarrow 0^+</math>:
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0^+} \sum_{a=0}^b f(x) \, \Delta x.</math>
The Riemann sum, which is a sum of areas of rectangles, is a rather inefficient
approximation of the definite integral. We can usually get a much closer approxi-
mation with the same amount of work by adding up areas of trapezoids instead of
rectangles, forming the Trapezoidal Rule suggested by Figure 4.6.1. The Trapezoidal
Rule also provides a formula, called an error estimate, which tells us how close the
approximation is to the exact value of the definite integral.

Figure 4.6.1
Choose a positive integer <math>n</math> and divide the interval <math>[a, b]</math> into <math>n</math> subintervals
of equal length <math>\Delta x = (b - a)/n</math>. The partition points are <math>a = x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n = b</math>.
The trapezoidal approximation is the area of the region under the broken line con-
necting the points
<math>(x_0, f(x_0)), (x_1, f(x_1)), \ldots, (x_n, f(x_n)).</math>
Since all of these points lie on the curve <math>y = f(x)</math>, the broken line closely follows the
curve. So one would expect the area of the region under the broken line to closely
approximate the area under the curve.
Consider a single subinterval <math>[x_m, x_{m+1}]</math> of width <math>\Delta x</math>. The region under the
line segment connecting the two points
<math>(x_m, f(x_m)), (x_{m+1}, f(x_{m+1}))</math>

is a trapezoid and its area is
<math display="block">\frac{f(x_m) + f(x_{m+1})}{2} \Delta x.</math>
The sum of the areas of the trapezoids is a modified Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{x=0}^{b} \frac{f(x) + f(x + \Delta x)}{2} \Delta x</math>
<math display="block">= \left( \frac{f(x_0) + f(x_1)}{2} + \frac{f(x_1) + f(x_2)}{2} + \dots + \frac{f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)}{2} \right) \Delta x</math>
<math display="block">= \left[ \frac{1}{2} f(x_0) + f(x_1) + f(x_2) + \dots + f(x_{n-1}) + \frac{1}{2} f(x_n) \right] \Delta x.</math>
We thus make the definition:
DEFINITION
Let <math>\Delta x = (b - a)/n</math> evenly divide <math>b - a</math>. Then by the trapezoidal approxi-
<b>mation</b> to the definite integral <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math> we mean the sum
<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{f(x) + f(x + \Delta x)}{2} \Delta x = \left[\frac{1}{2} f(x_0) + f(x_1) + \dots + f(x_{n-1}) + \frac{1}{2} f(x_n)\right] \Delta x.</math>
The Trapezoidal Approximation of an integral <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math> can be computed
very efficiently on most hand calculators. First compute the sum
<math>\frac{1}{2}f(x_0) + f(x_1) + f(x_2) + \cdots + \frac{1}{2}f(x_n)</math>
by cumulative addition. Then multiply this sum by <math>\Delta x</math> to obtain the Trapezoidal
Approximation.
THEOREM 1
For a continuous function <math>f</math> on <math>[a, b]</math>, the trapezoidal approximation approaches
the definite integral as <math>\Delta x \rightarrow 0^+</math>, that is,
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) dx = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0^+} \sum_{a=0}^b \frac{f(x) + f(x + \Delta x)}{2} \Delta x.</math>
PROOF Comparing the formulas for the trapezoidal approximation and the Riemann
sum, we see that
<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^{b} \frac{f(x) + f(x + \Delta x)}{2} \Delta x = \sum_{n=0}^{b} f(x) \Delta x + (\frac{1}{2} f(x_n) - \frac{1}{2} f(x_0)) \Delta x.</math>
For <math>dx</math> positive infinitesimal, the extra term
<math>(\frac{1}{2}f(x_H) - \frac{1}{2}f(x_0)) dx</math>
is infinitely small. It follows that
<math display="block">\sum_{a}^{b} \frac{f(x) + f(x + dx)}{2} dx \approx \sum_{a}^{b} f(x) dx \approx \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx.</math>

The trapezoidal approximation can be made as close to the definite integral
as we want by taking <math>\Delta x</math> small. From a practical standpoint, however, it is helpful
to know how small we should take <math>\Delta x</math> in order to be sure of a given degree of accuracy.
For instance, suppose we need to know the definite integral to three decimal places.
How small must we take <math>\Delta x</math> in our trapezoidal approximation? The answer is given

## PDF page 238

228
4 INTEGRATION
by the Trapezoidal Rule, which gives an error estimate for the trapezoidal
approximation.
The error in the trapezoidal approximation is the absolute value of the
difference between the trapezoidal sum and the definite integral,
error = <math display="block">\left| \sum_{a}^{b} \frac{f(x) + f(x + \Delta x)}{2} \Delta x - \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx \right|.</math>
An error estimate for the trapezoidal approximation is a function <math>E(\Delta x)</math>, which is
known to be greater than or equal to the error.
Thus if <math>E(\Delta x)</math> is an error estimate, the trapezoidal sum is within <math>E(\Delta x)</math> of
the definite integral. If we want to be sure that the trapezoidal approximation is
accurate to three decimal places—i.e., the error is less than 0.0005—we choose
<math>\Delta x</math> so that <math>E(\Delta x) \leq 0.0005</math>. We are now ready to state the Trapezoidal Rule.
TRAPEZOIDAL RULE
Let f be a function whose second derivative f" exists and has absolute value
at most M on a closed interval <math>[a, b]</math>,
<math>|f''(x)| \le M</math> for <math>a \le x \le b</math>.
If <math>\Delta x</math> evenly divides <math>b-a</math>, then the trapezoidal approximation of the definite
integral of f has the error estimate
<math display="block">\frac{b-a}{12}M(\Delta x)^2.</math>
That is,
<math display="block">\left| \sum_{a}^{b} \frac{f(x) + f(x + \Delta x)}{2} \Delta x - \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx \right| \le \frac{b - a}{12} M(\Delta x)^{2}.</math>
The proof is omitted.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> (Concluded) We let <math>f(x) = \sqrt{1 + x^2}</math>.
Then
<math display="block">f'(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}},</math>
<math display="block">f''(x) = \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2} - x^2/\sqrt{1+x^2}}{1+x^2} = \frac{1}{(1+x^2)^{3/2}}.</math>
Therefore <math>|f''(x)| \le 1</math> for all x in [0, 1]. We take <math>M = 1</math> and use the error
estimate given by the Trapezoidal Rule,
<math display="block">\frac{b-a}{12}M(\Delta x)^2 = \frac{1}{12} \cdot 1 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{300}.</math>
Thus our approximation is within an accuracy of 1/300,
<math display="block">\left| \int_{1}^{1} \sqrt{1 + x^{2}} \, dx - 1.150 \right| \le 1/300 \sim 0.0033.</math>
This shows that the integral is, at least, between 1.146 and 1.154.

We then add up the areas under each of the parabolic arcs to obtain an approximation

The lemma is proved at the end of this section. Using the lemma, we find
that the area of the region under one parabolic arc from <math>x_k</math> to <math>x_{k+2}</math> is

It follows that the sum of the <math>n/2</math> regions under the parabolic arcs is a modified
Riemann sum,
<math display="block">\sum_{x} \left[ \frac{f(x) + 4f(x + \Delta x) + f(x + 2 \Delta x)}{3} \right] \Delta x</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left\{ \left[ f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + f(x_2) \right] + \left[ f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + f(x_4) \right] + \cdots \right\}</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + 2f(x_4) + \dots + 4f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n) \right].</math>
This modified Riemann sum is Simpson's approximation to the definite
integral. Note the sequence of coefficients,
<math>1, 4, 2, 4, 2, \ldots, 2, 4, 1.</math>
Like the trapezoidal approximation, it is easily computed on a computer or hand
calculator.
THEOREM 2
For a continuous function <math>f</math> on <math>[a, b]</math>, Simpson's approximation approaches
the definite integral as <math>\Delta x \rightarrow 0^+</math>,
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0^{+}} \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_{0}) + 4f(x_{1}) + 2f(x_{2}) + 4f(x_{3}) + \dots + f(x_{n}) \right].</math>
Simpson's approximation is almost as easy to calculate as the trapezoidal
approximation, but is much more accurate. Simpson's Rule is an error estimate
that involves the fourth derivative of the function and the fourth power of <math>\Delta x</math>.

Suppose the function <math>f</math> has a fourth derivative on the interval <math>[a, b]</math> that has
absolute value at most M,
<math>|f^{(4)}(x)| \le M \text{ for } a \le x \le b.</math>
If <math>[a, b]</math> is divided into an even number of subintervals of length <math>\Delta x</math>, then
Simpson's approximation to the definite integral has the error estimate
<math display="block">\frac{b-a}{180}M(\Delta x)^4.</math>
Use Simpson's Rule with <math>\Delta x = 0.25</math> to approximate the integral

4 INTEGRATION
To get the Simpson approximation, we multiply this sum by <math>\Delta x/3</math>:
<math>S = (10.267816) \cdot (0.25)/3 = 0.855651.</math>
To find the error estimate we need the fourth derivative of
<math>v = e^{-x^2/2}</math>.
The fourth derivative can be computed as usual and turns out to be
<math>y^{(4)} = (x^4 - 6x^2 + 3)e^{-x^2/2}</math>
On the interval [0, 1], <math>y^{(4)}</math> is decreasing because both <math>x^4 - 6x^2 + 3</math> and
<math>-x^2/2</math> are decreasing, and therefore <math>y^{(4)}</math> has its maximum value at <math>x=0</math>
and its minimum value at <math>x = 1</math>,
maximum: <math>y^{(4)}(0) = 3</math>
minimum: <math>v^{(4)}(1) = -1.213061</math>
The maximum value of the absolute value <math>|y^{(4)}|</math> is thus <math>M=3</math>. The error
estimate in Simpson's Rule is then
<math display="block">\frac{b-a}{180}(\Delta x)^4 M = \frac{1}{180} \cdot (0.25)^4 \cdot 3 = 0.000065.</math>
This shows that the integral is within 0.000065 of the approximation; that is,
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{1} e^{-x^{2}/2} dx = 0.855651 \pm 0.000065,</math>
or using inequalities,
<math display="block">0.855586 \le \int_{0}^{1} e^{-x^{2}/2} dx \le 0.855716.</math>
For comparison, a more accurate computation with a smaller <math>\Delta x</math> shows
that the actual value to six places is
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{1} e^{-x^{2}/2} dx = 0.855624.</math>
The Trapezoidal Rule for this integral and the same value of <math>\Delta x = 0.25</math>
give an approximate value of 0.85246 for the integral and an error estimate
of 0.00521.

The algebra is simpler if the y-axis is drawn through the
second point, so that <math>u + h = 0</math>, and the three points have coordinates

Suppose the parabola has the equation <math>y = ax^2 + bx + c</math>. Then the area
under the parabola is
<math display="block">A = \int_{-b}^{b} (ax^2 + bx + c) dx</math>
<math>=\frac{ax^3}{3}+\frac{bx^2}{2}+cx\bigg|_{-h}^{h}</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{2}{3}ah^3+2ch.</math>

4.6 NUMERICAL INTEGRATION
When we substitute the coordinates of the three points <math>(-h, r)</math>, <math>(0, s)</math>, <math>(h, t)</math>
into the equation for the parabola, we obtain the three equations
<math display="block">r = ah^2 - bh + c.</math>
<math>s=c</math>
<math display="block">t = ah^2 + bh + c.</math>
Add the first and third equations and solve for a:
<math display="block">r + t = 2ah^2 + 2c</math>
<math display="block">a = \frac{r + t - 2c}{2h^2}</math>
Finally, substitute the above expression for <math>a</math> and <math>s</math> for <math>c</math> in the equation
for the area:
<math display="block">A = \frac{2}{3}ah^3 + 2ch</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{r+t-2c}{2h^2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot h^3+2ch</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{r+t-2c+6c}{3} \cdot h</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{h}{3}(r+4c+t).</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{h}{3}(r+4s+t).</math>

LIMITS,

5.1 INFINITE LIMITS
Up to this point we have studied three types of limits:
<math>\lim f(x) = L</math> means <math>f(x) \approx L</math> whenever <math>x \approx c</math> but <math>x \neq c</math>.
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c^+} f(x) = L \quad \text{means } f(x) \approx L \text{ whenever } x \approx c \text{ but } x > c.</math>
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = L \quad \text{means } f(x) \approx L \text{ whenever } x \approx c \text{ but } x < c.</math>
The limit notation <math>\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = L</math> means that whenever H is positive
infinite, <math>f(H) \approx L</math> (Figure 5.1.1(a)).
<math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = -\infty</math> means that whenever <math>x \approx c</math> and <math>x \neq c</math>, <math>f(x)</math> is negative
infinite (Figure 5.1.1(b)). The various other combinations have the meanings which
one would expect.

<math display="block">st\left(\frac{3H^4 + 5H - 2}{2H^4 - 6H^3 + 7}\right) = \frac{3 + 0 - 0}{2 - 0 + 0} = \frac{3}{2}.</math>
and therefore
Thus the limit exists and is <math>\frac{3}{2}</math>.

<b>EXAMPLE 4</b> Find <math>\lim_{x \to -\infty} (x^3 + 200x^2)</math>.
We have <math>x^3 + 200x^2 = x^2(x + 200)</math>. When H is negative infinite, <math>H^2</math> is
positive infinite and <math>(H + 200)</math> is negative infinite, so their product is negative
infinite. Thus
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to -\infty} (x^3 + 200x^2) = -\infty.</math>

5.1 INFINITE LIMITS
When
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \infty \quad \text{or} \quad -\infty,</math>
the limit does not exist, because <math>f(x)</math> has no standard part. The infinity symbol is
only used to indicate the behavior of <math>f(x)</math> and is not to be construed as a number.
<b>EXAMPLE 5</b> A student can get a score of <math>100t/(t+1)</math> on his math exam if he studies
t hours for it (Figure 5.1.2). If he studies infinitely long for the exam, his score
will be infinitely close to 100, because if H is positive infinite,
<math>st\left(\frac{100H}{H+1}\right) = st\left(\frac{100}{1+1/H}\right) = \frac{100}{1+0} = 100.</math>
In the notation of limits,
<math display="block">\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{100t}{t+1}=100.</math>

<b>EXAMPLE 6</b>
<math>f(t) = a_n t^n + a_{n-1} t^{n-1} + \dots + a_1 t + a_0</math>
of degree <math>n > 0</math>, the limits as t approaches <math>-\infty</math> or <math>+\infty</math> are as follows.
Suppose <math>a_n > 0</math>. When n is even, <math>\lim_{t \to -\infty} f(t) = \infty</math>, <math>\lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \infty</math>.
When <i>n</i> is odd, <math>\lim_{t\to -\infty} f(t) = -\infty</math>, <math>\lim_{t\to \infty} f(t) = \infty</math>.
The signs are all reversed when <math>a_n < 0</math>.
All these limits can be computed from
<math display="block">f(t) = t^{n} \left( a_{n} + \frac{a^{n-1}}{t} + \dots + \frac{a_{1}}{t^{n-1}} + \frac{a_{0}}{t^{n}} \right).</math>
In the special theory of relativity, a body which is moving at constant
EXAMPLE 7
velocity <math>v, -c < v < c</math>, will have mass
<math>m = \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}</math>
and its length in the direction of motion will be
<math>l = l_{00}\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}</math>.

5 LIMITS, ANALYTIC GEOMETRY, AND APPROXIMATIONS
Here <math>m_0</math>, <math>l_0</math>, and c are positive constants denoting the mass at rest (that is,
the mass when <math>v = 0</math>), the length at rest, and the speed of light.
Suppose the velocity <math>v</math> is infinitely close to the speed of light <math>c</math>, that is,
<math>v = c - \varepsilon</math>, <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> infinitesimal.
<math display="block">\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{(c - \varepsilon)^2}{c^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{c^2 - (c^2 - 2c\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2)}{c^2}}</math>
Then
<math display="block">=\sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon}{c}-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{c^2}}=\sqrt{\varepsilon\cdot\left(\frac{2}{c}-\frac{\varepsilon}{c^2}\right)},</math>
which is the square root of a positive infinitesimal. Thus <math>\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}</math> is a
positive infinitesimal. Therefore for <math>v</math> infinitely close to <math>c</math>, <math>m</math> is positive infinite
and l is positive infinitesimal. That is, a body moving at velocity infinitely
close to (but less than) the speed of light has infinite mass and infinitesimal
length in the direction of motion. In the notation of limits this means that
<math display="block">\lim_{v \to c^{-}} \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = +\infty,</math>
<math display="block">\lim_{v \to c^{-1}} l_0 \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = 0.</math>
Caution: This example must be understood in the light of our policy of
speaking as if a line in physical space really is like the hyperreal line. Actually,
there is no evidence one way or the other on whether a line in space is like
the hyperreal line, but the hyperreal line is a useful model for the purpose of
applications.
<b>EXAMPLE 8</b> Evaluate <math>\lim \frac{\sin x}{x}</math>
<math>\chi \to \infty</math> <math>\chi</math>
When H is positive infinite, <math>\sin H</math> is between <math>-1</math> and 1 and thus finite, so
<math>(\sin H)/H</math> is infinitesimal. The limit is therefore zero:
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 0.</math>
EXAMPLE 9 Find
<math>\lim \cos x</math>.
<math>x \to \infty</math>
If H is any integer or hyperinteger, then
<math>cos(2\pi H) = 1,</math> <math>cos(2\pi H + \pi) = -1.</math>
In fact, <math>\cos x</math> will keep oscillating between 1 and <math>-1</math> even for infinite x.
Therefore the limit does not exist.
Limits involving <math>e^x</math> and <math>\ln x</math> will be studied in Chapter 8.

5.2 L'HOSPITAL'S RULE
Suppose f and g are two real functions which are defined in an open interval con-
taining a real number a, and we wish to compute the limit
<math display="block">\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.</math>
Sometimes the answer is easy. Assume that the limits of <math>f(x)</math> and <math>g(x)</math> exist as <math>x \to a</math>,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L, \qquad \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M.</math>
If <math>M \neq 0</math>, then the limit of the quotient is simply the quotient of the limits,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{L}{M}.</math>
This is because for any infinitesimal <math>\Delta x \neq 0</math>,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = st \left( \frac{f(a + \Delta x)}{g(a + \Delta x)} \right) = \frac{st(f(a + \Delta x))}{st(g(a + \Delta x))} = \frac{L}{M}.</math>
If <math>L \neq 0</math> and <math>M = 0</math>, then the limit
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}</math>

## PDF page 253

243
5.2 L'HOSPITAL'S RULE
does not exist, because when <math>\Delta x \neq 0</math> is infinitesimal, <math>f(a + \Delta x)</math> has standard part
<math>L \neq 0</math> and <math>g(a + \Delta x)</math> has standard part 0.
But what happens if both L and M are 0? In some cases a simple algebraic
manipulation will enable us to compute the limit. For example,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to -1} \frac{x^2 - 1}{x + 1} = \lim_{x \to -1} \frac{(x + 1)(x - 1)}{x + 1} = \lim_{x \to -1} (x - 1) = -2,</math>
even though both the numerator <math>x^2 - 1</math> and the denominator <math>x + 1</math> approach 0 as
<math>x</math> approaches <math>-1</math>.
In other cases l'Hospital's Rule is useful in computing limits of quotients
where both L and M are 0. Before stating l'Hospital's Rule, we introduce the notion
of a neighborhood of a point <math>c</math> (Figure 5.2.1).
tummummum)
A neighborhood of c
Figure 5.2.1
DEFINITION
By a neighborhood of a real number c we mean an interval which contains c as
an interior point.
The set formed by removing the point c from a neighborhood I of c is called a
deleted neighborhood of c. Thus a deleted neighborhood is the set of all points
x in I such that <math>x \neq c</math>.
L'HOSPITAL'S RULE FOR 0/0
Suppose that in some deleted neighborhood of a real number <math>c</math>, <math>f'(x)</math> and <math>g'(x)</math>
exist and <math>g'(x) \neq 0</math>. Assume that
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to c} g(x) = 0.</math>
C11 \
If <math>\lim_{x\to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}</math> exists or is infinite, then
<math display="block">
\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}.
</math>
(See Figure 5.2.2.) Usually the limit will be given by
<math display="block">\lim_{x\to c}\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}=\frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)},</math>
and in this case the proof is very simple.

<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} = \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}</math>
PROOF IN THE CASE
Let <math>\Delta x</math> be a nonzero infinitesimal. Then <math>f(c) = 0</math>, <math>g(c) = 0</math>, and
<math display="block">\frac{f(c+\Delta x)}{g(c+\Delta x)} = \frac{(f(c+\Delta x) - f(c))/\Delta x}{(g(c+\Delta x) - g(c))/\Delta x} \approx \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}.</math>
Taking standard parts we get
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}.</math>
Intuitively, for <math>x \approx c</math> the graphs of <math>f(x)</math> and <math>g(x)</math> are almost straight lines of
slopes <math>f'(c)</math>, <math>g'(c)</math> passing through zero, so the graph of <math>f(x)/g(x)</math> is almost the hori-
zontal line through <math>f'(c)/g'(c)</math> (Figure 5.2.3).

The equation
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} = \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}</math>
is not always true. For example, <math>g'(c)</math> might be zero or undefined.
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}</math>
is sometimes another limit of type 0/0, that is,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} f'(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to c} g'(x) = 0.</math>
When this happens, l'Hospital's Rule can often be reapplied to <math>\lim_{x\to c} f'(x)/g'(x)</math>.
The proof of l'Hospital's Rule in general is fairly long and uses the Mean Value
Theorem. It will not be given here.
Here are some examples showing how the rule can be applied.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> Find <math>\lim_{x\to 1} \frac{(1/x)-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}</math>.

5.2 L'HOSPITAL'S RULE
Both <math>(1/x) - 1</math> and <math>\sqrt{x - 1}</math> approach 0 as x approaches 1. The limit is thus
of the form 0/0. Using l'Hospital's Rule,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{(1/x) - 1}{\sqrt{x} - 1} = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{-x^{-2}}{\frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2}} = \frac{-1}{\frac{1}{2}} = -2.</math>
Find <math>\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{\sqrt{x+1-1}}{3}</math>.
EXAMPLE 2
The limit is of the form 0/0. The limit of <math>f'(x)/g'(x)</math> as <math>x \to 0</math> is <math>\infty</math>,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{d(\sqrt{x+1}-1)/dx}{d(x^3)/dx} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{2}(x+1)^{-1/2}}{3x^2} = \infty.</math>
Thus by l'Hospital's Rule,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x+1-1}}{x^3} = \infty.</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 3</b> Find <math>\lim_{x \to 3} \left( x + \frac{1}{x-3} \right) (\sqrt{x+1} - 2)</math>.
This limit is not in a form where we can apply l'Hospital's Rule. We must
first use algebra to put it in another form,
<math>\left(x + \frac{1}{x - 3}\right)(\sqrt{x + 1} - 2) = x(\sqrt{x + 1} - 2) + \frac{\sqrt{x + 1} - 2}{x - 3}.</math>
By elementary computations, <math>\lim_{x \to 3} x(\sqrt{x+1} - 2) = 3 \cdot 0 = 0</math>.
Using l'Hospital's Rule,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{\sqrt{x+1}-2}{x} = \lim_{x \to 2} \frac{\frac{1}{2}(x+1)^{-1/2}}{1} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{4}.</math>
We then add the limits to get the desired answer,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 3} \left( x + \frac{1}{x - 3} \right) (\sqrt{x + 1} - 2) = \lim_{x \to 3} x (\sqrt{x + 1} - 2) + \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{\sqrt{x + 1} - 2}{x - 3}</math>
<math>=0+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{4}</math>.
Find <math>\lim \frac{(x-3)}{4} + \frac{1}{x+1}</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 4</b>
This limit is of the form 0/0. When l'Hospital's Rule is used the limit is still
of the form 0/0. But when it is used a second time we can compute the limit.
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\frac{x-3}{4} + \frac{1}{x+1}}{\frac{(x-1)^2}{(x-1)^2}} = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{(x+1)^2}}{\frac{2(x-1)}{2}} = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{2(x+1)^{-3}}{2} = \frac{1}{8}.</math>
L'Hospital's Rule also holds true for other types of limits. That is, it holds
true if <math>x \to c</math> is everywhere replaced by one of the following.
<math>x \to c^+, \qquad x \to c^-, \qquad x \to \infty, \qquad x \to -\infty.</math>

5 LIMITS, ANALYTIC GEOMETRY, AND APPROXIMATIONS
EXAMPLE 5 Find <math>\lim_{x\to 0^+} \frac{\sqrt{x+4-2}}{\sqrt{x}}</math>.
The limit as <math>x \to 0</math> does not exist because <math>\sqrt{x}</math> is defined only for <math>x > 0</math>.
However, the one-sided limit as <math>x \to 0^+</math> has the form <math>0/0</math> and can be found by
l'Hospital's Rule.
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\sqrt{x+4-2}}{\sqrt{x}} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\frac{1}{2}(x+4)^{-1/2}}{\frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2}} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x+4}} = 0.</math>
A second form of l'Hospital's Rule deals with the case where both <math>f(x)</math> and
<math>g(x)</math> approach <math>\infty</math> as x approaches c.
L'HOSPITAL'S RULE FOR ∞/∞
Suppose c is a real number, and in some deleted neighborhood of c, <math>f'(x)</math> and
<math>g'(x)</math> exist and <math>g'(x) \neq 0</math>. Assume that
<math display="block">\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = \infty, \qquad \lim_{x\to c} g(x) = \infty.</math>
If <math>\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}</math> exists or is infinite, then
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}.</math>
The rule for <math>\infty/\infty</math> is exactly the same, word for word, as the rule for <math>0/0</math>,
except that 0 is replaced by <math>\infty</math>. We omit the proof, which is more difficult in the case
<math>\infty/\infty</math>. Actually, the assumption
<math display="block">\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = \infty</math>
is not needed.
Again, l'Hospital's Rule for <math>\infty/\infty</math> also holds for the other types of limits,
<math>x \to c^+, \qquad x \to c^-, \qquad x \to \infty, \qquad x \to -\infty.</math>
Find <math>\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x + \sqrt{x} + 1}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{x} + 1}</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 6</b>
By l'Hospital's Rule for <math>\infty/\infty</math>,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x + \sqrt{x+1}}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{x+1}} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1 + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}}{\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1}}} = \infty.</math>
Before using l'Hospital's Rule, check to see whether the limit is
Warning:
of the form <math>0/0</math> or <math>\infty/\infty</math>. A common mistake is to use the rule when the limit is not of
one of these forms.

5.2 L'HOSPITAL'S RULE
Find <math>\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x - (1/x)}}{x}</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 7</b>
The limit has the form 0/1, so l'Hospital's Rule does not apply.
Correct: <math>\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x} - (1/x)}{x} = \frac{\lim_{x \to 1} (\sqrt{x} - (1/x))}{\lim x} = \frac{0}{1} = 0.</math>
Incorrect:
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x - (1/x)}}{x} = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{d(\sqrt{x} - (1/x))/dx}{dx/dx} = \lim_{x \to 1} \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} + \frac{1}{x^2}\right) = \frac{3}{2}.</math>

5.3 LIMITS AND CURVE SKETCHING
By definition, <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L</math> means that for every hyperreal number x which is
infinitely close but not equal to <math>c, f(x)</math> is infinitely close to L. What does <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) =</math>
L tell us about <math>f(x)</math> for real numbers x? It turns out that if <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L</math>, then for
every real number x which is close to but not equal to <math>c</math>, <math>f(x)</math> is close to <math>L</math>.
In the next section we shall justify the above intuitive statement by a math-
ematical theorem. The main difficulty is to make the word "close" precise. For the
time being we shall simply illustrate the idea with some examples.
Consider the limit <math>\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{2/x}{1/x} + \frac{1}{-1} = 2</math>.
EXAMPLE 1
This limit is evaluated by letting <math>x \neq 0</math> be infinitesimal:
<math>\frac{2/x+1}{1/x-1} = \frac{2+x}{1-x}</math>
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{2/x + 1}{1/x - 1} = st \left( \frac{2 + x}{1 - x} \right) = \frac{st(2 + x)}{st(1 - x)} = \frac{2 + 0}{1 - 0} = 2.</math>

Other types of limits also give information which is useful in drawing graphs.
For instance, if <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = \infty</math>, then for every number x which is close to but not
equal to c, the value of <math>f(x)</math> is large. And if <math>\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = L</math>, then for every large real
number <math>x, f(x)</math> is close to L.
In both the above statements, if we replace "close" by "infinitely close" and
"large" by "infinitely large" we get our official definition of a limit. We give two more
examples.

5.4 PARABOLAS
In this section we shall study the graph of the equation
<math display="block">y = ax^2 + bx + c,</math>
which is a U-shaped curve called a vertical parabola. We begin with the general
definition of a parabola in the plane.
Recall that the distance between a point <math>P</math> and a line <math>L</math> is the length of the
perpendicular line from P to L, as in Figure 5.4.1. If we are given a line L and a point
F not on L, the set of all points equidistant from L and F will form a U-shaped curve
that passes midway between L and F. This curve is a parabola, shown in Figure 5.4.2.

5.4 PARABOLAS
DEFINITION OF PARABOLA
Given a line L and a point F not on the line, the set of all points equidistant from
L and F is called the parabola with directrix L and focus F.
The line through the focus perpendicular to the directrix is called the axis
of the parabola. The point where the parabola crosses the axis is called the vertex.
These are illustrated in Figure 5.4.3.
As we can see from the figure, the parabola is symmetric about its axis. That
is, if we fold the page along the axis, the parabola will fold upon itself. The vertex is
just the point halfway between the focus and directrix. It is the point on the parabola
which is closest to the directrix and focus.
When a ball is thrown into the air, its path is the parabola shown in Figure
5.4.4, with the highest point at the vertex.
Telescope mirrors and radar antennae are in the shape of parabolas. This is
done because all light rays coming from the direction of the axis will be reflected to a
single point, the focus (see Figure 5.4.5). For the same reason, reflectors for search-
lights and automobile headlights are shaped like parabolas, with the light at the
focus.

We can now sketch the graph of any equation of the form
<math display="block">Ax^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0.</math>
In the ordinary case where both <math>A</math> and <math>E</math> are different from zero, proceed as follows.
First, solve the equation for <math>y</math>, obtaining the new equation
<math display="block">y = -\frac{A}{F}x^2 - \frac{D}{F}x - \frac{F}{F}.</math>
Second, use the method in this section to sketch the graph, which will be a vertical
parabola. There are also two degenerate cases. If <math>A = 0</math>, the graph is a straight line.
If <math>E = 0</math>, then y does not appear at all, and the graph is either two vertical lines,
one vertical line, or empty.
We can also sketch the graph of any equation of the form
<math display="block">Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0.</math>
In the ordinary case where C and D are different from zero, the graph will be a
horizontal parabola.

5.5 ELLIPSES AND HYPERBOLAS
In this section we shall study two important types of curves, the ellipses and
hyperbolas. The intersection of a circular cone and a plane will always be either a
parabola, an ellipse, a hyperbola, or one of three degenerate cases—one line, two
lines, or a point. For this reason, parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas are called
conic sections. We begin with the definition of an ellipse in the plane.
DEFINITION OF ELLIPSE
Given two points, <math>F_1</math> and <math>F_2</math>, and a constant, <math>L</math>, the ellipse with foci <math>F_1</math> and
<math>F_2</math> and length L is the set of all points the sum of whose distances from <math>F_1</math>
and <math>F_2</math> is equal to <math>L</math>.
If the two foci <math>F_1</math> and <math>F_2</math> are the same, the ellipse is just the circle with center
at the focus and diameter L. Circles are discussed in Section 1.1.
We shall concentrate on the case where the foci <math>F_1</math> and <math>F_2</math> are different.
The ellipse will be an oval curve shown in Figure 5.5.1. The orbit of a planet is an
ellipse with the sun at one focus. The eye sees a tilted circle as an ellipse.
major axis
minor axis
<math>\overline{PF}_1 + \overline{PF}_2 = \text{length}</math>
Figure 5.5.1
Ellipse
The line through the foci <math>F_1</math> and <math>F_2</math> is called the <i>major axis</i> of the ellipse.
The point on the major axis halfway between the foci is called the center. The line
through the center perpendicular to the major axis is called the minor axis.
An ellipse is symmetric about both its major and its minor axes. That is,
for any point P on the ellipse, the mirror image of P on the other side of either axis
is also on the ellipse. The equation of an ellipse has a simple form when the major
and minor axes are chosen for the x-axis and y-axis.

We turn next to the hyperbola. A hyperbola, like an ellipse, has two foci.
However, the distances between the foci and a point on the hyperbola must have a
constant difference instead of a constant sum.

<b>DEFINITION OF HYPERBOLA</b>
Given two distinct points, <math>F_1</math> and <math>F_2</math>, and a constant, <math>I</math>, the hyperbola with
foci <math>F_1</math> and <math>F_2</math> and difference <math>l</math> is the set of all points the difference of whose
distances from <math>F_1</math> and <math>F_2</math> is equal to 1.
In this definition, <i>l</i> must be a positive number less than the distance between
the foci. A hyperbola will have two separate branches, each shaped like a rounded V.
On one branch the points are closer to <math>F_1</math> than <math>F_2</math>; and on the other branch they
are closer to <math>F_2</math> than <math>F_1</math>. Figure 5.5.6 shows a typical hyperbola. The path of a comet
on an orbit that will escape the solar system is a hyperbola with the sun at one focus.
The shadow of a cylindrical lampshade on a wall is a hyperbola (the section of the
light cone cut by the wall).
The line through the foci is the transverse axis of the hyperbola, and the
point on the axis midway between the foci is the center. The hyperbola crosses the
transverse axis at two points called the vertices. The line through the center perpen-
dicular to the transverse axis is the <i>conjugate axis</i>. The hyperbola never crosses its
conjugate axis. A hyperbola is symmetric about both axes. A simple equation is
obtained when the transverse and conjugate axes are chosen for the coordinate axes.

For any positive a and b, the graph of the equation
<math>\frac{y^2}{h^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2} = 1</math>
is a hyperbola with its center at the origin. Its transverse axis is the y-axis,

and its conjugate axis is the x-axis. The vertices are at <math>(0, \pm b)</math>, and the foci
are at <math>(0, \pm c)</math>, where c is found by
<math display="block">a^2 + b^2 = c^2.</math>
The graph of the equation
<math>\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{h^2} = 1</math>
is a hyperbola with similar properties with the roles of <math>x</math>, <math>a</math> and <math>y</math>, <math>b</math> reversed. The
proof of Theorem 2 uses a computation like the proof of Theorem 1 on ellipses
and is omitted.
Using derivatives and limits, we can get additional information that is
helpful in sketching the graph of a hyperbola. By solving the equation
<math>\frac{y^2}{h^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2} = 1</math>
for y as a function of x, we see that the upper and lower branches have the equations
upper branch: <math>y = \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{a^2 + x^2}</math>,
lower branch: <math>y = -\frac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}</math>.
We concentrate on the upper branch. Its first two derivatives, after some algebraic
simplification, come out to be
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{bx}{a \cdot \sqrt{a^2 + x^2}}, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = ab(a^2 + x^2)^{-3/2}.</math>
Thus the first derivative is zero only at <math>x = 0</math> (the vertex), and the second derivative
is always positive. We have the following table of values for the upper branch.

All the limit computations are easy except for <math>dy/dx</math>, which we work out for <math>x \to \infty</math>.
Let <i>H</i> be positive infinite.
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to \infty} dy/dx = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{bx}{a\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}}</math>
<math>= st \left[ \frac{bH}{a\sqrt{a^2 + H^2}} \right]</math>
<math display="block">= st \left[ \frac{b}{a \cdot \sqrt{a^2 H^{-2} + 1}} \right] = \frac{b}{a}.</math>

<math>= st \left| \frac{b(-H)}{a\sqrt{a^2 + (-H)^2}} \right|</math>

In fact, we shall show now that the lines
<math>y = bx/a, \qquad y = -bx/a</math>
are asymptotes of the hyperbola. That is, as x approaches <math>\infty</math> or <math>-\infty</math>, the distance
between the line and the hyperbola approaches zero. We show that the upper branch
approaches the line <math>y = bx/a</math> as <math>x \to \infty</math>; that is,
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to \infty} \left| \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{a^2 + x^2} - \frac{bx}{a} \right| = 0.</math>
Let H be positive infinite. Then
<math>\frac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2+H^2} - \frac{bH}{a} = \frac{b}{a}\left[\sqrt{a^2+H^2} - H\right]</math>

<math display="block">= \frac{b}{a} \frac{a^2 + H^2 - H^2}{\sqrt{a^2 + H^2} + H}</math>
<math>= ab(\sqrt{a^2 + H^2} + H)^{-1}.</math>

5.6 SECOND DEGREE CURVES
A second degree equation is an equation of the form
<math>Ax^{2} + Bxy + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0.</math>
<b>(1)</b>
The graph of such an equation will be a conic section: a parabola, ellipse, hyperbola,
or one of several degenerate cases. In Section 5.4 we saw that the graph of a second
degree equation of one of the forms
<math display="block">Ax^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0</math>
(2)
or
<math display="block">Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0</math>
(3)
is a parabola or degenerate. In Section 5.5 we saw that the graph of a second degree
equation of the form

## PDF page 283

5.6 SECOND DEGREE CURVES
273
<math display="block">Ax^2 + Cv^2 + F = 0</math>
<b>(4)</b>
is an ellipse, a hyperbola, or degenerate.
In this and the next section we shall see how to describe and sketch the
graph of any second degree equation. We will begin with the Discriminant Test,
which shows at once whether a nondegenerate curve is a parabola, ellipse, or
hyperbola. The next topic in this section will be translation of axes, which can change
any second degree equation with no xy-term,
<math>Ax^{2} + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0</math>
<b>(5)</b>
into an equation of one of the simple forms (2), (3), or (4).
In the following section we will study rotation of axes, which can change
any second degree equation into an equation of the form (5) with no xy-term. We
will then be able to deal with any second degree equation by using first rotation
and then translation of axes.
Here is the Discriminant Test.
DEFINITION
The quantity <math>B^2 - 4AC</math> is called the <b>discriminant</b> of the equation
<math>Ax^{2} + Bxy + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0.</math>
DISCRIMINANT TEST
If we ignore the degenerate cases, the graph of a second degree equation is:
A parabola if the discriminant is zero.
An ellipse if the discriminant is negative.
A hyperbola if the discriminant is positive.
For example, the equation
<math>xy - 1 = 0</math>
has positive discriminant <math>1^2 - 4 \cdot 0 = 1</math>, and its graph is a hyperbola. The equation
<math>2x^2 + xy + y^2 - 1 = 0</math>
has negative discriminant <math>1^2 - 4 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = -7</math>, and its graph is an ellipse.
The degenerate graphs that can arise are: two straight lines, one straight
line, one point, and the empty graph. The Discriminant Test alone does not tell
whether or not the graph is degenerate. However, a degenerate case can usually be
recognized when one tries to sketch the graph. For the remainder of this section
we shall ignore the degenerate cases.
We now turn to the method of Translation of Axes. This method is useful
for graphing a second degree equation with no xy-term,
<math>Ax^{2} + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0.</math>
If A or C is zero, the graph will be a horizontal or vertical parabola, which can be
graphed by the method of Section 5.4. If both <math>A</math> and <math>C</math> are nonzero, the graph turns
out to be an ellipse or hyperbola with horizontal and vertical axes X and Y, as in

The new axes are found using a procedure from algebra called "completing
the squares." This procedure changes an expression like <math>Ax^2 + Dx</math> into a perfect
square plus a constant.
FORMULA FOR COMPLETING THE SQUARES
Let A be different from zero. Then
<math display="block">Ax^2 + Dx = AX^2 + K,</math>
<math display="block">X = x + \frac{D}{2A}, \qquad K = \frac{-D^2}{4A}.</math>

5.7 ROTATION OF AXES
We have seen how to graph any second degree equation with no xy-term. These
graphs are parabolas, ellipses, or hyperbolas with vertical and horizontal axes.
When the equation has a nonzero xy-term, the graph will have diagonal axes. By
rotating the axes, one can get new coordinate axes in the proper direction. The
method will give us a new equation that has no xy-term and can be graphed by
our previous method.
Suppose the x and y axes are rotated counterclockwise by an angle <math>\alpha</math>, and
the new coordinate axes are called <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>, as in Figure 5.7.1. A point <math>P</math> in the
plane will have a pair of coordinates <math>(x, y)</math> in the old coordinate system and <math>(X, Y)</math>
in the new coordinate system. The old and new coordinates of P are related to each
other by the equations for rotation of axes.

THEOREM 1
Given a second degree equation
<math>Ax^{2} + Bxy + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0</math>
with B nonzero. Rotate the coordinate axes counterclockwise through an

Here is an overall summary of the use of rotations and translations of axes.
The problem is to graph an equation of the form
<math>Ax^{2} + Bxy + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0.</math>
By Rotation of Axes, we get a new equation of the simpler form
<math>A_1X^2 + C_1Y^2 + D_1X + E_1Y + F_1 = 0.</math>
If either <math>A_1 = 0</math> or <math>C_1 = 0</math>, the curve is a parabola that can be sketched by the method
of Section 5.4. If <math>A_1</math> and <math>C_1</math> are both nonzero, Translation of Axes gives us a new
equation of the simpler form
<math>A_2U^2 + B_2V^2 + F_2 = 0.</math>
The graph of this equation is an ellipse or hyperbola, which can be sketched by the
method of Section 5.5. The degenerate cases—two lines, one line, a point, or an
empty graph—may also occur.

5.8 THE <math>\epsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> CONDITION FOR LIMITS
The traditional calculus course is developed entirely without infinitesimals. The
starting point is the concept of a limit. The intuitive idea of <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L</math> is: For
every real number x which is close to but not equal to <math>c</math>, <math>f(x)</math> is close to <math>L</math>.
It is hard to make this idea into a rigorous definition, because one must clarify
the word "close". Indeed, the whole point of our infinitesimal approach to calculus is
that it is easier to define and explain limits using infinitesimals. The definition of
limits in terms of real numbers is traditionally expressed using the Greek letters
<math>\varepsilon</math> (epsilon) and <math>\delta</math> (delta), and is therefore called the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition for limits.
The <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition will be based on the notion of distance between two real
numbers.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
The distance between two real numbers x and c is the absolute value of their
difference,
<math>distance = |x - c|</math>.
<i>x</i> is within <math>\delta</math> of <i>c</i> if <math>|x - c| \le \delta</math>.
x is strictly within <math>\delta</math> of c if <math>|x-c| < \delta</math>.
Notice that the distance <math>|x-c|</math> is just the difference between the larger and
the smaller of the two numbers <math>x</math> and <math>c</math>. This is a place where the absolute value sign
is especially convenient. The following simple but helpful lemma is illustrated in
Figure 5.8.1.

Suppose the real function f is defined for all real numbers <math>x \neq c</math> in some
neighborhood of c.
<b>DEFINITION OF LIMIT (Repeated)</b>
The equation
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L</math>
means that whenever a hyperreal number <math>x</math> is infinitely close to but not equal
to <math>c</math>, <math>f(x)</math> is infinitely close to <math>L</math>.
<math>\epsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> CONDITION FOR <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L</math>
For every real number <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> there is a real number <math>\delta > 0</math> which depends on <math>\varepsilon</math>
such that whenever x is strictly within <math>\delta</math> of c but not equal to c, <math>f(x)</math> is strictly
within <math>\varepsilon</math> of L. In symbols, if <math>0 < |x - c| < \delta</math>, then <math>|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon</math>.

There are also <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> conditions for one-sided limits and infinite limits. The
three cases below are typical.
<math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> CONDITION FOR <math>\lim_{x\to\varepsilon^-} f(x) = L</math>
For every real number <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, there is a real number <math>\delta > 0</math> which depends on <math>\varepsilon</math>
such that whenever <math>c < x < c + \delta</math>, we have <math>|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon</math>.
Intuitively, when x is close to c but greater than <math>c, f(x)</math> is close to L.
<math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> CONDITION FOR <math>\lim_{x\to x} f(x) = L</math>
For every real number <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> there is a real number <math>B > 0</math> which depends on <math>\varepsilon</math>
such that whenever <math>x > B</math>, we have <math>|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon</math>.
Intuitively, when x is large, <math>f(x)</math> is close to L.
<math>\epsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> CONDITION FOR <math>\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = \infty</math>
For every real number <math>A > 0</math> there is a real number <math>B > 0</math> which depends on A
such that whenever <math>x > B</math>, we have <math>f(x) > A</math>.
Intuitively, when <math>x</math> is large, <math>f(x)</math> is large.
