We conclude this section with the proof that the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition is equivalent
to the infinitesimal definition of a limit.
THEOREM 1
Let f be defined in some deleted neighborhood of c. Then the following are
equivalent:
(i) <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L</math>.
(ii) The <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition for <math>\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L</math> is true.
<b>PROOF</b> We first assume the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition and prove that
<math display="block">\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L.</math>
Let <math>x</math> be any hyperreal number which is infinitely close but not equal to <math>c</math>.
To prove that <math>f(x)</math> is infinitely close to L we must show that
for every real <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, <math>|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon</math>.
Let <math>\varepsilon</math> be any positive real number, and let <math>\delta > 0</math> be the corresponding number
in the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition. Since x is infinitely close to c and <math>\delta > 0</math> is real, we have
<math>0 < |x - c| < \delta</math>.
By the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition and the Transfer Principle,
<math>|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon</math>.
We conclude that <math>f(x)</math> is infinitely close to L. This proves that
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L.</math>
For the other half of the proof we assume that
<math display="block">\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L,</math>
and prove the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition. This will be done by an indirect proof. Assume
that the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition is false for some real number <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>. That means that
for every real <math>\delta > 0</math> there is a real number <math>x = x(\delta)</math> such that
<math>x \neq c</math>, <math>|x - c| < \delta</math>, <math>|f(x) - L| \ge \varepsilon</math>.
<b>(1)</b>
Now let <math>\delta_1 > 0</math> be a positive infinitesimal. By the Transfer Principle,
Equation (1) holds for <math>\delta_1</math>. Therefore <math>x_1 = x(\delta_1)</math> is infinitely close but not

equal to c. But since
<math>|f(x_1) - L| \ge \varepsilon</math>
and <math>\varepsilon</math> is a positive real number, <math>f(x_1)</math> is not infinitely close to L. This con-
tradicts the equation
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L.</math>
We conclude that the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition must be true after all.
The theorem is also true for the other types of limits.
The concept of continuity can be described in terms of limits, as we saw in
Section 3.4. Therefore continuity can be defined in terms of the real number system
only.
COROLLARY
The following are equivalent.
(i) f is continuous at c.
(ii) For every real <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> there is a real <math>\delta > 0</math> depending on <math>\varepsilon</math> such that:
whenever <math>|x-c| < \delta</math>, <math>|f(x)-f(c)| < \varepsilon</math>.
PROOF Both (i) and (ii) are equivalent to
<math display="block">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c).</math>
Intuitively, this corollary says that f is continuous at c if and only if <math>f(x)</math> is
close to <math>f(c)</math> whenever x is close to c.

5.9 NEWTON'S METHOD
The Increment Theorem for derivatives shows that when <math>f'(c)</math> exists and <math>x \approx c</math>, <math>f(x)</math>
is infinitely close to the tangent line <math>f(c) + f'(c)(x - c)</math> even compared to <math>x - c</math>.
Thus intuitively, when x is real and close to <math>c, f(x)</math> is closely approximated by the
tangent line <math>f(c) + f'(c)(x - c)</math>. Newton's method uses the tangent line to
approximate a zero of <math>f(x)</math>. It is an iterative method that does not always work
but usually gives a very good approximation.
Consider a real function f that crosses the x-axis as in Figure 5.9.1. From the
graph we make a first rough approximation <math>x_1</math> to the zero of <math>f(x)</math>. To get a better
approximation, we take the tangent line at <math>x_1</math> and compute the point <math>x_2</math> where the
tangent line intersects the x-axis. At <math>x_2</math>, the curve <math>f(x)</math> is very close to zero, so we
take <math>x_2</math> as our new approximation. The tangent line has the equation
<math>y = f(x_1) + f'(x_1)(x - x_1).</math>
We get a formula for <math>x_2</math> by setting <math>y = 0</math> and <math>x = x_2</math> and then solving for <math>x_2</math>.

5.10 DERIVATIVES AND INCREMENTS
In Section 3.3 we found that the derivative of <math>f</math> is given by the limit
<math display="block">f'(c) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{f(c + \Delta x) - f(c)}{\Delta x}.</math>
<math>\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}</math>.
If <math>y = f(x)</math>,
By definition this means that when the hyperreal number <math>\Delta x</math> is infinitely close to
but not equal to zero, <math>\Delta y/\Delta x</math> is infinitely close to <math>dy/dx</math>.
By contrast, the <math>\varepsilon, \delta</math> condition for this limit says intuitively that when the
real number <math>\Delta x</math> is close to but not equal to zero, <math>\Delta y/\Delta x</math> is close to <math>dy/dx</math>.

5 LIMITS, ANALYTIC GEOMETRY, AND APPROXIMATIONS
The <math>\varepsilon, \delta</math> condition for the derivative is of theoretical importance but does
not give an error estimate for the limit. When the function <math>f</math> has a continuous second
derivative, we can get a useful error estimate in a different way. It is more convenient
to work with one-sided limits.
By an error estimate for a limit
<math display="block">\lim_{\Delta x \to 0^+} g(\Delta x) = L</math>
we mean a real function <math>E(\Delta x)</math>, <math>0 < \Delta x \le b</math>, such that the approximation <math>g(\Delta x)</math>
is always within <math>E(\Delta x)</math> of the limit L. In symbols,
<math>|g(\Delta x) - L| \le E(\Delta x)</math> for <math>0 < \Delta x \le b</math>.
THEOREM 1
Suppose f has a continuous second derivative and <math>|f''(t)| \leq M</math> for all t in the
interval [c, b]. Then:
Whenever <math>c < c + \Delta x \le b</math>, <math>f(c + \Delta x)</math> is within <math>\frac{1}{2}M \Delta x^2</math> of <math>f(c) + f'(c) \Delta x</math>.
(i)
(ii) Whenever <math>c < c + \Delta x \le b</math>, <math>\frac{f(c + \Delta x) - f(c)}{\Delta x}</math> is within <math>\frac{1}{2}M \Delta x</math> of
<math>f'(c)</math>. That is, <math>\frac{1}{2}M \Delta x</math> is an error estimate for the right-sided limit
<math display="block">\lim_{\Delta x \to 0+} \frac{f(c + \Delta x) - f(c)}{\Delta x} = f'(c).</math>
There is a similar theorem for the left-sided limit
<math display="block">\lim_{\Delta x \to 0^{-}} \frac{f(c + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} = f'(c)</math>
with the error estimate <math>\frac{1}{2}M[\Delta x]</math>.
<i>PROOF</i> Let <math>x = c + \Delta x</math>. Then
<math>-M \le f''(t) \le M</math> for <math>c \le t \le x</math>.
Integrating from <math>c</math> to <math>t</math>,
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{t} -M dt \leq \int_{0}^{t} f''(t) dt \leq \int_{0}^{t} M dt,</math>
<math display="block">-M(t-c) \le f'(t) - f'(c) \le M(t-c).</math>
Integrating again from <math>c</math> to <math>x</math>,
<math display="block">\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} -M(t-c) dt \le \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f'(t) - f'(c) dt \le \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} M(t-c) dt,</math>
<math display="block">-M\frac{(x-c)^2}{2} \le f(t) - f'(c)t \bigg|^x \le M\frac{(x-c)^2}{2},</math>
<math display="block">-M\frac{\Delta x^2}{2} \le (f(x) - f(c)) - f'(c)\Delta x \le M\frac{\Delta x^2}{2},</math>
or
<math display="block">-M\frac{\Delta x^2}{2} \le f(x) - (f(c) + f'(c)\Delta x) \le M\frac{\Delta x^2}{2}.</math>

We shall now turn the problem around. Instead of using the increment <math>\Delta y</math>
to approximate the derivative <math>dy/dx</math>, we shall use the derivative <math>dy/dx</math> to approximate
the increment <math>\Delta y</math>. When <math>\Delta x</math> is small, <math>f(c + \Delta x)</math> will be close to <math>f(c) + f'(c) \Delta x</math> even
compared to <math>\Delta x</math>. Part (i) of Theorem 1 gives the error estimate <math>\frac{1}{2}M \Delta x^2</math> for this
approximation. This method is especially useful for approximating <math>f(x)</math> when there
is a number c close to x such that both <math>f(c)</math> and <math>f'(c)</math> are known.

5.10 DERIVATIVES AND INCREMENTS
INCREMENT THEOREM (Repeated)
Hypotheses <math>f'(c)</math> exists and <math>\Delta x</math> is infinitesimal.
Conclusion <math>f(c + \Delta x) = f(c) + f'(c) \Delta x + \varepsilon \Delta x</math> for some infinitesimal <math>\varepsilon</math> which
depends on c and <math>\Delta x</math>.
THEOREM 1 OF THIS SECTION (in an equivalent form)
Hypotheses <math>f''(u)</math> exists and <math>|f''(u)| \leq M</math> for all u between the real numbers c and
<math>c + \Delta x</math>.
Conclusion <math>f(c + \Delta x) = f(c) + f'(c) \Delta x + \varepsilon \Delta x</math> for some real <math>\varepsilon</math> within <math>\frac{1}{2}M|\Delta x|</math> of 0.
Thus Theorem 1 has more hypotheses but also gives more specific information
about <math>\varepsilon</math> in its conclusion.

6.1 INFINITE SUM THEOREM
In Chapter 4 we obtained the formula
Area = <math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx</math>

In this chapter we shall obtain integral formulas for several other quantities
arising in geometry and physics, such as volumes, curve lengths, and work. We begin
with the Infinite Sum Theorem, which will be useful in justifying these formulas. It
tells when a given function <math>B(a, b)</math> is equal to the definite integral <math>\int_a^b h(x) dx</math>.
Any two infinitesimals are infinitely close to each other. The following
definition helps us to keep track of how close to each other they are.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
Let <math>\varepsilon, \delta</math> be infinitesimals and let <math>\Delta x</math> be a nonzero infinitesimal. We say that
<math>\varepsilon</math> is infinitely close to <math>\delta</math> compared to <math>\Delta x</math>,
<math>\varepsilon \approx \delta</math> (compared to <math>\Delta x</math>), if <math>\varepsilon/\Delta x \approx \delta/\Delta x</math>.
In Figure 6.1.1, an infinitesimal microscope within an infinitesimal micro-
scope is used to show <math>\varepsilon \approx \delta</math> (compared to <math>\Delta x</math>).
For example, <math>3 \Delta x + 5 \Delta x^2 \approx 3 \Delta x - \Delta x^2 + \Delta x^3</math> (compared to <math>\Delta x</math>)
<math>3 \Delta x + 5 \Delta x^2 \approx 2 \Delta x</math> (compared to <math>\Delta x</math>).

INFINITE SUM THEOREM
Let B(u, w) be a real function of two variables that has the Addition Property
in the interval <math>[a, b]</math>—i.e.,
<math>B(u, w) = B(u, v) + B(v, w)</math> for <math>u < v < w</math> in <math>[a, b]</math>.
Suppose <math>h(x)</math> is a real function continuous on <math>[a, b]</math> and for any infinitesimal
subinterval <math>[x, x + \Delta x]</math> of <math>[a, b]</math>,
<math>\Delta B \approx h(x) \Delta x</math> (compared to <math>\Delta x</math>).
Then <math>B(a, b)</math> is equal to the integral
<math display="block">B(a,b) = \int_a^b h(x) \, dx.</math>
Intuitively, the theorem says that if each infinitely small piece <math>\Delta B</math> is infinitely
close to <math>h(x) \Delta x</math> compared to <math>\Delta x</math>, then the sum <math>B(a, b)</math> of all these pieces is infinitely
close to <math>\sum_{a}^{b} h(x) \Delta x</math> (Figure 6.1.2). This is why we call it the Infinite Sum Theorem.

6.1 INFINITE SUM THEOREM
Place the pyramid on its side with the apex at <math>x = 0</math> and the base at <math>x = h</math>.
We use the fact that at any point <math>x</math> between 0 and <math>h</math>, the cross section has
area proportional to <math>x^2</math>, so that
<math display="block">\frac{A(x)}{x^2} = \frac{B}{h^2},</math>
<math display="block">A(x) = \frac{Bx^2}{h^2}.</math>
The volume is then
<math display="block">V = \int_0^h \frac{Bx^2}{h^2} dx = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{Bx^3}{h^2} \bigg|_0^h = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{Bh^3}{h^2} = \frac{1}{3} Bh.</math>
The solution is <math>V = (\frac{1}{3})Bh</math>.

We shall work with the region under a curve and the region between two

the usual formula for the volume of a right circular cylinder (Figure 6.2.2).

The circle of radius r and center at the origin has the equation
<math>x^2 + y^2 = r^2</math>.
The region R inside this circle in the first quadrant will generate a hemisphere
of radius <math>r</math> when it is rotated about the <math>x</math>-axis (Figure 6.2.14).

First take x as the independent variable and use the Disc Method. R is the
region under the curve
<math display="block">y = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}, \qquad 0 \le x \le r.</math>
The hemisphere has volume
<math display="block">\frac{1}{2}V = \int_0^x \pi(f(x))^2 dx</math>
<math display="block">= \int_0^r \pi(r^2 - x^2) dx = \pi r^2 x - \frac{1}{3}\pi x^3 \bigg|_0^r</math>
<math>=\pi r^3 - \frac{1}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3.</math>
Therefore the sphere has volume
<math>V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3</math>.
Now take y as the independent variable and use the Cylindrical Shell Method.
R is the region under the curve
<math display="block">x = \sqrt{r^2 - y^2}, \qquad 0 \le y \le r.</math>
The hemisphere has volume
<math display="block">\frac{1}{2}V = \int_0^r 2\pi y \sqrt{r^2 - y^2} \, dy.</math>

assign a length to a segment of a smooth curve.

<b>DEFINITION</b>
Assume the function <math>y = f(x)</math> has a continuous derivative for x in [a, b], that is,
the curve
<math>y = f(x), \quad a \le x \le b</math>
is smooth. The length of the curve is defined as
<math display="block">s = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + (dy/dx)^2} \, dx.</math>
Because <math>\sqrt{1 + (dy/dx)^2} dx = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}</math>, the equation is sometimes
<math display="block">s = \int_{-\infty}^{b} \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}</math>
written in the form
with the understanding that <math>x</math> is the independent variable. The length <math>s</math> is always
greater than or equal to 0 because <math>a < b</math> and
<math>\sqrt{1 + (dy/dx)^2} > 0.</math>
JUSTIFICATION Let <math>s(u, w)</math> be the intuitive length of the curve between <math>t = u</math> and
<math>t = w</math>. The function <math>s(u, w)</math> has the Addition Property; the length of the
curve from <math>u</math> to <math>w</math> equals the length from <math>u</math> to <math>v</math> plus the length from <math>v</math> to <math>w</math>.
Figure 6.3.2 shows an infinitesimal piece of the curve from x to <math>x + \Delta x</math>. Its
length is <math>\Delta s = s(x, x + \Delta x)</math>.

The slope <math>dy/dx</math> is a continuous function of x, and therefore changes only by

<math display="block">s = \int_a^b \sqrt{(dx/dy)^2 + 1} \, dy.</math>

We next prove a theorem which shows the connection between the length of
an arc and the area of a sector of a circle. Given two points P and Q on a circle with
center O, the arc PQ is the portion of the circle traced out by a point moving from P
to <math>Q</math> in a counterclockwise direction. The sector <math>POQ</math> is the region bounded by the
arc PQ and the radii OP and OQ as shown in Figure 6.3.7.

<b>THEOREM</b>
Let P and Q be two points on a circle with center O. The area A of the sector
<i>POQ</i> is equal to one half the radius r times the length s of the arc PQ,
<math>A = \frac{1}{2}rs</math>.
The theorem is intuitively plausible because if we consider an
DISCUSSION
infinitely small arc <math>\Delta s</math> of the circle as in Figure 6.3.8, then the corresponding
sector is almost a triangle of height r and base <math>\Delta s</math>, so it has area

Figure 6.3.8
We can derive the formula <math>C = 2\pi r</math> for the circumference of a circle using the
theorem. By definition, <math>\pi</math> is the area of a circle of radius one,
<math display="block">\pi = \int_{-1}^{1} 2\sqrt{1 - y^2} \, dy.</math>
Then a circle of radius r has area
<math display="block">A = \int_{-r}^{r} 2\sqrt{r^2 - y^2} \, dy = \int_{-1}^{1} 2r^2 \sqrt{1 - (y/r)^2} \, d(y/r) = \pi r^2.</math>
Therefore the circumference C is given by
<math>A = \frac{1}{2}rC, \qquad \pi r^2 = \frac{1}{2}rC, \qquad C = 2\pi r.</math>

Cone frustum
Figure 6.4.4
Figure 6.4.4 shows the frustum of a cone with smaller radius <math>r_1</math>, larger radius
<math>r_2</math>, and slant height l. The formula for the area of the lateral surface of a frustum of a
cone is
lateral area of frustum = <math>\pi(r_1 + r_2)l</math>.
This formula is justified as follows. The frustum is formed by removing
a cone of radius <math>r_1</math> and slant height <math>l_1</math> from a cone of radius <math>r_2</math> and slant height <math>l_2</math>.
The frustum therefore has lateral area
<math>A = \pi r_1 l_2 - \pi r_1 l_1</math>.
The slant heights are proportional to the radii,
<math>\frac{l_1}{r} = \frac{l_2}{r}</math>, so <math>r_1 l_2 = r_2 l_1</math>.
The slant height <i>l</i> of the frustum is
<math>l = l_2 - l_1</math>.
Using the last two equations,
<math display="block">\pi(r_1 + r_2)l = \pi(r_2 + r_1)(l_2 - l_1)</math>
<math>=\pi(r_2l_2+r_1l_2-r_2l_1-r_5l_1)</math>
<math>= \pi r_2 l_2 - \pi r_1 l_1 = A.</math>

curve segment
<math>y = f(x), \quad a \le x \le b</math>

surface of revolution (Figure 6.4.5).
Here is the formula for the area.

In finding a formula for surface area, why did we divide the surface into
frustums of cones instead of into cylinders (as we did for volumes)? The reason is that
to use the Infinite Sum Theorem we need something which is infinitely close to a small
piece <math>\Delta A</math> of area compared to <math>\Delta x</math>. The small frustum has area
<math>(2x + \Delta x)\pi \Delta s</math>
which is infinitely close to <math>\Delta A</math> compared to <math>\Delta x</math> because it almost has the same shape
as <math>\Delta A</math> (Figure 6.4.9). The small cylinder has area <math>2x\pi \Delta y</math>. While this area is infi-
nitesimal, it is not infinitely close to <math>\Delta A</math> compared to <math>\Delta x</math>, because on dividing by <math>\Delta x</math>
we get
<math display="block">\frac{\text{area of frustum}}{\Delta x} = 2x\pi \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta x} + \pi \Delta x \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta x} \approx 2x\pi \frac{ds}{dx},</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\text{area of cylinder}}{\Delta x} = 2x\pi \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} \approx 2x\pi \frac{dy}{dx}.</math>

6.5 AVERAGES
Given n numbers <math>y_1, \ldots, y_n</math>, their average value is defined as
<math display="block">y_{\text{ave}} = \frac{y_1 + \dots + y_n}{n}.</math>
If all the <math>y_i</math> are replaced by the average value <math>y_{ave}</math>, the sum will be unchanged,
<math>y_1 + \cdots + y_n = y_{ave} + \cdots + y_{ave} = ny_{ave}</math>.
If <math>f</math> is a continuous function on a closed interval <math>[a, b]</math>, what is meant by the
average value of <math>f</math> between <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> (Figure 6.5.1)? Let us try to imitate the procedure
for finding the average of <math>n</math> numbers. Take an infinite hyperreal number <math>H</math> and
divide the interval <math>[a, b]</math> into infinitesimal subintervals of length <math>dx = (b - a)/H</math>. Let

us "sample" the value of f at the H points <math>a, a + dx, a + 2 dx, \dots, a + (H-1) dx</math>.
Then the average value of <math>f</math> should be infinitely close to the sum of the values of <math>f</math>
at <math>a, a + dx, \dots, a + (H - 1) dx</math>, divided by H. Thus
<math>f_{\text{ave}} \approx \frac{f(a) + f(a + dx) + f(a + 2 dx) + \dots + f(a + (H - 1) dx)}{H}.</math>
Since <math>dx = \frac{b-a}{H}</math>, <math>\frac{1}{H} = \frac{dx}{b-a}</math> and we have
<math display="block">f_{\text{ave}} \approx \frac{f(a) dx + f(a + dx) dx + \dots + f(a + (H - 1) dx) dx}{b - a},</math>
<math>f_{\text{ave}} \approx \frac{\sum_{a}^{b} f(x) dx}{b - a}</math>.
Taking standard parts, we are led to
<b>DEFINITION</b>
Let <math>f</math> be continuous on <math>[a, b]</math>. The average value of <math>f</math> between <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> is
<math display="block">f_{\text{ave}} = \frac{\int_a^b f(x) \, dx}{b - a}.</math>
Geometrically, the area under the curve <math>y = f(x)</math> is equal to the area under
the constant curve <math>y = f_{ave}</math> between a and b,
<math>f_{\text{ave}} \cdot (b - a) = \int_a^b f(x) \, dx.</math>
Find the average value of <math>y = \sqrt{x}</math> from <math>x = 1</math> to <math>x = 4</math> (Figure 6.5.2).
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b>
<math>y_{\text{ave}} = \frac{\int_{1}^{4} \sqrt{x} \, dx}{(4-1)} = \frac{\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2} \Big]_{1}^{4}}{3} = \frac{\frac{2}{3}(8-1)}{3} = \frac{14}{9}.</math>

Recall that in Section 3.8, we defined the average slope of a function F
between a and b as the quotient
average slope = <math>\frac{F(b) - F(a)}{b - a}</math>.
Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus we can find the connection between
the average value of <math>F'</math> and the average slope of <math>F</math>.
THEOREM 1
Let F be an antiderivative of a continuous function f on an open interval I.
Then for any <math>a < b</math> in I, the average slope of F between a and b is equal to
the average value of f between a and b,
<math display="block">\frac{F(b) - F(a)}{b - a} = \frac{\int_a^b f(x) dx}{b - a}.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> By the Fundamental Theorem,
<math display="block">F(b) - F(a) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx.</math>
THEOREM 2 (Mean Value Theorem for Integrals)
Let f be continuous on [a, b]. Then there is a point c strictly between a and b
where the value of f is equal to its average value,
<math display="block">f(c) = \frac{\int_a^b f(x) \, dx}{b}.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> Theorem 2 is illustrated in Figure 6.5.3. We can make <math>f</math> continuous on the
whole real line by defining <math>f(x) = f(a)</math> for <math>x < a</math> and <math>f(x) = f(b)</math> for <math>x > b</math>.
By the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, f has an antiderivative F.
By the Mean Value Theorem there is a point c strictly between a and b at
which <math>F'(c)</math> is equal to the average slope of <math>F</math>,
<math display="block">F'(c) = \frac{F(b) - F(a)}{b - a}.</math>
But <math>F'(c) = f(c)</math> and <math>F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b f(x) dx</math>, so
<math display="block">f(c) = \frac{\int_a^b f(x) \, dx}{b - a}.</math>

6.5 AVERAGES
A car starts at rest and moves with velocity <math>v = 3t^2</math>. Find its average
EXAMPLE 2
velocity between times <math>t = 0</math> and <math>t = 5</math>. At what point of time is its velocity
equal to the average velocity?
<math>v_{\text{ave}} = \frac{\int_0^3 3t^2 dt}{5 - 0} = \frac{t^3 \int_0^3}{5} = \frac{125}{5} = 25.</math>
To find the value of t where <math>v = v_{ave}</math>, we put
<math>3t^2 = 25</math>, <math>t = \sqrt{25/3} = 5/\sqrt{3}</math>.
Suppose a car drives from city A to city B and back, a distance of 120 miles
each way. From A to B it travels at a speed of 30 mph, and on the return trip it travels
at 60 mph. What is the average speed?
If we choose distance as the independent variable we get one answer, and if we
choose time we get another.
Average speed with respect to time: The car takes <math>120/30 = 4</math> hours to go
from A to B and <math>120/60 = 2</math> hours to return to A. The total trip takes 6 hours.
<math>v_{\text{ave}} = \frac{30 \cdot 4 + 60 \cdot 2}{6} = \frac{240}{6} = 40 \text{ mph.}</math>
Average speed with respect to distance: The car goes 120 miles at 30 mph
and 120 miles at 60 mph, with a total distance of 240 miles. Therefore
<math>v_{\text{ave}} = \frac{30 \cdot 120 + 60 \cdot 120}{240} = 45 \text{ mph.}</math>
From Figure 6.5.4 we see that the average with respect to time is smaller
because most of the time was spent at the lower speed of 30 mph.

6.6 SOME APPLICATIONS TO PHYSICS
The Infinite Sum Theorem can frequently be used to derive formulas in physics.
1 MASS AND DENSITY, ONE DIMENSION
Consider a one-dimensional object such as a length of wire. We ignore the atomic
nature of matter and assume that it is distributed continuously along a line seg-
ment. If the density <math>\rho</math> per unit length is the same at each point of the wire, then the
mass is the product of the density and the length, <math>m = \rho L</math>. If L is in centimeters and <math>\rho</math>
in grams per centimeter, then m is in grams. (<math>\rho</math> is the Greek letter "rho".)
Now suppose that the density of the wire varies continuously with the posi-
tion. Put the wire on the x-axis between the points <math>x = a</math> and <math>x = b</math>, and let the
density at the point x be <math>\rho(x)</math>. Consider the piece of the wire of infinitesimal length
<math>\Delta x</math> and mass <math>\Delta m</math> shown in Figure 6.6.1. At each point between x and <math>x + \Delta x</math>, the
density is infinitely close to <math>\rho(x)</math>, so
<math>\Delta m \approx \rho(x) \Delta x</math>
(compared to <math>\Delta x</math>).

<b>EXAMPLE 2</b> A circular disc of radius r has density at each point equal to the distance
of the point from the y-axis. Find its mass. (The center of the circle, shown in
Figure 6.6.4, is at the origin.) The circle is the region between the curves
<math>-\sqrt{r^2-x^2}</math> and <math>\sqrt{r^2-x^2}</math> from <math>-r</math> to r. The density at a point <math>(x, y)</math> in the
disc is <math>|x|</math>. By symmetry, all four quadrants have the same mass. We shall
find the mass <math>m_1</math> of the first quadrant and multiply by four.
<math>m_1 = \int_0^r \sqrt{r^2 - x^2} \, x \, dx.</math>
Put <math>u = r^2 - x^2</math>, <math>du = -2x dx</math>; <math>u = r^2</math> when <math>x = 0</math>, and <math>u = 0</math> when <math>x = r</math>.
<math display="block">m_1 = \int_{r^2}^0 -\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{u} \, du = \frac{1}{2} \int_0^{r^2} \sqrt{u} \, du = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3} u^{3/2} \bigg|_0^{r^2} = \frac{1}{3} r^3.</math>
Then <math>m = 4m_1 = \frac{4}{3}r^3</math>.

For example, a 60 lb child 6 feet from the fulcrum will balance a 40 lb child 9 feet
from the fulcrum, <math>60 \cdot 6 = 40 \cdot 9</math>. If the fulcrum is at the origin <math>x = 0</math>, the masses <math>m_1</math>
and <math>m_2</math> have coordinates <math>x_1 = -d_1</math> and <math>x_2 = d_2</math>. The equation for balancing becomes
<math>m_1x_1 + m_2x_2 = 0.</math>
Similarly, finitely many masses <math>m_1, \ldots, m_k</math> at the points <math>x_1, \ldots, x_k</math> will balance about
the point <math>x = 0</math> if
<math display="block">m_1 x_1 + \cdots + m_k x_k = 0.</math>
Given a mass <math>m</math> at the point <math>x</math>, the quantity <math>mx</math> is called the moment about the origin.

6 APPLICATIONS OF THE INTEGRAL
The moment of a finite collection of point masses <math>m_1, \ldots, m_k</math> at <math>x_1, \ldots, x_k</math>
about the origin is defined as the sum
<math>M = m_1 x_1 + \cdots + m_k x_k</math>
Suppose the point masses are rigidly connected to a rod of mass zero. If the moment
M is equal to zero, the masses will balance at the origin. In general they will balance
at a point <math>\bar{x}</math> called the center of gravity (Figure 6.6.6). <math>\bar{x}</math> is equal to the moment divided
by the total mass <math>m</math>,
<math display="block">\bar{x} = \frac{M}{m} = \frac{m_1 x_1 + \dots + m_k x_k}{m_1 + \dots + m_k}.</math>
Since the mass m is positive, the moment M has the same sign as the center of gravity <math>\bar{x}</math>.

Now consider a length of wire between <math>x = a</math> and <math>x = b</math> whose density at
x is <math>\rho(x)</math>. The moment of the wire about the origin is defined as the integral
<math display="block">M = \int_{-\infty}^{b} x \rho(x) \, dx.</math>
This formula is justified by considering a piece of the wire of infinitesimal length <math>\Delta x</math>.
On the piece from x to <math>x + \Delta x</math> the density remains infinitely close to <math>\rho(x)</math>. Thus if
<math>\Delta M</math> is the moment of the piece,
<math>\Delta M \approx x \, \Delta m \approx x \rho(x) \, \Delta x</math> (compared to <math>\Delta x</math>).
The moment of an object is equal to the sum of the moments of its parts. Hence by
the Infinite Sum Theorem,
<math display="block">M = \int_{-\infty}^{b} x \rho(x) \, dx.</math>
If the wire has moment M about the origin and mass m, the center of mass
of the wire is defined as the point
<math>\bar{x} = M/m</math>.
A point of mass m located at <math>\bar{x}</math> has the same moment about the origin as the whole
wire, <math>M = \bar{x}m</math>. Physically, the wire will balance on a fulcrum placed at the center of
mass.
A wire between <math>x = 0</math> and <math>x = 1</math> has density <math>\rho(x) = x^2</math> (Figure 6.6.7).
<b>EXAMPLE 3</b>
The moment is
<math>M = \int_0^1 x^2 x \, dx = \frac{x^4}{4} \Big|_0^1 = \frac{1}{4}.</math>

The center of mass of a two-dimensional object is defined as the point <math>(\bar{x}, \bar{y})</math>
with coordinates
<math>\bar{x} = M_y/m, \quad \bar{y} = M_x/m.</math>

body, <math>M_x = m\bar{y}</math>, <math>M_y = m\bar{x}</math>. The object will balance on a pin placed at the center of
mass.
If a two-dimensional object has constant density, the center of mass depends
only on the region R which it occupies. The centroid of a region R is defined as the
center of mass of an object of constant density which occupies R. Thus if R is the
region below the continuous curve <math>y = f(x)</math> from <math>x = a</math> to <math>x = b</math>, then the centroid
has coordinates
<math>\overline{x} = \int_a^b x f(x) dx/A, \qquad \overline{y} = \int_a^b \frac{1}{2} f(x)^2 dx/A,</math>
where A is the area <math>A = \int_a^b f(x) dx</math>.

The following principle often simplifies a problem in moments.
If an object is symmetrical about an axis, then its moment about that axis is
zero and its center of mass lies on the axis.
PROOF Consider the y-axis. Suppose a plane object occupies the region under the
curve <math>y = f(y)</math> from <math>-a</math> to <math>a</math> and its density at a point <math>(x, y)</math> is <math>\rho(x)</math> (Figure
6.6.12). The object is symmetric about the y-axis, so for all x between 0 and <math>\vec{a}</math>,
<math>f(-x) = f(x), \qquad \rho(-x) = \rho(x).</math>
Then <math>M_y = \int_{-a}^a x f(x) \rho(x) dx = \int_{-a}^0 x f(x) \rho(x) dx + \int_0^a x f(x) \rho(x) dx</math>
<math display="block">= \int_{-\infty}^{0} (-x)f(-x)\rho(-x) d(-x) + \int_{0}^{a} xf(x)\rho(x) dx = 0.</math>
Also, <math>\bar{x} = M_v/m = 0</math>.

5 WORK
A constant force F acting along a straight line for a distance s requires the amount of
work
<math>W = Fs</math>.
For example, the force of gravity on an object of mass m near the surface of the
earth is very nearly a constant g times the mass, <math>F = gm</math>. Thus to lift an object of mass
<math>m</math> a distance <math>s</math> against gravity requires the work <math>W = gms</math>. The following principle is
useful in computing work done against gravity.
The amount of work done against gravity to move an object is the same as it
would be if all the mass were concentrated at the center of mass. Moreover,
the work against gravity depends only on the vertical change in position of the
center of mass, not on the actual path of its motion.
That is, <math>W = gms</math> where s is the vertical change in the center of mass.

To justify this formula we consider an infinitesimal length <math>\Delta s</math>. On the interval
from s to <math>s + \Delta s</math> the force is infinitely close to <math>F(s)</math>, so the work <math>\Delta W</math> done on this
interval satisfies
<math>\Delta W \approx F(s) \Delta s</math> (compared to <math>\Delta s</math>).
By the Infinite Sum Theorem,
<math display="block">W = \int_{a}^{b} F(s) \, ds.</math>

6.7 IMPROPER INTEGRALS
What is the area of the region under the curve <math>y = 1/\sqrt{x}</math> from <math>x = 0</math> to <math>x = 1</math>
(Figure 6.7.1(a))? The function <math>1/\sqrt{x}</math> is not continuous at <math>\dot{x} = 0</math>, and in fact <math>1/\sqrt{\varepsilon}</math> is
infinite for infinitesimal <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>. Thus our notion of a definite integral does not apply.
Nevertheless we shall be able to assign an area to the region using improper integrals.
We see from the figure that the region extends infinitely far up in the vertical direction.
However, it becomes so thin that the area of the region turns out to be finite.

6 APPLICATIONS OF THE INTEGRAL
extends infinitely far in the horizontal direction. We shall see that this region, too,
has a finite area which is given by an improper integral.
Improper integrals are defined as follows.
DEFINITION
Suppose f is continuous on the half-open interval (a, b]. The improper integral
of f from a to b is defined by the limit
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) dx = \lim_{u \to a^+} \int_u^b f(x) dx.</math>
If the limit exists the improper integral is said to converge. Otherwise the
improper integral is said to diverge.
The improper integral can also be described in terms of definite integrals
with hyperreal endpoints. We first recall that the definite integral
<math display="block">D(u,v) = \int_{-\infty}^{v} f(x) \, dx</math>
is a real function of two variables <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>. If <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> vary over the hyperreal numbers
instead of the real numbers, the definite integral <math>\int_{u}^{v} f(x) dx</math> stands for the natural
extension of <math>D</math> evaluated at <math>(u, v)</math>,
<math display="block">D^*(u,v) = \int^v f(x) \, dx.</math>
Here is the description of the improper integral using definite integrals with hyperreal
endpoints.
Let <math>f</math> be continuous on <math>(a, b]</math>.
(1) <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx = S</math> if and only if <math>\int_{a+\varepsilon}^b f(x) dx \approx S</math> for all positive infinite-
simal <math>\varepsilon</math>.
(2) <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx = \infty</math> (or <math>-\infty</math>) if and only if <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math> is positive infinite
(or negative infinite) for all positive infinitesimal <math>\varepsilon</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> Find <math>\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} dx</math>. For <math>u > 0</math>,
<math display="block">\int_{u}^{1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} dx = 2\sqrt{x} \bigg]_{u}^{1} = 2 - 2\sqrt{u}.</math>
<math display="block">\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} dx = \lim_{u \to 0^+} \int_u^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} dx = \lim_{u \to 0^+} (2 - 2\sqrt{u}) = 2.</math>
Then
Therefore the region under the curve <math>y = 1/\sqrt{x}</math> from 0 to 1 shown in Figure
6.7.1(a) has area 2, and the improper integral converges.

Notice that we use the same symbol for both the definite and the improper
integral. The theorem below justifies this practice.
THEOREM 1
If f is continuous on the closed interval <math>[a, b]</math> then the improper integral of f
from a to b converges and equals the definite integral of f from a to b.
PROOF We have shown in Section 4.2 on the Fundamental Theorem that the
function
<math display="block">F(u) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx</math>
is continuous on <math>[a, b]</math>. Therefore
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx = \lim_{u \to a^{+}} \int_{u}^{a} f(x) dx,</math>
where <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math> denotes the definite integral.
We now define a second kind of improper integral where the interval is
infinite.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
Let f be continuous on the half-open interval <math>[a, \infty)</math>. The improper integral
of f from a to <math>\infty</math> is defined by the limit
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{\infty} f(x) dx = \lim_{u \to \infty} \int_{a}^{u} f(x) dx.</math>
The improper integral is said to converge if the limit exists and to diverge
otherwise.
Here is a description of this kind of improper integral using definite integrals
with hyperreal endpoints.
Let f be continuous on <math>[a, \infty)</math>.
(1) <math>\int_a^{\infty} f(x) dx = S</math> if and only if <math>\int_a^H f(x) dx \approx S</math> for all positive infinite <math>H</math>.

There are other types of improper integrals. If f is continuous on the half-open
interval [a, b) then we define
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \lim_{u \to b^-} \int_a^u f(x) \, dx.</math>
If f is continuous on <math>(-\infty, b]</math> we define
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx = \lim_{u \to -\infty} \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx.</math>

By piecing together improper integrals of these four types we can assign an improper
integral to most functions which arise in calculus.
DEFINITION
A function f is said to be <b>piecewise continuous</b> on an interval I if f is defined
and continuous at all but perhaps finitely many points of I. In particular, every
continuous function is piecewise continuous.
We can introduce the improper integral <math>\int_a^b f(x) dx</math> whenever f is piecewise
continuous on I and a, b are either the endpoints of I or the appropriate infinity
symbol. A few examples will show how this can be done.
Let <math>f</math> be continuous at every point of the closed interval <math>[a, b]</math> except at one
point <math>c</math> where <math>a < c < b</math>. We define
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \int_a^c f(x) \, dx + \int_a^b f(x) \, dx.</math>

Then

Similarly,

If f is continuous on the open interval <math>(a, b)</math>, the improper integral is defined
as the sum
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) dx = \int_a^c f(x) dx + \int_a^b f(x) dx,</math>
where <math>c</math> is any point in the interval <math>(a, b)</math>. The endpoints <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> may be finite or infinite.
It does not matter which point <math>c</math> is chosen, because if <math>e</math> is any other point in <math>(a, b)</math>, then
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{c} f(x) \, dx + \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = \int_{a}^{c} f(x) \, dx + \left( \int_{a}^{e} f(x) \, dx + \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx \right)</math>
<math display="block">= \left( \int_{a}^{c} f(x) dx + \int_{a}^{e} f(x) dx \right) + \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx</math>
<math display="block">= \int_a^e f(x) dx + \int_a^b f(x) dx.</math>

7.1 TRIGONOMETRY
In this chapter we shall study the trigonometric functions, i.e., the sine and cosine
function and other functions that are built up from them. Let us start from the
beginning and introduce the basic concepts of trigonometry.
The unit circle <math>x^2 + y^2 = 1</math> has radius 1 and center at the origin.
Two points P and Q on the unit circle determine an arc <math>PQ</math>, an angle <math>\angle POQ</math>,
and a sector POQ. The arc starts at P and goes counterclockwise to Q along the
circle. The sector <math>POQ</math> is the region bounded by the arc <math>\widehat{PQ}</math> and the lines <math>OP</math> and <math>OQ</math>.
As Figure 7.1.1 shows, the arcs <math>\widehat{PQ}</math> and <math>\widehat{QP}</math> are different.

Trigonometry is based on the notion of the length of an arc. Lengths of
curves were introduced in Section 6.3. Although that section provides a useful
background, this chapter can also be studied independently of Chapter 6. As a starting
point we shall give a formula for the length of an arc in terms of the area of a sector.
(This formula was proved as a theorem in Section 6.3 but can also be taken as the
definition of arc length.)

<b>DEFINITION</b>
The <b>length</b> of an arc <math>PQ</math> on the unit circle is equal to twice the area of the
sector <math>POQ</math>, <math>s = 2A</math>.
This formula can be seen intuitively as follows. Consider a small arc <math>\hat{P}\hat{Q}</math> of
length <math>\Delta s</math> (Figure 7.1.2). The sector <math>POQ</math> is a thin wedge which is almost a right
triangle of altitude one and base <math>\Delta s</math>. Thus <math>\Delta A \sim \frac{1}{2} \Delta s</math>. Making <math>\Delta s</math> infinitesimal and
adding up, we get <math>A = \frac{1}{2}s</math>.
The number <math>\pi \sim 3.14159</math> is defined as the area of the unit circle. Thus the
unit circle has circumference <math>2\pi</math>.
The area of a sector <i>POQ</i> is a definite integral. For example, if <i>P</i> is the point
<math>P(1,0)</math> and the point <math>Q(x, y)</math> is in the first quadrant, then we see from Figure 7.1.3 that
the area is
<math display="block">A(x) = \frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{1-x^2} + \int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1-t^2} dt.</math>
Notice that <math>A(x)</math> is a continuous function of x. The length of an arc has the following
basic property.

THEOREM 1
Let P be the point <math>P(1,0)</math>. For every number s between 0 and <math>2\pi</math> there is a point
<math>Q</math> on the unit circle such that the arc <math>\widehat{PQ}</math> has length <math>s</math>.
<i>PROOF</i> We give the proof for s between 0 and <math>\pi/2</math>, whence
<math>0 \le \frac{1}{2}s \le \pi/4</math>.
Let <math>A(x)</math> be the area of the sector <math>POQ</math> where <math>Q = Q(x, y)</math> (Figure 7.1.4).
Then <math>A(0) = \pi/4</math>, <math>A(1) = 0</math> and the function <math>A(x)</math> is continuous for <math>0 \le x \le 1</math>.
By the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a point <math>x_0</math> between 0 and 1
where the sector has area <math>\frac{1}{2}s</math>,
<math>A(x_0) = \frac{1}{2}s</math>.
Therefore the arc <math>\widehat{PQ}</math> has length
<math>2A(x_0) = s</math>.

Arc lengths are used to measure angles. Two units of measurement for angles
are radians (best for mathematics) and degrees (used in everyday life).
DEFINITION
Let P and Q be two points on the unit circle. The measure of the angle <math>\angle POQ</math>
in <b>radians</b> is the length of the arc <math>P\hat{Q}</math>. A <b>degree</b> is defined as
<math>1^{\circ} = \pi/180</math> radians,
whence the measure of <math>\angle POQ</math> in degrees is <math>180/\pi</math> times the length of <math>\widehat{PQ}</math>.
Approximately,
<math>1^{\circ} \sim 0.01745</math> radians,
1 radian <math>\sim 57^{\circ}18' = (57\frac{18}{60})^{\circ}</math>.
A complete revolution is 360° or <math>2\pi</math> radians. A straight angle is 180° or <math>\pi</math> radians. A
right angle is 90° or <math>\pi/2</math> radians.
It is convenient to take the point (1, 0) as a starting point and measure arc
length around the unit circle in a counterclockwise direction. Imagine a particle
which moves with speed one counterclockwise around the circle and is at the point
<math>(1,0)</math> at time <math>t=0</math>. It will complete a revolution once every <math>2\pi</math> units of time. Thus if the
particle is at the point P at time t, it will also be at P at all the times <math>t + 2k\pi</math>, k an
integer. Another way to think of the process is to take a copy of the real line, place the
origin at the point (1, 0), and wrap the line around the circle infinitely many times with
the positive direction going counterclockwise. Then each point on the circle will
correspond to an infinite family of real numbers spaced <math>2\pi</math> apart (Figure 7.1.5).

Sin <math>\theta</math> and cos <math>\theta</math> are periodic functions with period <math>2\pi</math>. That is,
<math>\sin (\theta + 2\pi n) = \sin \theta</math>,
<math>\cos(\theta + 2\pi n) = \cos\theta</math>
for all integers n. The graphs of <math>\sin \theta</math> and <math>\cos \theta</math> are infinitely repeating waves which
oscillate between <math>-1</math> and <math>+1</math> (Figure 7.1.7).
For infinite values of <math>\theta</math>, the values of <math>\sin \theta</math> and <math>\cos \theta</math> continue to oscillate
between <math>-1</math> and 1. Thus the limits
<math display="block">\lim_{\theta \to \infty} \sin \theta, \qquad \lim_{\theta \to -\infty} \sin \theta,</math>
<math display="block">\lim_{\theta \to x} \cos \theta, \qquad \lim_{\theta \to -x} \cos \theta,</math>
do not exist. Figure 7.1.8 shows parts of the hyperreal graph of <math>\sin \theta</math>, for positive and
negative infinite values of <math>\theta</math>, through infinite telescopes.

THEOREM 3
(i) <math>d(\sin \theta) = \cos \theta \ d\theta</math>, <math>d(\cos \theta) = -\sin \theta \ d\theta</math>,<br>

(iii) <math>d(\sec \theta) = \sec \theta \tan \theta \ d\theta</math>, <math>d(\csc \theta) = -\csc \theta \cot \theta \ d\theta</math>.
<b>PROOF</b> We prove the formula for <math>d(\tan \theta)</math> and leave the rest as problems.

<math display="block">= \frac{\cos\theta\cos\theta - \sin\theta(-\sin\theta)}{\cos^2\theta}d\theta = \frac{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{1}{\cos^2 \theta} d\theta = \sec^2 \theta d\theta.</math>

7.3 INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS
Inverse functions were studied in Section 2.4. We now take up the topic again and
apply it to trigonometric functions. A binary relation on the real numbers is any set
of ordered pairs of real numbers. Thus a real function <math>f</math> of one variable is a binary
relation such that for each x, either there is exactly one y with <math>(x, y)</math> in f or there is
no y with <math>(x, y)</math> in f. (Other important relations are <math>x < y, x \le y, x \ne y, x = y</math>.)
DEFINITION
Let S be a binary relation on the real numbers. The inverse relation of S is the
set T of all ordered pairs <math>(y, x)</math> such that <math>(x, y)</math> is in S. If S and T are both
functions they are called inverse functions of each other.
The inverse of a function <math>f</math> may or may not be a function. For example, the
inverse of <math>y = x^2</math> is the relation <math>x = \pm \sqrt{y}</math>, which is not a function (Figure 7.3.1).
But the inverse of <math>y = x^2</math>, <math>x \ge 0</math>, is the function <math>x = \sqrt{y}</math> (Figure 7.3.2).

Figures 7.3.1 and 7.3.2). This flipping interchanges the x- and y-axes. This is because
<math>f(x) = y</math> means <math>(x, y)</math> is in <math>f</math>, and <math>g(y) = x</math> means <math>(y, x)</math> is in <math>g</math>. It follows that:
If <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are inverse functions then the range of <math>f</math> is the domain of <math>g</math> and vice
versa.
Which functions have inverse functions? We can answer this question with
a definition and a simple theorem.
DEFINITION
A real function <math>f</math> with domain <math>X</math> is said to be one-to-one if <math>f</math> never takes the
same value twice, that is, for all <math>x_1 \neq x_2</math> in X we have <math>f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)</math>.
THEOREM 1
<math>f</math> has an inverse function if and only if <math>f</math> is one-to-one.

COROLLARY
Every function which is increasing on its domain I has an inverse function. So
does every function decreasing on its domain I.
<b>PROOF</b> Let f be increasing on I. For any two points <math>x_1 \neq x_2</math> in I, the value of f
at the smaller of <math>x_1</math>, <math>x_2</math> is less than the value of <math>f</math> at the greater, so <math>f(x_1) \neq f</math>
<math>f(x_2)</math>.
For example, the function <math>y = x^2</math> is not one-to-one because <math>(-1)^2 = 1^2</math>,
whence it has no inverse function. The function <math>y = x^2, x \ge 0</math>, is increasing on its
domain <math>[0, \infty)</math> and thus has an inverse.
Now let us examine the trigonometric functions. The function <math>y = \sin x</math> is
not one-to-one. For example, <math>\sin 0 = 0</math>, <math>\sin \pi = 0</math>, <math>\sin 2\pi = 0</math>, etc. We can see in
Figure 7.3.3 that the inverse relation of <math>y = \sin x</math> is not a function.

The other trigonometric functions also are not one-to-one and thus do not
have inverse functions. However, in each case we obtain a one-to-one function by
restricting the domain to a suitable interval, either <math>[-\pi/2, \pi/2]</math> or <math>[0, \pi]</math>. The resulting
inverse functions are called the arccosine, arctangent, etc.
DEFINITION
The inverse trigonometric functions are defined as follows.
<math>x = \arcsin y</math> is the inverse of <math>y = \sin x</math>, <math>-\pi/2 \le x \le \pi/2</math>
<math>x = \arccos y \text{ is the inverse of } y = \cos x, \qquad 0 \le x \le \pi</math>
<math>x = \arctan y</math> is the inverse of <math>y = \tan x</math>, <math>-\pi/2 \le x \le \pi/2</math>
<math>x = \operatorname{arccot} y \text{ is the inverse of } y = \cot x, \qquad 0 \le x \le \pi</math>
<math>x = \operatorname{arcsec} y \text{ is the inverse of } y = \operatorname{sec} x, \qquad 0 \le x \le \pi</math>
<math>x = \operatorname{arccsc} y \text{ is the inverse of } y = \operatorname{csc} x, \qquad -\pi/2 \le x \le \pi/2</math>
The graphs of these functions are shown in Figure 7.3.5. The domains of the
inverse trigonometric functions can be read off from the graphs, and are shown in
the table below.

We shall next study the derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions.
Here is a general theorem which tells us when the derivative of the inverse function
exists and gives a rule for computing its value.
<b>INVERSE FUNCTION THEOREM</b>
Suppose a real function <math>f</math> is differentiable on an open interval <math>I</math> and <math>f</math> has an
inverse function g. Let x be a point in I where <math>f'(x) \neq 0</math> and let <math>y = f(x)</math>.

The Inverse Function Rule from Chapter 2 says that (ii) is true if we assume

7.4 INTEGRATION BY PARTS
One reason it is harder to integrate than differentiate is that for derivatives there is
both a Sum Rule and a Product Rule,
<math>d(u + v) = du + dv,</math> <math>d(uv) = u dv + v du</math>
while for integrals there is only a Sum Rule,
<math display="block">\int du + dv = \int du + \int dv.</math>
The Sum Rule for integrals is obtained in a simple way by reversing the sum
rule for derivatives.
There is a way to turn the Product Rule for derivatives into a rule for integrals.
It no longer looks like a product rule, and is called integration by parts. Integration
by parts is a basic method which is needed for many integrals involving trigonometric
functions (and later exponential functions).
INDEFINITE INTEGRATION BY PARTS
Suppose, for x in an open interval I, that u and v depend on x and that du and
dv exist. Then
<math display="block">\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> We use the Product Rule
<math>u dv + v du = d(uv),</math> <math>u dv = d(uv) - v du.</math>
Integrating both sides with x as the independent variable,
<math display="block">\int u \, dv = \int (d(uv) - v \, du) = \int d(uv) - \int v \, du = uv - \int v \, du.</math>
No constant of integration is needed because there are indefinite integrals on
both sides of the equation.
Integration by parts is useful whenever <math>\int v \, du</math> is easier to evaluate than a
given integral <math>\int u \, dv</math>.

Evaluate <math>\int x \sin x \, dx</math>. Our plan is to break <math>x \sin x \, dx</math> into a product of
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b>
the form <math>u dv</math>, evaluate the integrals <math>\int dv</math> and <math>\int v du</math>, and then use integration
by parts to get <math>\int u \, dv</math>. There are several choices we might make for u and <math>dv</math>,
and not all of them lead to a solution of the problem. Some guesswork is
required.
First try: <math>u = \sin x</math>, <math>dv = x dx</math>. <math>\int dv = \int x dx = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C</math>. Take <math>v = \frac{1}{2}x^2</math>.
Next we find <math>du</math> and try to evaluate <math>\int v \, du</math>.
<math>du = \cos x \, dx, \qquad \int v \, du = \int \frac{1}{2} x^2 \cos x \, dx.</math>
This integral looks harder than the one we started with, so we shall start
over with another choice of <math>u</math> and <math>dv</math>.
Second try: <math>u = x</math>, <math>dv = \sin x \, dx</math>.
<math display="block">\int dv = \int \sin x \, dx = -\cos x + C.</math>
We take <math>v = -\cos x</math>. This time we find du and easily evaluate <math>\int v \, du</math>.
<math>du = dx</math>, <math>\int v \, du = \int -\cos x \, dx = -\sin x + C_1</math>.
Finally we use the rule
<math display="block">\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du,</math>
<math display="block">\int x \sin x \, dx = x(-\cos x) - (-\sin x + C_1),</math>
<math display="block">\int x \sin x \, dx = -x \cos x + \sin x + C.</math>
or
<b>EXAMPLE 2</b> Evaluate <math>\int \arcsin x \, dx</math>. A choice of u and dv which works is
<math>u = \arcsin x</math>, <math>dv = dx</math>.
We may take <math>v = x</math>. Then
<math display="block">du = \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}},</math>
<math display="block">\int v \, du = \int \frac{x \, dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} = -\sqrt{1 - x^2} + C_1.</math>
<math display="block">\int \arcsin x \, dx = x \arcsin x - (-\sqrt{1 - x^2} + C_1),</math>
Finally,
<math display="block">\int \arcsin x \, dx = x \arcsin x + \sqrt{1 - x^2} + C.</math>
This integral and the similar formula for <math>\int \arccos x \, dx</math> are included in our
table at the end of the book. We shall see how to integrate the other inverse trigono-
metric functions in the next chapter.

<math>du = 2x dx</math>, <math>\int dv = \int \sin x dx = -\cos x + C</math>.
We take <math>v = -\cos x</math>.
<math display="block">\int x^2 \sin x \, dx = uv - \int v \, du = -x^2 \cos x + \int 2x \cos x \, dx.</math>
Step 2 Evaluate <math>\int 2x \cos x \, dx</math>.
<math>u_1 = 2x,</math> <math>dv_1 = \cos x \, dx,</math>
<math>du_1 = 2 dx</math>, <math>\int dv_1 = \int \cos x dx = \sin x + C</math>.
We take <math>v_1 = \sin x</math>.
<math display="block">\int 2x \cos x \, dx = u_1 v_1 - \int v_1 \, du_1</math>
<math display="block">= 2x \sin x - \int 2 \sin x \, dx</math>
<math display="block">= 2x \sin x + 2 \cos x + C.</math>
Combining the two steps,
<math display="block">\int x^2 \sin x \, dx = -x^2 \cos x + 2x \sin x + 2 \cos x + C.</math>
Sometimes integration by parts will yield an equation in which the given
integral occurs on both sides. One can often solve for the answer.
<b>EXAMPLE 4</b> Evaluate <math>\int \sin^2 \theta \ d\theta</math>. Let
<math>u = \sin \theta</math>,
<math display="block">dv = \sin\theta \, d\theta.</math>
<math>du = \cos\theta \, d\theta, \qquad v = -\cos\theta.</math>
Then
<math display="block">\int \sin^2 \theta \, d\theta = -\sin \theta \cos \theta - \int -\cos^2 \theta \, d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= -\sin\theta\cos\theta + \int\!\cos^2\theta\,d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= -\sin\theta\cos\theta + \int (1-\sin^2\theta)\,d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= -\sin\theta\cos\theta + \theta - \int \sin^2\theta \,d\theta.</math>
We solve this equation for <math>\int \sin^2 \theta \ d\theta</math>,
<math display="block">\int \sin^2 \theta \, d\theta = -\frac{1}{2} \sin \theta \cos \theta + \frac{1}{2} \theta + C.</math>

7 TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS
Here is another way to evaluate <math>\int \sin^2 \theta \, d\theta</math>. Instead of using integration by
parts, we can use the half-angle formula
<math display="block">\sin^2\theta = \frac{1 - \cos(2\theta)}{2}.</math>
This is derived from the addition formula,
<math>\cos(\theta + \phi) = \cos\theta\cos\phi - \sin\theta\sin\phi</math>
<math>cos(2\theta) = cos^2 \theta - sin^2 \theta = 1 - 2 sin^2 \theta</math>
<math display="block">\sin^2\theta = \frac{1-\cos(2\theta)}{2}.</math>
<math display="block">\int \sin^2 \theta \, d\theta = \int \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2} d\theta = \frac{1}{2} \int d\theta - \frac{1}{2} \int \cos 2\theta \, d\theta</math>
Then
<math display="block">= \frac{1}{2} \int d\theta - \frac{1}{4} \int \cos 2\theta \, d(2\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \theta - \frac{1}{4} \sin 2\theta + C.</math>
This answer agrees with Example 4 because
<math>\sin 2\theta = \sin (\theta + \theta) = 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta</math>
<math display="block">\frac{1}{2}\theta - \frac{1}{4}\sin 2\theta = \frac{1}{2}\theta - \frac{1}{2}\sin \theta\cos\theta.</math>

Integration by parts requires a great deal of guesswork. Given a problem
<math>\int h(x) dx</math> we try to find a way to split <math>h(x) dx</math> into a product <math>f(x)g'(x) dx</math> where we can
evaluate both of the integrals <math>\int g'(x) dx</math> and <math>\int g(x) f'(x) dx</math>.
Definite integrals take the following form when integration by parts is
applied.
DEFINITE INTEGRATION BY PARTS
If <math>u = f(x)</math> and <math>v = g(x)</math> have continuous derivatives on an open interval I,
then for a, b in I,
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} f(x)g'(x) \, dx = f(x)g(x) \bigg|_{a}^{b} - \int_{a}^{b} g(x)f'(x) \, dx.</math>
PROOF The Product Rule gives
<math display="block">f(x)g'(x) dx + g(x)f'(x) dx = d(f(x)g(x)).</math>
Then by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b} (f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x)) dx = f(x)g(x) \Big|_{a}^{b},</math>
and the desired result follows by the Sum Rule.
If we plot <math>u = f(x)</math> on one axis and <math>v = g(x)</math> on the other, we get a picture
of definite integration by parts (Figure 7.4.1). The picture is easier to interpret if we
change variables in the definite integrals and write the formula for integration by

7.5 INTEGRALS OF POWERS OF TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS
It is often possible to transform an integral into one of the forms
<math display="block">\int \sin^n u \, du, \qquad \int \cos^n u \, du, \qquad \int \tan^n u \, du, \quad \text{etc.}</math>
These integrals can be evaluated by means of reduction formulas, which express the
integral of the <i>n</i>th power of a trigonometric function in terms of the <math>(n-2)</math>nd power.
The easiest reduction formulas to prove are those for the tangent and cotangent, so
we shall give them first.
THEOREM 1
Let <math>n \neq 1</math>. Then
(i) <math>\int \tan^n x \, dx = \frac{\tan^{n-1} x}{n-1} - \int \tan^{n-2} x \, dx</math>.
(ii) <math>\int \cot^n x \, dx = -\frac{\cot^{n-1} x}{n-1} - \int \cot^{n-2} x \, dx</math>.
PROOF We recall that
<math>\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1</math>, <math>d(\tan x) = \sec^2 x \, dx</math>.
<math display="block">\int \tan^n x \, dx = \int \tan^{n-2} x \tan^2 x \, dx = \int \tan^{n-2} x (\sec^2 x - 1) \, dx</math>
Then
<math display="block">= \int \tan^{n-2} x \sec^2 x \, dx - \int \tan^{n-2} x \, dx</math>
<math display="block">= \int \tan^{n-2} x \, d(\tan x) - \int \tan^{n-2} x \, dx</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{\tan^{n-1}x}{n-1}-\int \tan^{n-2}x\ dx.</math>
These reduction formulas are true for any rational number <math>n \neq 1</math>. They are
most useful, however, when <math>n</math> is a positive integer.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> <math display="block">\int \tan^2 x \, dx = \frac{\tan x}{1} - \int \tan^0 x \, dx = \tan x - x + C.</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 2</b> <math>\int \tan^4 x \, dx = \frac{\tan^3 x}{3} - \int \tan^2 x \, dx = \frac{\tan^3 x}{3} - \tan x + x + C.</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 3</b> <math display="block">\int \tan^3 x \, dx = \frac{\tan^2 x}{2} - \int \tan x \, dx.</math>
We will evaluate <math>\int \tan x \, dx</math> in the next chapter.

## PDF page 408

7 TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS
Each time we use the reduction formula the exponent in the integral goes
down by two. By repeated use of the reduction formulas we can integrate any even
power of tanx or cotx. We can also work the integral of any odd power of tanx or
<math>\cot x</math> down to an expression involving <math>\int \tan x</math> or <math>\int \cot x</math>.
The reduction formulas for the other trigonometric functions are obtained
by using integration by parts.
THEOREM 2
Let <math>n \neq 0</math>. Then
(i) <math display="block">\int \sin^n x \, dx = -\frac{1}{n} \sin^{n-1} x \cos x + \frac{n-1}{n} \int \sin^{n-2} x \, dx.</math>
(ii) <math display="block">\int \cos^n x \, dx = \frac{1}{n} \cos^{n-1} x \sin x + \frac{n-1}{n} \int \cos^{n-2} x \, dx.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> (i) Break the term <math>\sin^n x \, dx</math> into two parts,
<math display="block">\sin^n x \, dx = \sin^{n-1} x (\sin x \, dx).</math>
We shall let
<math>u = \sin^{n-1} x</math>, <math>v = -\cos x</math>,
<math>du = (n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x \, dx, \qquad dv = \sin x \, dx,</math>
and use integration by parts. Then
<math display="block">\int \sin^n x \, dx = \int u \, dv = uv - \int v \, du</math>
<math display="block">= -\sin^{n-1} x \cos x - \int (n-1)(-\cos x)\sin^{n-2} x \cos x \, dx.</math>
<math display="block">= -\sin^{n-1} x \cos x + (n-1) \int \sin^{n-2} x (1 - \sin^2 x) dx</math>
<math display="block">= -\sin^{n-1} x \cos x + (n-1) \int \sin^{n-2} x \, dx - (n-1) \int \sin^n x \, dx.</math>
We find that <math>\int \sin^n x \, dx</math> appears on both sides of the equation, and we solve
for it,
<math display="block">n \int \sin^{n} x \, dx = -\sin^{n-1} x \cos x + (n-1) \int \sin^{n-2} x \, dx,</math>
<math display="block">\int \sin^n x \, dx = -\frac{1}{n} \sin^{n-1} x \cos x + \frac{n-1}{n} \int \sin^{n-2} x \, dx.</math>
We already know the integrals
<math display="block">\int \sin x \, dx = -\cos x + C, \qquad \int \cos x \, dx = \sin x + C.</math>
We can use the reduction formulas to integrate any positive power of <math>\sin x</math> or <math>\cos x</math>.
Again, the formulas are true where n is any rational number, <math>n \neq 0</math>.

form <math>\int \sin^m x \cos^n x \, dx</math> where m and n are positive integers. If either m or n is odd we
let <math>u = \sin x</math> or <math>u = \cos x</math> and transform the integral into a polynomial in u.
<b>EXAMPLE 8</b> <math display="block">\int \sin^4 x \cos^3 x \, dx. \text{ Let } u = \sin x, \, du = \cos x \, dx.</math>
<math display="block">\int \sin^4 x \cos^3 x \, dx = \int u^4 (1 - u^2) \, du</math>
<math>=\frac{1}{5}u^5-\frac{1}{7}u^7+C</math>
<math>=\frac{1}{5}\sin^5 x - \frac{1}{2}\sin^7 x + C.</math>
This method also works for an odd power of <math>\sin x</math> times any power of <math>\cos x</math>,
and vice versa.
<b>EXAMPLE 9</b> <math>\sqrt{\cos x} \sin^3 x \, dx</math>. Let <math>u = \cos x</math>, <math>du = -\sin x \, dx</math>.
<math display="block">\int \sqrt{\cos x} \sin^3 x \, dx = \int \sqrt{u} (1 - u^2)(-1) \, du</math>
<math display="block">= \int -u^{1/2} + u^{5/2} du = -\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} + \frac{2}{7}u^{7/2} + C</math>
<math>=-\frac{2}{3}(\cos x)^{3/2}+\frac{2}{3}(\cos x)^{7/2}+C</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 10</b> <math display="block">\int \sin^5 x \, dx. \text{ Let } u = \cos x, \, du = -\sin x \, dx.</math>
<math display="block">\int \sin^5 x \, dx = \int (1 - u^2)^2 (-1) \, du</math>
<math display="block">= -\int (1 - 2u^2 + u^4) du = -u + \frac{2}{3}u^3 - \frac{1}{5}u^5 + C</math>
<math>= -\cos x + \frac{2}{3}\cos^3 x - \frac{1}{5}\cos^5 x + C.</math>
If m and n are both even, the integral <math>\int \sin^m x \cos^n x \, dx</math> can be transformed
into the integral of a sum of even powers of sin x. Then the reduction formula can
be used.
<math display="block">\int \sin^4 x \cos^4 x \, dx = \int \sin^4 x (1 - \sin^2 x)^2 \, dx</math>
EXAMPLE 11
<math display="block">= \int \sin^4 x - 2\sin^6 x + \sin^8 x \, dx.</math>
We can also evaluate integrals of the form
<math display="block">\int \tan^m x \sec^n x \, dx,</math>
<math display="block">\int \cot^m x \csc^n x \, dx.</math>

7.6 TRIGONOMETRIC SUBSTITUTIONS
Integrals containing one of the terms
<math>\sqrt{a^2+x^2}</math>, <math>\sqrt{a^2-x^2}</math>, or <math>\sqrt{x^2-a^2}</math>
can often be integrated by a trigonometric substitution. The idea is to take <math>x</math>, <math>a</math>, and the
square root as the three sides of a right triangle and use one of its acute angles as a
new variable <math>\theta</math>. The three kinds of trigonometric substitutions are shown in Figure
7.6.1. These figures do not have to be memorized. Just remember that the sides must
be labeled so that
<math>(opposite)^2 + (adjacent)^2 = (hypotenuse)^2</math>.
These substitutions frequently give an integral of powers of trigonometric functions
discussed in the preceding section.

Find <math>\int (a^2 + x^2)^{-3/2} dx</math>.
EXAMPLE 1
Let <math>\theta = \arctan(x/a)</math>. Then from Figure 7.6.2,
<math>x = a \tan \theta</math>, <math>dx = a \sec^2 \theta d\theta</math>, <math>\sqrt{a^2 + x^2} = a \sec \theta</math>.
So
<math display="block">\int (a^2 + x^2)^{-3/2} dx = \int (a \sec \theta)^{-3} a \sec^2 \theta d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{1}{a^2} \int (\sec \theta)^{-1} d\theta = \frac{1}{a^2} \int \cos \theta d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{1}{a^2} \sin \theta + C = \frac{1}{a^2} \frac{\tan \theta}{\sec \theta} + C = \frac{x}{a^2 \sqrt{a^2 + x^2}} + C.</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 2</b> Find <math>\int \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} dx</math>.
Let <math>\theta = \operatorname{arcsec}(x/a)</math> (Figure 7.6.3), so
<math>x = a \sec \theta</math>, <math>dx = a \tan \theta \sec \theta d\theta</math>, <math>\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} = a \tan \theta</math>.
So
<math display="block">\int \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} \, dx = \int a \tan \theta \, a \tan \theta \, \sec \theta \, d\theta = a^2 \int \tan^2 \theta \, \sec \theta \, d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= a^2 \int (\sec^2 \theta - 1) \sec \theta \, d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= a^2 \int \sec^3 \theta \, d\theta - a^2 \int \sec \theta \, d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= \left(\frac{1}{2}a^2 \sec^2 \theta \sin \theta + \frac{1}{2}a^2 \int \sec \theta \, d\theta\right) - a^2 \int \sec \theta \, d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{1}{2}a^2 \sec^2 \theta \sin \theta - \frac{1}{2}a^2 \int \sec \theta \, d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= \frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} - \frac{1}{2}a^2 \int \sec\theta \, d\theta.</math>
This is as far as we can go on this problem until we find out how to integrate
<math>\int \sec \theta \ d\theta</math> in the next chapter.

7.7 POLAR COORDINATES
A pair of polar coordinates of P is given by <math>(r, \theta)</math> where r is the distance from the
origin to P and <math>\theta</math> is the angle XOP.
Each pair of real numbers <math>(r, \theta)</math> determines a point P in polar coordinates.
To find P we first rotate the line OX through an angle <math>\theta</math>, forming a new line OX',
and then go out a distance r along the line <math>OX'</math>. If <math>\theta</math> is negative then the rotation is in
the negative, or clockwise direction. If r is negative the distance is measured along
the line <math>OX'</math> in the direction away from <math>X'</math> (see Figure 7.7.2).

Any coordinate pair <math>(0, \theta)</math> with <math>r = 0</math> determines the origin. As we see in
Figure 7.7.5, the coordinates of a point <math>P</math> in rectangular and in polar coordinates are
related by the equations
<math>x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.</math>
The graph, or locus in polar coordinates of a system of formulas in the variables <math>r, \theta</math>
is the set of all points <math>P(r, \theta)</math> for which the formulas are true.
<b>EXAMPLE 2</b> The graph of the equation <math>r = a</math> is the circle of radius <math>a</math> centered at the
origin (Figure 7.7.6(a)). The graph of the equation <math>\theta = b</math> is a straight line
through the origin (Figure 7.7.6(b)).
<b>EXAMPLE 3</b> The graph of the system of formulas
<math>r = \theta, \quad 0 \le \theta</math>
is the spiral of Archimedes formed by moving a pencil along the line <math>OX</math>
while the line is rotating, with the pencil moving at the same speed as the
point X. The graph is shown in Figure <math>7.7.6(c)</math>.
An equation in rectangular coordinates can readily be transformed into an
equation in polar coordinates with the same graph by using <math>x = r \cos \theta</math>, <math>y = r \sin \theta</math>.

7.8 SLOPES AND CURVE SKETCHING IN POLAR COORDINATES
Derivatives can be used to measure direction in polar as well as in rectangular
coordinates. We begin with two theorems, one about the direction of a curve at the
origin (an unusual point in polar coordinates) and the other about the direction of a
curve elsewhere. Then we shall use these theorems for sketching curves.
THEOREM 1
At any value <math>\theta_0</math> where the curve <math>r=f(\theta)</math> passes through the origin, the curve
is tangent to the line <math>\theta = \theta_0</math>.
More precisely, if <math>r = 0</math> at <math>\theta = \theta_0</math> but <math>r \neq 0</math> for all <math>\theta \neq \theta_0</math> in some neighbor-
hood of <math>\theta_0</math>, then
<math display="block">\lim_{\theta \to \theta_0} \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \tan \theta_0, \qquad \lim_{\theta \to \theta_0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y} = \cot \theta_0.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> Suppose <math>\cos \theta_0 \neq 0</math>, so <math>\tan \theta_0</math> exists. Let <math>\Delta \theta</math> be a nonzero infinitesimal. Then
<math>\Delta r \neq 0</math> and r changes from 0 to <math>\Delta r</math>. We compute <math>\Delta y/\Delta x</math>.
<math display="block">\Delta y = (0 + \Delta r)\sin(\theta_0 + \Delta \theta) - 0\sin\theta_0</math>
<math display="block">= \Delta r \sin(\theta_0 + \Delta \theta),</math>
<math display="block">\Delta x = \Delta r \cos(\theta_0 + \Delta \theta),</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{\Delta r \sin(\theta_0 + \Delta \theta)}{\Delta r \cos(\theta_0 + \Delta \theta)} = \tan(\theta_0 + \Delta \theta).</math>
Taking standard parts,
<math display="block">\lim_{\theta \to \theta_0} \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \tan \theta_0.</math>
Similarly, when <math>\sin \theta_0 \neq 0</math>,
<math display="block">\lim_{\theta \to \theta_0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta v} = \cot \theta_0.</math>

7.9 AREA IN POLAR COORDINATES
In this section we derive a formula for the area of a region in polar coordinates.
Section 6.3 on the length of a curve in rectangular coordinates should be studied
before this and the following section.
Our starting point for areas in rectangular coordinates was the formula for
the area of a rectangle. In polar coordinates our starting point is the formula for the
area of a sector of a circle.
THEOREM 1
A sector of a circle with radius r and central angle <math>\theta</math> has area
<math display="block">A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta.</math>
An arc of a circle with radius r and central angle <math>\theta</math> has length
<math>s = r\theta</math>.
PROOF Consider a sector POQ shown in Figure 7.9.1. To simplify notation let O
be the origin, and put the sector POQ in the first quadrant with P on the

<math>P = (r, 0),</math> <math>Q = (r \cos \theta, r \sin \theta).</math>
The arc <math>QP</math> has the equation
<math>y = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}, \quad r \cos \theta \le x \le r.</math>
We see from the figure that
<math display="block">A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta + \int_{r=0}^{r} \sqrt{r^2 - x^2} dx.</math>
Integrating by the trigonometric substitution <math>x = r \sin \phi</math>, we get
<math display="block">\int_{r\cos\theta}^{r} \sqrt{r^2 - x^2} \, dx = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta - \frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta.</math>
Therefore <math>A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta</math>. By definition, <math>A = \frac{1}{2}rs</math>, so
<math>s = \frac{2A}{r} = r\theta.</math>
The next theorem gives the formula for area in polar coordinates.
THEOREM 2
Let <math>r = f(\theta)</math> be continuous and <math>r \ge 0</math> for <math>a \le \theta \le b</math>, where <math>b \le a + 2\pi</math>.
Then the region R bounded by the curve <math>r = f(\theta)</math> and the lines <math>\theta = a</math> and
<math>\theta = b</math> has area
<math display="block">A = \frac{1}{2} \int_{a}^{b} f(\theta)^2 d\theta.</math>
Discussion Imagine a point P moving along the curve <math>r = f(\theta)</math> from <math>\theta = a</math> to <math>\theta = b</math>.
The line <i>OP</i> will sweep out the region R in Figure 7.9.2. Since <math>b \le a + 2\pi</math>,
the line will complete at most one revolution, so no point of R will be counted
more than once.

7.10 LENGTH OF A CURVE IN POLAR COORDINATES
Consider a curve
<math>r = f(\theta), \quad a \le \theta \le b</math>
in polar coordinates. The curve is called <i>smooth</i> if <math>f'(\theta)</math> is continuous for <math>\theta</math> between
a and b. In Chapter 6 we obtained a formula for the length of a smooth parametric
curve in rectangular coordinates. We may now apply this to get a formula for the
length of a smooth curve in polar coordinates.
THEOREM
The length of a smooth curve
<math>r = f(\theta), \quad a \le \theta \le b</math>
in polar coordinates which does not retrace itself is
<math display="block">s = \int_{-\infty}^{b} \sqrt{f(\theta)^2 + f'(\theta)^2} d\theta,</math>
<math display="block">s = \int_{-\infty}^{b} \sqrt{r^2 + (dr/d\theta)^2} \, d\theta.</math>
or equivalently
The formula can be seen intuitively as follows. We see from Figure
Discussion
7.10.1 that
<math>\Delta s \approx \sqrt{(r \Delta \theta)^2 + \Delta r^2} = \sqrt{r^2 + (\Delta r / \Delta \theta)^2} \Delta \theta</math>
<math>\approx \sqrt{r^2 + (dr/d\theta)^2} \,\Delta\theta</math> (compared to <math>\Delta\theta</math>).
By the Infinite Sum Theorem,
<math display="block">s = \int_{0}^{\theta} \sqrt{r^{2} + (\overline{dr}/d\theta)^{2}} d\theta.</math>

The length of a curve has already been defined using rectangular coordinates,
and the theorem states that the new formula will give the same number for the length.
PROOF The curve is given in rectangular coordinates by the parametric equation
<math>x = f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y = f(\theta)\sin\theta.</math>
The derivatives are
<math display="block">\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -f(\theta)\sin\theta + f'(\theta)\cos\theta,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{d\theta} = f(\theta)\cos\theta + f'(\theta)\sin\theta.</math>
Since <math>f(\theta)</math> and <math>f'(\theta)</math> are continuous, <math>dx/d\theta</math> and <math>dy/d\theta</math> are continuous. Recall
the length formula for parametric equations:
<math display="block">s = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^{2}} d\theta.</math>
We compute
<math display="block">\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^2 = f(\theta)^2 \sin^2\theta - 2f(\theta)f'(\theta)\sin\theta\cos\theta + f'(\theta)\cos^2\theta</math>
<math>+f(\theta)^2\cos^2\theta + 2f(\theta)f'(\theta)\sin\theta\cos\theta + f'(\theta)^2\sin^2\theta</math>
<math display="block">= f(\theta)^2(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta) + f'(\theta)^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta)</math>
<math>= f(\theta)^2 + f'(\theta)^2</math>.
The desired formula now follows by substitution.

EXPONENTIAL
AND LOGARITHMIC
<b>FUNCTIONS</b>
8.1 EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS
Any positive real number a can be raised to a rational exponent,
<math display="block">a^{m/n} = \sqrt[n]{a^m}, \qquad a > 0.</math>
But what does <math>a^b</math> mean if b is an irrational number? For example, what are <math>2^{\pi}</math> and <math>2^{\sqrt{3}}</math>?
We shall approach the problem of defining <math>a^b</math> by considering <math>a^x</math> as a function
of x. Given a positive real number a, the function <math>a^x</math> is defined for all rational numbers
x. Its graph may be thought of as a "dotted" line as in Figure 8.1.1.
<math>a^x</math>, x rational
.<u>---</u>
х
Figure 8.1.1
Our idea is to define <math>a^x</math> for all x by "connecting the dots." This will make <math>a^x</math>
into a continuous function which agrees with the original dotted curve when <math>x</math> is
rational. A number such as <math>2^{\pi}</math> will thus be approximated by raising 2 to a rational
exponent close to <math>\pi</math>. <math>2^{3.14}</math> will be close to <math>2^{\pi}</math> and <math>2^{3.14159}</math> will be even closer.
To get the exact value of <math>2^{\pi}</math> we use hyperrational numbers; if r is a hyper-
rational number infinitely close to <math>\pi</math>, then <math>2^r</math> will be infinitely close to <math>2^{\pi}</math>. The function
<math>y = a^x</math> will be called the exponential function with base a.
Hyperintegers were introduced in Section 3.8. To get an exact value of
<math>2^{\pi}</math>, we use hyperintegers. A quotient <math>K/H</math> of two hyperintegers is called a hyper-
rational number. Our idea is to take a hyperrational number <math>K/H</math> that is infinitely
close to <math>\pi</math> and define <math>2^{\pi}</math> to be the standard part of <math>2^{K/H}</math>.
In general, given a real number <math>r</math>, we can find a hyperrational number
431

## PDF page 442

8 EXPONENTIAL AND LOGARITHMIC FUNCTIONS
432
<math>K/H</math> infinitely close to r as follows. Choose a positive infinite hyperinteger H. Let K
be the greatest hyperinteger <math>\leq Hr</math>, <math>K = [Hr]</math>. Then
<math>K < Hr < K + 1</math>.
Dividing by <math>H</math>,
<math>\frac{K}{H} \le r < \frac{K}{H} + \frac{1}{H}, \qquad \frac{K}{H} \approx r.</math>
Given a positive real number a, we then define <math>a^r</math> to be the standard part of <math>a^{K/H}</math>.
It can be proved that the value for a obtained in this way does not depend on our
choice of <math>H</math>. Thus the exponent <math>a^x</math> is defined for all real <math>x</math>. We summarize our
procedure as a lemma and a definition.
LEMMA 1
Let a and r be real numbers, <math>a > 0</math>.
There is a hyperrational number <math>K/H</math> infinitely close to <math>r</math>.
(i)
(ii) The hyperrational exponent <math>a^{K/H}</math> is defined and finite.
For any other hyperrational number <math>L/M \approx r</math>, <math>st(a^{K/H}) = st(a^{L/M})</math>.
(iii)
DEFINITION
Let a and r be real, <math>a > 0</math>. We define <math>a^r = st(a^{K/H})</math>, where <math>K/H \approx r</math>.
The function <math>y = a^x</math>, also written <math>y = \exp_a x</math>, is called the exponential
function with base a. If <math>a < 0</math>, we leave <math>a^x</math> undefined except when <math>x = m/n</math>, n odd.
The following rules for exponents should be familiar to the student when
the exponents are rational, except for inequality (vii). They can be proved for real
exponents by forming hyperrational exponents and taking standard parts.
RULES FOR EXPONENTS
Let a, b be positive real numbers.
(i) <math>1^x = 1</math>, <math>a^0 = 1</math>.
(ii) <math>a^{x+y} = a^x a^y</math>, <math>a^{x-y} = a^x / a^y</math>.
(iii) <math>a^{xy} = (a^x)^y</math>.
(iv) <math>a^x b^x = (ab)^x</math>, <math>(a^x/b^x) = (a/b)^x</math>.
INEQUALITIES FOR EXPONENTS
Let a, b be positive real numbers.
(v) If <math>a < b</math> and <math>x > 0</math>, then <math>a^x < b^x</math>.
(vi) If <math>1 < a</math> and <math>x < y</math>, then <math>a^x < a^y</math>.
(vii) If <math>x \ge 1</math>, then <math>(a + 1)^x \ge ax + 1</math>.
PROOF (vii) Since this inequality is probably new to the student, we give a proof
for the case where x is a rational number <math>x = q</math>.

so

The case <math>a \le 1</math> is similar.
An example of an exponential function is given by the growth of a population
