THEOREM 2
If <math>f(x, y)</math> is continuous at <math>(a, b)</math> and <math>g(u)</math> is continuous at <math>f(a, b)</math>, then
(i)
<math display="block">h(x, y) = g(f(x, y))</math>
is continuous at (a, b).
Sums, differences, products, quotients, and exponents of continuous
(ii)
functions are continuous.
<b>PROOF</b> (i) If <math>(x, y) \approx (a, b)</math> then <math>f(x, y) \approx f(a, b)</math>, hence <math>g(f(x, y)) \approx g(f(a, b))</math>, and
thus <math>h(x, y) \approx h(a, b)</math>.
(ii) Let <math>f(x, y)</math> and <math>g(x, y)</math> be continuous at <math>(a, b)</math>. As an illustration we show
that if <math>f(x, y) > 0</math> then
<math display="block">h(x, y) = f(x, y)^{g(x, y)}</math>
is continuous at <math>(a, b)</math>. Let <math>(x, y) \approx (a, b)</math>. Then
<math>st(h(x, y)) = st(f(x, y)^{g(x,y)}) = st(f(x, y))^{st(g(x,y))} = f(a, b)^{g(a,b)} = h(a, b).</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 2</b> By (i), <math>h(x, y) = \sin(x + y)</math> is continuous for all <math>(x, y)</math>.
By (ii), <math>h(x, y) = \sin x \cos y</math> is continuous for all <math>(x, y)</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 3</b>
A function is said to be continuous on a set S of points in the plane if it is
continuous at every point in S. Thus the quotient function <math>f(x, y) = x/y</math> is con-
tinuous on the set of all <math>(x, y)</math> such that <math>y \neq 0</math>. The function <math>f(x, y) = x^y</math> is continuous
on the set of all <math>(x, y)</math> such that <math>x > 0</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 4</b> Find a set on which <math>h(x, y) = \ln(x + y)</math> is continuous.
By Theorems 1 and 2,
<math>x + y</math> is continuous for all <math>(x, y)</math>,
<math>\ln u</math> is continuous for <math>u > 0</math>,
<math>ln(x + y)</math> is continuous for <math>x + y > 0</math>.
Answer <math>ln(x + y)</math> is continuous on the set of all <math>(x, y)</math> such that <math>x + y > 0</math>, shown in
Figure 11.2.3.

11.3 PARTIAL DERIVATIVES
Partial derivatives are used to study the rates of change of functions of two or more
variables. In general the rate of change of <math>z = f(x, y)</math> will depend both on the rate
of change of x and the rate of change of y. Partial derivatives deal with the simplest
case, where only one of the independent variables is changing and the other is held
constant.
Given a function <math>z = f(x, y)</math>, if we hold y fixed at some constant value b we
obtain a function
<math>g(x) = f(x, b)</math>
of x only. Geometrically the curve <math>z = g(x)</math> is the intersection of the surface <math>z = f(x, y)</math>
with the vertical plane <math>y = b</math>. The rate of change of z with respect to x with y held
constant is the slope of the curve <math>z = g(x)</math>. This slope is called the partial derivative
of <math>f(x, y)</math> with respect to x (Figure 11.3.1(a)). There is also a partial derivative with
respect to y (Figure 11.3.1(b)).
Here is a precise definition.
DEFINITION
The partial derivatives of <math>f(x, y)</math> at the point <math>(a, b)</math> are the limits
<math>f_x(a,b) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{f(a + \Delta x, b) - f(a, b)}{\Delta x},</math>

<math>f_{y}(a,b) = \lim_{\Delta y \to 0} \frac{f(a,b+\Delta y) - f(a,b)}{\Delta y}.</math>
A partial derivative is undefined if the limit does not exist.
When <math>f_x(a, b)</math> exists, it is equal to the standard part
<math>f_x(a,b) = st \left( \frac{f(a + \Delta x, b) - f(a,b)}{\Delta x} \right)</math>
for any nonzero infinitesimal <math>\Delta x</math>. Similarly when <math>f_y(a, b)</math> exists,
<math>f_{y}(a,b) = st \left( \frac{f(a,b+\Delta y) - f(a,b)}{\Delta y} \right)</math>
for any nonzero infinitesimal <math>\Delta y</math>.
Just as the one-variable derivative <math>f'(x)</math> is a function of x, the partial deriva-
tives <math>f_x(x, y)</math> and <math>f_y(x, y)</math> are again functions of x and y. At each point <math>(x, y)</math>, the partial
derivative <math>f_x(x, y)</math> either has exactly one value or is undefined.

Another convenient notation for the partial derivatives uses the Cyrillic
lower case D, <math>\partial</math>, called a "round d". If <math>z = f(x, y)</math>, we use:
<math>\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}(x, y)</math>, <math>\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}</math>, or <math>\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}</math> for <math>f_x(x, y)</math>,
<math>\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}(x, y), \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial v}, \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial v} \quad \text{for } f_y(x, y).</math>
Partial derivatives, like ordinary derivatives, may be represented as quotients
of infinitesimals.
In <math>\partial z/\partial x</math>, <math>\partial x</math> means <math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\partial z</math> means <math>f_x(x, y) \Delta x</math>.
In <math>\partial z/\partial y</math>, <math>\partial y</math> means <math>\Delta y</math> and <math>\partial z</math> means <math>f_y(x, y) \Delta y</math>.
Notice that <math>\partial z</math> has a different meaning in <math>\partial z/\partial x</math> than it has in <math>\partial z/\partial y</math>. For this
reason we shall avoid using the symbol <math>\partial z</math> alone.
Partial derivatives are easily computed using the ordinary rules of differentia-
tion with all but one variable treated as a constant.

Functions of three or more variables cannot easily be represented graphically.
However, they can be given other physical interpretations. For example, <math>w = f(x, y, t)</math>
may be pictured as a moving surface in <math>(x, y, w)</math> space where t is time. Alternatively,
<math>w = f(x, y, z)</math> may be thought of as assigning a number to each point of <math>(x, y, z)</math> space
where it is defined; for example, w could be the density of a three-dimensional object
at the point <math>(x, y, z)</math>.
Partial derivatives of functions of three or more variables are defined in a
manner analogous to the two-variable case.
DEFINITION
The partial derivatives of <math>f(x, y, z)</math> at the point <math>(a, b, c)</math> are the limits
<math display="block">f_x(a,b,c) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{f(a+\Delta x,b,c) - f(a,b,c)}{\Delta x},</math>

<math display="block">f_z(a,b,c) = \lim_{\Delta z \to 0} \frac{f(a,b,c+\Delta z) - f(a,b,c)}{\Delta z}.</math>
A partial derivative is undefined if the limit does not exist.
When <math>f_x(a, b, c)</math> exists we have
<math>f_x(a,b,c) = st \left( \frac{f(a+\Delta x,b,c) - f(a,b,c)}{\Delta x} \right)</math>
for nonzero infinitesimal <math>\Delta x</math>.
Thus <math>f_x(x, y, z)</math> is the rate of change of <math>f(x, y, z)</math> with respect to x when y and
z are held constant.
We also use the round d notation. If <math>w = f(x, y, z)</math>, we use:

<math>f_z(x, y, z) = -\cos(x^2y - z).</math>

<math>f_z(1,0,0) = -\cos(1^2 \cdot 0 - 0) = -1.</math>

11.4 TOTAL DIFFERENTIALS AND TANGENT PLANES
Most of the functions we encounter have continuous partial derivatives. To keep
our theory simple we shall concentrate on such functions in this chapter.
DEFINITION
A function <math>f(x, y)</math> is said to be <b>smooth</b> at <math>(a, b)</math> if both of its partial derivatives
exist and are continuous at (a, b).
The definition for three or more variables is similar.
The Increment Theorem for a differentiable function of one variable shows
that the increment <math>\Delta z</math> is very close to the differential dz, and leads to the notion of a
tangent line. In this section we introduce the increment and total differential for a
function of two variables. Then we state an Increment Theorem for a smooth function
of two variables, which leads to the notion of a tangent plane.
Let z depend on the two independent variables x and y, <math>z = f(x, y)</math>. Let <math>\Delta x</math>
and <math>\Delta y</math> be two new independent variables, called the <i>increments</i> of x and y. Usually
<math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\Delta y</math> are taken to be infinitesimals.
We now introduce two new dependent variables, the increment <math>\Delta z</math> and the
total differential dz.
DEFINITION
When <math>z = f(x, y)</math>, the <b>increment</b> of z is the dependent variable <math>\Delta z</math> given by
<math>\Delta z = f(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) - f(x, y)</math>
The increment <math>\Delta z</math> depends on the four independent variables x, y, <math>\Delta x</math>, <math>\Delta y</math>,
and is equal to the change in z as x changes by <math>\Delta x</math> and y changes by <math>\Delta y</math>. Thus
<math>\Delta z = \Delta f(x, y, \Delta x, \Delta y),</math>
where <math>\Delta f</math> is the function
<math>\Delta f(x, y, \Delta x, \Delta y) = f(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) - f(x, y).</math>
DEFINITION
When <math>z = f(x, y)</math>, the <b>total differential</b> of z is the dependent variable dz given by
<math display="block">dz = f_x(x, y) dx + f_y(x, y) dy,</math>
<math display="block">dz = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} dx + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} dy.</math>
or equivalently

The following corollary is analogous to the theorem that a differentiable
function of one variable is continuous.
<b>COROLLARY 1</b>
If a function <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is smooth at <math>(a, b)</math> then it is continuous at <math>(a, b)</math>.
<b>PROOF</b> Let <math>(x, y)</math> be infinitely close to <math>(a, b)</math> and let
<math>\Delta x = x - a, \qquad \Delta y = y - b.</math>
<math display="block">\Delta z = dz + \varepsilon_1 \, \Delta x + \varepsilon_2 \, \Delta y</math>
Then
<math display="block">= \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \Delta x + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \Delta y + \varepsilon_1 \Delta x + \varepsilon_2 \Delta y.</math>
Since <math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\Delta y</math> are infinitesimal, <math>\Delta z</math> is infinitesimal, so <math>f(x, y) \approx f(a, b)</math>.
Some examples of what can happen when the function is not smooth are
given in the problem set.
If a function <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is smooth at <math>(a, b)</math>, the curve <math>z = f(x, b)</math> has a tangent
line <math>L_1</math> on the plane <math>y = b</math>, and the curve <math>z = f(a, y)</math> has a tangent line <math>L_2</math> on the
plane <math>x = a</math>.
<math>L_1</math> has the equation <math>z - f(a, b) = f_x(a, b)(x - a)</math>
and <math>L_2</math> has the equation <math>z - f(a, b) = f_v(a, b)(y - b)</math>.
The plane determined by the lines <math>L_1</math> and <math>L_2</math> is called the tangent plane. It has the
equation
<math>z - f(a, b) = f_{x}(a, b)(x - a) + f_{y}(a, b)(y - b),</math>
because the graph p of this equation is a plane and intersects the plane <math>y = b</math> in <math>L_1</math> and
the plane <math>x = a</math> in <math>L_2</math> (Figure 11.4.4).
DEFINITION
The tangent plane of a smooth function <math>z = f(x, y)</math> at <math>(a, b)</math> is the plane with
the equation
<math>z - f(a, b) = f_{x}(a, b)(x - a) + f_{y}(a, b)(y - b).</math>
If we set <math>x = a</math> and <math>y = b</math> in this equation we get <math>z = f(a, b)</math>. If we set <math>x - a = dx</math>
and <math>y - b = dy</math> we get <math>z - f(a, b) = dz</math>. Therefore:
The tangent plane touches the surface at (a, b).

11.5 CHAIN RULE
The Chain Rule is useful when several variables depend on each other. A typical case
is where z depends on x and y, while x and y depend on another variable <math>t</math>. We shall
call <math>t</math> the independent variable, <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> the intermediate variables, and <math>z</math> the dependent
variable. Figure 11.5.1 shows which variables depend on which.

CHAIN RULE
If z is a smooth function of x and y, while x and y are differentiable functions
of t, then dz/dt exists and
<math display="block">\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}.</math>
Discussion If <math>z = F(x, y)</math> and <math>x = g(t)</math>, <math>y = h(t)</math>, then z as a function of t is
<math>z = f(t) = F(g(t), h(t)).</math>
We can give a more precise statement of the Chain Rule using functional
notation:
If <math>g(t)</math> and <math>h(t)</math> are differentiable at <math>t_0</math>, and <math>F(x, y)</math> is smooth at <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> where
<math>x_0 = g(t_0)</math> and <math>y_0 = h(t_0)</math>, then <math>f'(t_0)</math> exists and
<math display="block">f'(t_0) = F_{\nu}(x_0, y_0)g'(t_0) + F_{\nu}(x_0, y_0)h'(t_0).</math>

<i>PROOF OF THE CHAIN RULE</i> We use the Increment Theorem. Let <math>\Delta t</math> be a non-
zero infinitesimal, and let <math>\Delta x</math>, <math>\Delta y</math>, and <math>\Delta z</math> be the corresponding increments of
x, y and z. Then <math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\Delta y</math> are infinitesimal, and
<math display="block">\Delta z = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \Delta x + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \Delta y + \varepsilon_1 \Delta x + \varepsilon_2 \Delta y,</math>
where <math>\varepsilon_1</math> and <math>\varepsilon_2</math> are infinitesimal. Dividing by <math>\Delta t</math>,
<math display="block">\frac{\Delta z}{\Delta t} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t} + \varepsilon_1 \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} + \varepsilon_2 \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t}.</math>
Taking standard parts, we see that
<math display="block">\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \frac{dy}{dt}.</math>
There is a Chain Rule for any number of independent and intermediate
variables. We state the simplest cases here.
The Chain Rules for two or more independent variables follow from the
Chain Rules for one independent variable.
If z depends on x and x depends on s and t, we have the diagram in Figure
11.5.3. The Chain Rule for this case is:
If z is a differentiable function of x and x is a smooth function of s and t, then
<math display="block">\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = \frac{dz}{dx} \frac{\partial x}{\partial s}, \qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial t} = \frac{dz}{dx} \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}.</math>
This follows from the ordinary Chain Rule in Chapter 2 by holding s or t
constant.
If z depends on x and y while x and y depend on s and t, we have the diagram
in Figure 11.5.4. The Chain Rule for this case is:
If z is a smooth function of x and y while x and y are smooth functions of s and
t, then
<math display="block">\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}, \qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \frac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}.</math>

11.6 IMPLICIT FUNCTIONS
In many applications of the Chain Rule, one or more of the independent variables
is also used as an intermediate variable. The simplest case where this occurs is when
z depends on x and y while y depends on <math>x</math>,
<math>y = g(x),</math> <math>z = F(x, y).</math>
Figure 11.6.1 shows which variables depend on which.
Assuming <math>F(x, y)</math> is smooth and <math>dy/dx = g'(x)</math> exists, the Chain Rule gives
<math display="block">\frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dx} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dx}, \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dx}.</math>

In many problems we are given a relationship between x and y which can be
expressed by an equation of the form <math>F(x, y) = 0</math>, and we wish to find <math>dy/dx</math>. The
graph of <math>F(x, y) = 0</math> is usually a curve in the <math>(x, y)</math> plane. If we put <math>z = F(x, y) = 0</math>,
then <math>dz/dx = 0</math> while <math>dy/dx</math> is the slope of the curve. Ordinarily such a curve can be
divided into finitely many pieces each of which is the graph of a function <math>y = g(x)</math>.

<b>DEFINITION</b>
An implicit function of the curve <math>F(x, y) = 0</math> at <math>(a, b)</math> is a function <math>y = g(x)</math>
such that:
(i) <math>g(a) = b</math>;
The domain of <math>g(x)</math> is an open interval containing a;
(ii)
The graph of <math>y = g(x)</math> is a subset of the graph of <math>F(x, y) = 0</math>.
(iii)
If every implicit function of <math>F(x, y) = 0</math> has the same slope S at <math>(a, b)</math>, we call
S the slope of the curve.
Figure 11.6.3 shows an implicit function <math>y = g(x)</math> of a curve <math>F(x, y) = 0</math>.
It is often hard or impossible to express an implicit function in terms of known
(or elementary) functions. However, the next theorem gives an easy test for showing
that there is an implicit function and finding its slope.

<b>THEOREM</b>
Suppose the function <math>w = F(x, y, z)</math> is smooth at the point <math>(a, b, c)</math>, and

and the tangent plane
<math>F_x(a, b, c)(x - a) + F_y(a, b, c)(y - b) + F_z(a, b, c)(z - c) = 0.</math>

and finally <math>F_x(a, b, c)(x - a) + F_y(a, b, c)(y - b) + F_z(a, b, c)(z - c) = 0</math>.

11.7 MAXIMA AND MINIMA
The theory of maxima and minima for functions of two variables is similar to the
theory for one variable. The student should review the one-variable case at this time.
DEFINITION
Let <math>z = f(x, y)</math> be a function with domain D. f is said to have a maximum
at a point <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> in D if
<math>f(x_0, y_0) \ge f(x, y)</math>
for all <math>(x, y)</math> in D. The value <math>f(x_0, y_0)</math> is called the maximum value of <math>f</math>.
A minimum and the minimum value of f are defined analogously.

11.7 MAXIMA AND MINIMA
We shall first study functions defined on closed regions, which correspond
to closed intervals. By a closed region in the plane we mean a set D defined by
inequalities
<math>a \le x \le b</math>, <math>f(x) \le y \le g(x)</math>,
where f and g are continuous and <math>f(x) \le g(x)</math> on [a, b]. D is called the region between
<math>f(x)</math> and <math>g(x)</math> for <math>a \le x \le b</math> (Figure 11.7.1).

The points of D on the four curves
<math>x = a</math>, <math>x = b</math>, <math>y = f(x)</math>, <math>y = g(x)</math>
are called boundary points. All other points of D are called interior points.
EXTREME VALUE THEOREM
Suppose <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is continuous at every point of a closed region D. Then
the function <math>f</math> with its domain restricted to <math>D</math> has a maximum and a minimum.
The proof is similar to the corresponding proof for one variable.
CRITICAL POINT THEOREM
Suppose the domain of <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is a closed region D and f is smooth at every
interior point of D. If f has a maximum or minimum at <math>(x_0, y_0)</math>, then either
(i) <math>f_x(x_0, y_0) = 0</math> and <math>f_y(x_0, y_0) = 0</math>, or
(ii) <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> is a boundary point of D.
Figure 11.7.2 illustrates the two cases when f has a maximum at <math>(x_0, y_0)</math>.
An interior point where both partial derivatives are zero is called a critical point.
Thus a critical point is a point where the tangent plane is horizontal. On the graph
of a surface, an interior point looks like a mountain summit if it is a maximum and
a valley bottom if it is a minimum. The theorem states that every interior maximum
or minimum is a critical point. An interesting kind of critical point which is neither

We shall now develop a method for finding maxima and minima of functions
defined on open regions.
A bounded open region D is a set of points given by strict inequalities
<math>a < x < b</math>, <math>f(x) < y < g(x)</math>
where f and g are continuous and <math>f(x) < g(x)</math> on <math>(a, b)</math>. A closed region with its
boundary removed is a bounded open region.
We shall also consider unbounded open regions, which are given by strict
inequalities where one or more of <math>a, b, f(x), g(x)</math> are replaced by infinity symbols.
For example, the following are unbounded open regions:
(1) <math>-\infty < x < \infty</math>, <math>f(x) < y < g(x)</math>.
(2) <math>0 < x < \infty</math>, <math>0 < y < \infty</math>.
(3) The whole plane <math>-\infty < x < \infty</math>, <math>-\infty < y < \infty</math>.
Unbounded open regions are pictured in Figure 11.7.8.
A smooth function whose domain is an open region may or may not have
a maximum or minimum. Many problems have at most one critical point, and we
shall concentrate on that case. The method can readily be extended to the case of
two or more critical points. The Critical Point Theorem holds for open regions as
well as closed regions. The corollary below shows how it can be used in maximum
or minimum problems.
COROLLARY
Suppose the domain of the function <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is an open region D, and f is
smooth on D.
(i) If f has no critical points it has no maximum or minimum.

If we know a function has a maximum or minimum, we can find it simply
by finding the critical point. But usually we are not sure whether a function has a
maximum or minimum. Here is a method that can be used when a function has a
unique critical point in an open region. It is based on the fact that the Extreme
Value Theorem holds for closed regions of the hyperreal plane as well as the real
plane (because of the Transfer Principle).
Given a real open region <math>D</math> we can find a hyperreal closed region <math>E</math> which
contains the same real points as D (Figure 11.7.11).
For example, if <math>D</math> is the real region
<math>a < x < b</math>, <math>f(x) < y < g(x)</math>,
we can take for E the hyperreal region
<math>a + \varepsilon \le x \le b - \varepsilon</math>, <math>f(x) + \varepsilon \le y \le g(x) - \varepsilon</math>
where <math>\varepsilon</math> is positive infinitesimal.

METHOD FOR FINDING MAXIMA AND MINIMA ON AN OPEN REGION
When to Use <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is a smooth function whose domain is an open region D, and
f has exactly one critical point.
Step 1 Set up the problem and sketch D if necessary.
Step 2 Compute <math>\partial z/\partial x</math> and <math>\partial z/\partial y</math>.
Step 3 Find the critical point <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> and the value <math>f(x_0, y_0)</math>. If we already know
there is a maximum (or minimum), it must be <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> and we can stop here.
Step 4 Find a hyperreal closed region E with the same real points as D.
Step 5 Compare <math>f(x_0, y_0)</math> with the values of f on the boundary of E.
<b>CONCLUSION</b> f has a maximum at <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> if <math>f(x_0, y_0) \ge f(x, y)</math> for every boundary
point <math>(x, y)</math> of E. Otherwise f has no maximum.
A similar rule holds for the minimum.

Find the four second partial derivatives of
EXAMPLE 1
<math>z = e^x \sin y + xy^2</math>.
<math>\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = e^x \sin y + y^2, \qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = e^x \cos y + 2xy.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} (e^x \sin y + y^2) = e^x \sin y,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial v^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial v} (e^x \cos y + 2xy) = -e^x \sin y + 2x.</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y \, \partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y} (e^x \sin y + y^2) = e^x \cos y + 2y,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x \, \partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} (e^x \cos y + 2xy) = e^x \cos y + 2y.</math>
Notice that in this example the two mixed second partials <math>\partial^2 z/\partial y \partial x</math> and
<math>\partial^2 z/\partial x \partial y</math> are equal. The following theorem shows that it is not just a
coincidence.
THEOREM 1 (Equality of Mixed Partials)
Suppose that the first and second partial derivatives of <math>z = f(x, y)</math> are con-
tinuous at <math>(a, b)</math>. Then at <math>(a, b)</math>,
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y \, \partial x} = \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x \, \partial y}.</math>
This is a surprising theorem. <math>\partial^2 z/\partial y \partial x</math> is the rate of change with respect
Discussion
to y of the slope <math>\partial z/\partial x</math>, while <math>\partial^2 z/\partial x \partial y</math> is the rate of change with respect to
x of the slope <math>\partial z/\partial y</math>. There is no simple intuitive way to see that these should
be equal.
As a matter of fact, there are functions <math>f(x, y)</math> whose mixed second partial
derivatives exist but are not equal. One such example is the function

11 PARTIAL DIFFERENTIATION
<math display="block">f(x, y) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } (x, y) = (0, 0), \\ xy \frac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 - 1 - y^2} & \text{if } (x, y) \neq (0, 0). \end{cases}</math>
We have left the computation of the second partials of <math>f(x, y)</math> as a problem. It turns
out that at <math>(0, 0)</math>,
<math>\partial^2 f/\partial x \, \partial y = 1, \qquad \partial^2 f/\partial y \, \partial x = -1.</math>
How can this be in view of Theorem 1? The answer is that in this example the second
partial derivatives exist but are not continuous at <math>(0, 0)</math>, so the theorem does not apply.
We shall only rarely encounter functions whose second partial derivatives are not
continuous, so in all ordinary problems it is true that the mixed partials are equal.
We shall prove the theorem later. We now turn to some applications. Our first ap-
plication concerns mixed third partial derivatives.
If the third partial derivatives of <math>z = f(x, y)</math> are continuous, then
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial x \, \partial x \, \partial y} = \frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial x \, \partial y \, \partial x} = \frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial y \, \partial x \, \partial x},</math>
so we write <math>\frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial x^2 \partial y}</math> for each of them. Similarly,
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial x \, \partial y \, \partial y} = \frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial y \, \partial x \, \partial y} = \frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial v \, \partial x \, \partial x}</math>
and we write <math>\frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial x \partial y^2}</math> for each of them.
We prove the first equation as an illustration.
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial x \, \partial x \, \partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x \, \partial y} \right) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y \, \partial x} \right) = \frac{\partial^3 z}{\partial x \, \partial y \, \partial x}.</math>

<math display="block">=\frac{h(a+\Delta x)-h(a)}{\Delta x}=\frac{\Delta^2 f}{\Delta x \Delta y}.</math>
By the Mean Value Theorem,
<math display="block">\frac{\Delta^2 f}{\Lambda v \Lambda x} = \frac{g(b + \Delta y) - g(b)}{\Lambda v} = g'(y_1),</math>
where <math>b < y_1 < b + \Delta y</math>. Using the Mean Value Theorem again,
<math display="block">g'(y_1) = \frac{\partial \left( \frac{\int (a + \Delta x, y) - \int (a, y)}{\Delta x} \right)}{\partial y} (a, y_1)</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(a+\Delta x,y_1)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(a,y_1)}{\Delta x}</math>
<math display="block">=\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \, \partial v}(x_1, y_1),</math>

We conclude this section by stating a Second Derivative Test for maxima
and minima of functions of two variables. In practice the test often fails except on
small regions D. We therefore have emphasized the tests in the preceding section
rather than the Second Derivative Test.
SECOND DERIVATIVE TEST
Suppose <math>z = f(x, y)</math> has continuous first and second partial derivatives on a
rectangle D, and <math>(a, b)</math> is a critical point of <math>f</math> in D.
(i) <math>f</math> has a minimum at <math>(a, b)</math> if
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2} \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2} - \left( \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x \partial y} \right)^2 > 0, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2} > 0</math>
at every point of D.
(ii) <math>f</math> has a maximum at <math>(a, b)</math> if
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2} \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2} - \left( \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x \partial y} \right)^2 > 0, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2} < 0</math>
at every point of D.
f has a saddle point at (a, b) if
(iii)
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2} \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2} - \left( \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x \, \partial y} \right)^2 < 0 \qquad at (a, b).</math>
For an indication of the proof of the Second Derivative Test, see Extra
Problem 55 at the end of this chapter.

INTEGRALS
The first seven sections of this chapter develop the double and triple integral. They
depend on Sections 11.1 and 11.2 on surfaces and continuous functions, but are
independent of Chapter 10 on vectors.
Sections 8 through 10 of this chapter discuss the relationship between
multiple integrals, line integrals, and surface integrals. Chapters 10 on vectors and 11
on partial derivatives are prerequisites.
12.1 DOUBLE INTEGRALS
The double integral is the analogue of the single integral (definite integral) suggested
by Figure 12.1.1. Figure 12.1.1(a) shows the area A bounded by the interval <math>[a, b]</math> and
the curve <math>y = f(x)</math>, and corresponds to the single integral
<math display="block">A = \int_a^b f(x) \, dx.</math>
Figure 12.1.1(b) shows the volume <math>V</math> bounded by the plane region <math>D</math> and the surface
<math>z = f(x, y)</math>, and corresponds to the double integral
<math display="block">V = \iint_D f(x, y) \, dx \, dy.</math>
Our development of double integrals will be similar to our development of
single integrals in Chapter 4. Before going into detail, we give a brief intuitive preview.
Instead of closed intervals <math>[u, v]</math> in the line, we deal with closed regions D
in the plane. A volume function for <math>f(x, y)</math> is a function B, which assigns a real number
<math>B(D)</math> to each closed region <math>D</math>, and has the following two properties: Addition Property
and Cylinder Property.

ADDITION PROPERTY
If D is divided into two regions <math>D_1</math> and <math>D_2</math> which meet only on a common
boundary curve, then
<math>B(D) = B(D_1) + B(D_2).</math>
(Intuitively, the volume over <math>D</math> is the sum of the volumes over <math>D_1</math> and <math>D_2</math>.)
This property is illustrated in Figure 12.1.2(a).
CYLINDER PROPERTY
Let m and M be the minimum and maximum values of <math>f(x, y)</math> on D and let A be
the area of D. Then
<math>mA \leq B(D) \leq MA</math>.
(Intuitively, the volume over D is between the volumes of the cylinders over
<math>D</math> of height <math>m</math> and <math>M</math>. This corresponds to the Rectangle Property for single
integrals.)
This property is illustrated in Figure 12.1.2(b).
We shall see at the end of this section that the double integral
<math display="block">\iiint_{\mathbb{R}} f(x, y) \, dx \, dy</math>
is the unique volume function for a continuous function <math>f(x, y)</math>. The double integral
will be constructed using double Riemann sums, just as the single integral was
constructed from single Riemann sums.
We now begin the construction of the double integral, starting with a careful
discussion of closed regions in the plane.
A closed region in the <math>(x, y)</math> plane is a set D of real points <math>(x, y)</math> given by
inequalities
<math display="block">a_1 \le x \le a_2, \qquad b_1(x) \le y \le b_2(x),</math>

12 MULTIPLE INTEGRALS
We shall usually be working with closed regions. So from now on when we
use the word region alone we mean closed region.
To simplify our treatment we shall consider only continuous functions.
PERMANENT ASSUMPTION FOR CHAPTER 12
Whenever we refer to a function <math>f(x, y)</math> and a region D, we assume that <math>f(x, y)</math>
is continuous on some open region containing D.
If <math>f(x, y) \ge 0</math> on D, the double integral is intuitively the volume of the solid
over D between the surfaces <math>z = 0</math> and <math>z = f(x, y)</math>; i.e., the solid consisting of all
points <math>(x, y, z)</math> where <math>(x, y)</math> is in D and
<math>0 \le z \le f(x, y)</math>.
If <math>f(x, y) \le 0</math> on D the double integral is intuitively the negative of the volume
of the solid under D between the surfaces <math>z = f(x, y)</math> and <math>z = 0</math>. Thus volumes above
the plane <math>z = 0</math> are counted positively and volumes below <math>z = 0</math> are counted
negatively (Figure 12.1.4).

The double Riemann sum for a rectangle D is the sum
<math display="block">\sum_{D} f(x, y) \Delta x \Delta y = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \sum_{l=0}^{p} f(x_k, y_l) \Delta x \Delta y.</math>
This is the sum of the volume of the rectangular solids with base <math>\Delta x \Delta y</math> and height
<math>f(x_k, y_l)</math>.
As we can see from Figure 12.1.7,
<math display="block">\sum_{D} f(x, y) \, \Delta x \, \Delta y</math>
approximates the volume of the solid over D between <math>z = 0</math> and <math>z = f(x, y)</math>.

Given positive real numbers <math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\Delta y</math>, we partition the circumscribed

DEFINITION
The double Riemann sum over D is defined as the sum of the volumes of the
rectangular solids with base <math>\Delta x \Delta y</math> and height <math>f(x_k, y_l)</math> corresponding to
partition points <math>(x_k, y_l)</math> which belong to D. In symbols,
<math display="block">\sum_{D} f(x, y) \Delta x \Delta y = \sum_{(x_k, y_l) \text{ in } D} f(x_k, y_l) \Delta x \Delta y.</math>
Notice that in the double Riemann sum over D, we only use partition points
<math>(x_k, y_l)</math> which belong to D (Figure 12.1.9).

12.1 DOUBLE INTEGRALS
Given the function <math>f(x, y)</math> and the region D, the double Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{D} f(x, y) \, \Delta x \, \Delta y</math>
is a real function of <math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\Delta y</math>. When we replace <math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\Delta y</math> by positive infinitesimals
dx and dy (Figure 12.1.12), we obtain (by the Function Axiom) the infinite double
Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{D} \int f(x, y) dx dy.</math>
The infinite double Riemann sum is in general a hyperreal number. Intuitively, it is
equal to the sum of the volumes of infinitely many rectangular solids of infinitesimal
base <math>dx dy</math> and height <math>f(x_K, y_L)</math>. The double integral is defined as the standard part of
the infinite double Riemann sum. The following lemma, based on our Permanent
Assumption for Chapter 12, shows that this sum has a standard part.

LEMMA
For any positive infinitesimals dx and dy, the double Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{D} \int f(x, y) dx dy</math>
is a finite hyperreal number and thus has a standard part.
We omit the proof, which is similar to the proof that single Riemann sums
are finite. We are now ready to define the double integral.
DEFINITION
Given positive infinitesimals dx and dy, the double integral of a continuous
function <math>f(x, y)</math> over D is the standard part of the double Riemann sum-
<math display="block">\iint_{\mathbb{R}} f(x, y) dx dy = \operatorname{st} \left( \sum_{D} f(x, y) dx dy \right).</math>

Here is a list of properties of the double integral. Each property is analogous
to a property of the single integral given in Chapter Four and has a similar proof.
INDEPENDENCE OF dx AND dy
The value of the double integral <math>\iint_D f(x, y) dx dy</math> does not depend on <math>dx</math> and <math>dy</math>.
That is, if <math>dx</math>, <math>d_1x</math>, <math>dy</math>, and <math>d_1y</math> are positive infinitesimals then
<math display="block">\iint f(x, y) dx dy = \iint f(x, y) d_1 x d_1 y.</math>
This theorem shows that the value of the double integral depends only on
the function <math>f</math> and the region <math>D</math>. From now on we shall usually use the simpler notation
<math>dA = dx dy</math> for the area of an infinitesimal dx by dy rectangle, and
<math display="block">\iint_{\mathbb{R}} f(x, y) dA \qquad \text{for } \iint_{\mathbb{R}} f(x, y) dx dy.</math>
ADDITION PROPERTY
Let D be divided into two regions <math>D_1</math> and <math>D_2</math> which meet only on a common
boundary as in Figure 12.1.13. Then
<math display="block">\iint_{\mathcal{D}} f(x, y) dA = \iint_{\mathcal{D}} f(x, y) dA + \iint_{\mathcal{D}} f(x, y) dA.</math>

A continuous function <math>z = f(x, y)</math> always has a minimum and maximum

CYLINDER PROPERTY
Let m and M be the minimum and maximum values of <math>f(x, y)</math> on D and let A be
the area of D. Then
<math>mA \le \iint_{D} f(x, y) dA \le MA.</math>
This corresponds to the Rectangle Property for single integrals. The solid
with base D and constant height m is called the inscribed cylinder, and the solid with
base D and height M is called the circumscribed cylinder. The inscribed cylinder and
the circumscribed cylinder are shown in Figure 12.1.15. Intuitively, the volume of a
cylinder is equal to the area of the base A times the height. Thus the Cylinder Property
states that the volume of the solid is between the volumes of the inscribed and circum-
scribed cylinders.
Here are two consequences of the Cylinder Property.

PROOF Both m and M are equal to 1, so <math>1 \cdot A \leq \iint dA \leq 1 \cdot A</math>.
<b>COROLLARY 2</b>
If <math>f(x, y) \ge 0</math> on D then <math>\iint_D f(x, y) dA \ge 0</math>. If <math>f(x, y) \le 0</math> on D then
<math display="block">\iint_D f(x, y) \, dA \le 0.</math>
To really be sure that the double integral corresponds to the volume, we
need to know that it is the only operation that has the Addition and Cylinder
Properties. To make this precise, we introduce the notion of a volume function.
We suppose <math>f(x, y)</math> is continuous at every point of an open region <math>D_0</math>, and
consider subregions <math>D</math> of <math>D_0</math>. A volume function for <math>f</math> is a function <math>B</math> which assigns
a real number <math>B(D)</math> to each subregion D of <math>D_0</math> and has the Addition Property
<math display="block">B(D) = B(D_1) + B(D_2)</math>
and the Cylinder Property
<math>mA \leq B(D) \leq MA</math>,
where <math>m</math> is the minimum and <math>M</math> the maximum value of <math>f</math> on <math>D</math>.
UNIQUENESS THEOREM
The double integral <math>\iint_D f(x, y) dA</math> is the only volume function for <math>f</math>. That is,
if B is a function which has the Addition and Cylinder Properties, then
<math display="block">B(D) = \iint_{D} f(x, y) dA \qquad \text{for every } D.</math>

12.2 ITERATED INTEGRALS
In this section we shall learn how to evaluate double integrals. A double integral
can be evaluated by two single integrations. The Iterated Integral Theorem gives the
key formula.
The iterated integral
<math display="block">\int_{a_1}^{a_2} \left| \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f(x, y) \, dy \right| dx</math>
is an integral of an integral of <math>f(x, y)</math>. It is evaluated in two stages. First evaluate the
inside integral
<math>g(x) = \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f(x, y) dy</math>

## PDF page 735

12.2 ITERATED INTEGRALS
725
by ordinary definite integration, treating x as a constant. This gives us a function of x
alone. Second, evaluate the outside integral
<math display="block">\int_{a_1}^{a_2} g(x) dx = \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \left[ \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f(x, y) dy \right] dx</math>
by a second definite integration.
We shall usually drop the brackets around the inside integral and write the
iterated integral as
<math display="block">\int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f(x, y) \, dy \, dx.</math>
ITERATED INTEGRAL THEOREM
Let D be a region
<math>a_1 \le x \le a_2</math>, <math>b_1(x) \le y \le b_2(x)</math>.
The double integral over D is equal to the iterated integral:
<math display="block">\iint f(x, y) dA = \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f(x, y) dy dx.</math>
Discussion For a fixed <math>x_0</math>, <math>\int_{b_1(x_0)}^{b_2(x_0)} f(x_0, y) dy</math> is the area of the cross section shown
in Figure 12.2.1. The Iterated Integral Theorem states that the volume is
equal to the integral of the areas of the cross sections.
The proof of the Iterated Integral Theorem is given at the end of this section.
When using iterated integrals we must be sure that:
(1) <math>a_1 \le a_2</math> and <math>b_1(x) \le b_2(x)</math>.
(2) The differentials <math>dx</math> and <math>dy</math> appear in the right order.
(3) The outer integral sign has constant limits.

12 MULTIPLE INTEGRALS
While the order of the differentials, <math>dx dy</math> or <math>dy dx</math>, does not matter in a
double integral, it is important in an iterated integral. The inside integral sign goes
with the inside differential, and is performed first.
<math display="block">\int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f(x, y) \, dy \, dx</math>
do first
do second
When the region D is a rectangle, there are two possible orders of integration,
because all the boundaries are constant. Thus there are two different iterated integrals
over a rectangle. Integrating first with respect to y we have
<math display="block">\int_a^{a_2} \int_b^{b_2} f(x, y) \, dy \, dx,</math>
and integrating first with respect to x we have
<math display="block">\int_{a_{-}}^{b_{2}} \int_{a_{-}}^{a_{2}} f(x, y) \, dx \, dy.</math>
Using the Iterated Integral Theorem twice, we see that both iterated integrals must
equal the double integral.
<math display="block">\int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1}^{b_2} f(x, y) \, dy \, dx = \iint_{D} f(x, y) \, dA,</math>
<math display="block">\int_{b_1}^{b_2} \int_{a_1}^{a_2} f(x, y) \, dx \, dy = \iiint f(x, y) \, dA.</math>
Therefore the two iterated integrals are equal to each other. We have proved a
corollary.
COROLLARY
The two iterated integrals over a rectangle are equal:
<math display="block">\int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1}^{b_2} f(x, y) \, dy \, dx = \int_{b_1}^{b_2} \int_{a_1}^{a_2} f(x, y) \, dx \, dy.</math>
This corollary is the simplest form of a result known as Fubini's Theorem.
Discussion
Remember that by our Permanent Assumption, <math>f(x, y)</math> is continuous on D.
For an idea of the difficulties that arise when <math>f(x, y)</math> is not assumed to be
continuous, see Problem 49 at the end of this section.
There are also other regions besides rectangles over which we can integrate
in either of two orders, such as Example 5 in this section.
In the following two examples we evaluate the double integrals which were
approximated by double Riemann sums in the preceding section.

where <math>D_1</math> is the unit square

The limits of the outside integral are given by <math>0 \le x \le 1</math>, and those of the
inside integral are given by <math>0 \le y \le 1</math>. The iterated integral is thus
<math display="block">\iint x^2 y \, dA = \int_0^1 \int_0^1 x^2 y \, dy \, dx.</math>
The inside integral is
<math display="block">\int_0^1 x^2 y \, dy = \frac{1}{2} x^2 y^2 \bigg|_{y=0}^{y=1} = \frac{1}{2} x^2.</math>
<math display="block">\iint x^2 y \, dA = \int_0^1 \frac{1}{2} x^2 \, dx = \frac{1}{6} x^3 \bigg|_0^1 = \frac{1}{6} \sim 0.16667.</math>
Then
Since <math>D_1</math> is a rectangle we may also integrate in the other order, and should
get the same answer.
<math display="block">\iint x^2 y \, dA = \int_0^1 \int_0^1 x^2 y \, dx \, dy.</math>
<math display="block">\int_0^1 x^2 y \, dx = \frac{1}{3} x^3 y \bigg|_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} y.</math>

PROOF OF THE ITERATED INTEGRAL THEOREM For any region D, let <math>B(D)</math> be
the iterated integral over D. Our plan is to prove that B has the Addition and
Cylinder Properties, so that by the Uniqueness Theorem <math>B(D)</math> will equal the
double integral.
PROOF OF ADDITION PROPERTY
Case 1 Let D be divided into <math>D_1</math> and <math>D_2</math> as in Figure 12.2.8(a). By the Addition
Property for single integrals,
<math display="block">B(D) = \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f \, dy \, dx</math><br>= <math display="block">\int_{a_1}^{a_3} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f \, dy \, dx + \int_{a_3}^{a_2} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f \, dy \, dx</math>
<math display="block">= B(D_1) + B(D_2).</math>
Case 2 Let D be divided into <math>D_1</math> and <math>D_2</math> as in Figure 12.2.8(b). Then
<math display="block">B(D) = \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f \, dy \, dx</math>
<math display="block">= \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \left[ \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_3(x)} f \, dy + \int_{b_3(x)}^{b_2(x)} f \, dy \right] dx</math>

<math display="block">= B(D_1) + B(D_2).</math>

The Constant, Sum, and Inequality Rules for double integrals follow easily
from the corresponding rules for single integrals, using the Iterated Integral Theorem.
CONSTANT RULE
<math display="block">\iint_D cf(x, y) dA = c \iint_D f(x, y) dA.</math>
SUM RULE
<math display="block">\iint\limits_{\Omega} f(x, y) + g(x, y) \, dA = \iint\limits_{\Omega} f(x, y) \, dA + \iint\limits_{\Omega} g(x, y) \, dA.</math>

<b>INEQUALITY RULE</b>
If <math>f(x, y) \leq g(x, y)</math> for all <math>(x, y)</math> in D,
<math display="block">\iint f(x, y) dA \le \iint g(x, y) dA.</math>

<math display="block">\iint f + g \, dA = \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f + g \, dy \, dx</math>
<math display="block">= \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \left[ \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} f \, dy + \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} g \, dy \right] dx</math>

<math display="block">= \iiint f \, dA + \iiint g \, dA.</math>

12.3 INFINITE SUM THEOREM AND VOLUME
The double integral, like the single integral, has a number of applications to geometry
and physics. The basic theorem which justifies these applications is the Infinite Sum
Theorem. It shows how to get an integration formula by considering an infinitely
small element of area.
An element of area is a rectangle <math>\Delta D</math> whose sides are infinitesimal and parallel
to the x and y axes. Given an element of area <math>\Delta D</math>, we let
<math>(x, y) = \text{lower left corner of } \Delta D</math>,
<math>\Delta x, \Delta y = \text{dimensions of } \Delta D,</math>
<math>\Delta A = \Delta x \, \Delta y = \text{area of } \Delta D.</math>
<math>\Delta D</math> is illustrated in Figure 12.3.1.

(i)
<math>B(D) \ge 0</math> for every D.
(ii)
For every element of area <math>\Delta D</math>, <math>B(\Delta D) \approx h(x, y) \Delta A</math> (compared to <math>\Delta A</math>).
(iii)
<math display="block">B(D) = \iint h(x, y) \, dA.</math>

We shall use the notation

Given (i) and (ii), the theorem shows that if we always have

<math>B(D) \approx \sum_{n} \sum_{n} h(x, y) \Delta A</math>.

12.3
<b>PROOF</b> WHEN D IS A RECTANGLE Choose positive infinitesimal <math>\Delta x</math> and <math>\Delta y</math> and
partition D into elements of area <math>\Delta D</math> (Figure 12.3.2). Since B has the Addition
Property, <math>B(D)</math> is the sum of the <math>\Delta B</math>'s. Let c be any positive real number. For
each <math>\Delta D</math> we have
<math>\Delta B \approx h(x, y) \Delta A</math>
(compared to <math>\Delta A</math>),
<math display="block">\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta A} \approx h(x, y),</math>
<math>\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta A} - c < h(x, y) < \frac{\Delta B}{\Delta A} + c,</math>
<math>\Delta B - c \Delta A < h(x, y) \Delta A < \Delta B + c \Delta A</math>.
Letting A be the area of D and adding up,

12.4 APPLICATIONS TO PHYSICS
In this section we obtain double integrals for mass, center of mass, and moment of
inertia.
DEFINITION
If a plane object fills a region D and has continuous density <math>\rho(x, y)</math>, its mass is
<math display="block">m = \iint \rho(x, y) \, dA.</math>
On an element of area <math>\Delta D</math>, the density is infinitely close to <math>\rho(x, y)</math> (Figure
12.4.1). Therefore the mass is
<math>\Delta m \approx \rho(x, y) \Delta A</math> (compared to <math>\Delta A</math>).
By the Infinite Sum Theorem <math>m = \iint_D \rho(x, y) dx dy</math>.

A plane object which fills a region D and has continuous density <math>\rho(x, y)</math> has
moments about the x and y axes given by

<math display="block">M_x = \iint_D y \rho(x, y) \, dA.</math>
<math display="block">M_{y} = \iint_{D} x \rho(x, y) \, dA.</math>
<math>M_x</math> and <math>M_y</math> are sometimes called first moments to distinguish them from
moments of inertia (which are called second moments).
The <b>center of mass</b> of the object is the point <math>(\bar{x}, \bar{y})</math> with coordinates
<math display="block">\bar{x} = \frac{M_y}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{D} x \rho(x, y) \, dA}{\iint\limits_{D} \rho(x, y) \, dA},</math>
<math display="block">\bar{y} = \frac{M_x}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{D} y \rho(x, y) \, dA}{\iint\limits_{\rho(x, y)} \rho(x, y) \, dA}.</math>
The piece of the object on an element of area <math>\Delta D</math> has mass
<b>JUSTIFICATION</b>
<math>\Delta m \approx \rho(x, y) \Delta A</math> (compared to <math>\Delta A</math>).
A point mass <math>\overline{m}</math> at <math>(x, y)</math> has moments
<math>\overline{M}_{x} = y\overline{m}, \qquad \overline{M}_{y} = x\overline{m}.</math>
Therefore the piece of the object at <math>\Delta D</math> has moments
<math>\Delta M_{\rm x} \approx y \, \Delta m \approx y \rho(x, y) \, \Delta A</math> (compared to <math>\Delta A</math>),
<math>\Delta M_y \approx x \, \Delta m \approx x \rho(x, y) \, \Delta A</math> (compared to <math>\Delta A</math>).
The double integrals for <math>M_x</math> and <math>M_y</math> now follow from the Infinite Sum
Theorem.

We use the formula
<math>W = mgs</math>.
From Example 2, <math>m = \frac{1}{2}</math>. We must find s.
<math>s = \text{minimum distance from } \left(\frac{5}{12}, \frac{9}{12}\right) \text{ to the line } x = y.</math>
<math>s = \text{minimum value of } z = \sqrt{\left(x - \frac{5}{12}\right)^2 + \left(x - \frac{9}{12}\right)^2}.</math>
<math>z = \sqrt{2x^2 - \frac{28}{12}x + \frac{106}{144}}</math>.
<math display="block">\frac{dz}{dx} = \left(4x - \frac{28}{12}\right) \frac{1}{2} z^{-1/2}.</math>
<math>\frac{dz}{dx} = 0</math> at <math>4x = \frac{28}{12}</math>, <math>x = \frac{7}{12}</math>.
<math display="block">s = \sqrt{2\left(\frac{7}{12}\right)^2 - \frac{28}{12} \cdot \frac{7}{12} + \frac{106}{144}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}.</math>
<math>W = mgs = \frac{1}{2} \cdot g \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12} g.</math>

<math display="block">I = m(x^2 + v^2).</math>
The moment of inertia is related to the kinetic energy of rotation. A mass m moving at
speed v has kinetic energy
<math>KE = \frac{1}{2} mv^2</math>.
Hence if m is rotating about the origin with angular velocity <math>\omega</math> radians per second,
its speed is <math>v = \omega \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}</math> and
<math>KE = \frac{1}{2}m(\omega_{2}/x^{2} + y^{2})^{2} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}</math>
Thus moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass.
DEFINITION
Given a plane object on the region D with continuous density <math>\rho(x, y)</math>, the
moment of inertia about the origin is
<math display="block">I = \iint \rho(x, y)(x^2 + y^2) dA.</math>
JUSTIFICATION On an element of volume <math>\Delta D</math>, the moment of inertia is
<math>\Delta I \approx (x^2 + y^2) \Delta m \approx \rho(x, y)(x^2 + y^2) \Delta A</math>
(compared to <math>\Delta A</math>).
The integral for <i>I</i> follows by the Infinite Sum Theorem.

<math display="block">\int_{-1/2}^{1/2} x^2 + y^2 \, dy = x^2 y + \frac{1}{3} y^3 \bigg]_{-1/2}^{1/2} = x^2 + \frac{1}{12}.</math>
<math display="block">I = \int_{-1/2}^{1/2} x^2 + \frac{1}{12} dx = \frac{1}{6}.</math>

<b>DEFINITION</b>
A polar region is a region D in the <math>(x, y)</math> plane given by polar coordinate
inequalities
<math>\alpha \le \theta \le \beta</math>, <math>a(\theta) \le r \le b(\theta)</math>,
where <math>a(\theta)</math> and <math>b(\theta)</math> are continuous. To avoid overlaps, we also require that
for all <math>(\theta, r)</math> in <math>D</math>,
<math>0 \le \theta \le 2\pi</math> and <math>0 \le r</math>.
The last requirement means that the limits <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are between 0 and <math>2\pi</math>,
while the limits <math>a(\theta)</math> and <math>b(\theta)</math> are <math>\geq 0</math>. Figure 12.5.1 shows a polar region.
The simplest polar regions are the polar rectangles
<math>\alpha \le \theta \le \beta</math>, <math>a \le r \le b</math>.
We see in Figure 12.5.2 that the <math>\theta</math> boundaries are radii and the r boundaries are
circular arcs.

We shall use the Infinite Sum Theorem to get a formula for the double
integral over a polar region. In the proof we take for <math>\Delta D</math> an infinitely small polar
rectangle.
POLAR INTEGRATION FORMULA
Let D be the polar region
<math>\alpha \le \theta \le \beta</math>, <math>a(\theta) \le r \le b(\theta)</math>.
The double integral of <math>f(x, y)</math> over D is
<math display="block">\iint_{\Omega} f(x, y) dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{a(\theta)}^{b(\theta)} f(x, y) r dr d\theta</math>
<math display="block">= \int_{-\pi}^{\beta} \int_{\sigma(\theta)}^{b(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) r \, dr \, d\theta.</math>
Notice that in the iterated integral for a polar region we do not integrate
<math>f(x, y)</math> but the product of <math>f(x, y)</math> and r. Intuitively, the extra r comes from the fact
that a polar element of area is almost a rectangle of area <math>r \Delta \theta \Delta r</math> (see Figure 12.5.6(b)).
<b>PROOF</b> We shall work with the rectangular <math>(\theta, r)</math> plane. Let C be the region in the
<math>(\theta, r)</math> plane given by the inequalities
<math>\alpha \le \theta \le \beta</math>, <math>a(\theta) \le r \le b(\theta)</math>.
Thus C has the same inequalities as D but they refer to the <math>(\theta, r)</math> plane instead
of the <math>(x, y)</math> plane. D and C are shown in Figure 12.5.5.
We must prove that
<math display="block">\iint_{\mathbb{R}} f(x, y) dx dy = \iint_{\mathbb{R}} f(x, y) r d\theta dr.</math>

A closed region in space, or solid region, is a set E of points given by inequalities
<math>a_1 \le x \le a_2</math>, <math>b_1(x) \le y \le b_2(x)</math>, <math>c_1(x, y) \le z \le c_2(x, y)</math>
where the functions <math>b_1(x)</math>, <math>b_2(x)</math> and <math>c_1(x, y)</math>, <math>c_2(x, y)</math> are continuous.
The boundary of E is the part of E on the following surfaces:
The planes <math>x = a_1, x = a_2</math>.

An open region in space is defined in a similar way but with strict inequalities.
As in the two-dimensional case, the word region alone will mean closed region.
PERMANENT ASSUMPTION
Whenever we refer to a function <math>f(x, y, z)</math> and a solid region <math>E</math>, we assume that
<math>f(x, y, z)</math> is continuous on some open region containing E.
The triple integral
<math display="block">\iiint_{z} f(x, y, z) \, dx \, dy \, dz</math>
is analogous to the double integral.
The first step in defining the triple integral is to form the circumscribed
rectangular box of E (Figure 12.6.2). This is the rectangular box
<math>a_1 \le x \le a_2</math>, <math>B_1 \le y \le B_2</math>, <math>C_1 \le z \le C_2</math>,
<math>B_1 = \text{minimum value of } b_1(x),</math>
where
<math>B_2</math> = maximum value of <math>b_2(x)</math>,
<math>C_1 = \text{minimum value of } c_1(x, y),</math>
<math>C_2 = \text{maximum value of } c_2(x, y).</math>

Our next step is to define the triple Riemann sum. Given positive real
numbers <math>\Delta x</math>, <math>\Delta y</math>, and <math>\Delta z</math>, we partition the circumscribed rectangular box of E into
rectangular boxes with sides <math>\Delta x</math>, <math>\Delta y</math>, and <math>\Delta z</math> (Figure 12.6.3). The partition points of
this three-dimensional partition have the form
<math>(x_k, y_l, z_m), \qquad 0 \le k \le n, \qquad 0 \le l \le p, \qquad 0 \le m \le q.</math>
The triple Riemann sum of <math>f(x, y, z) \Delta x \Delta y \Delta z</math> over E is defined as the sum
<math display="block">\sum \sum_{E} \sum f(x, y, z) \Delta x \Delta y \Delta z = \sum_{(x_k, y_l, z_m) \text{ in } E} \int f(x_k, y_l, z_m) \Delta x \Delta y \Delta z.</math>
When we replace <math>\Delta x</math>, <math>\Delta y</math>, <math>\Delta z</math> by positive infinitesimals <math>dx</math>, <math>dy</math>, <math>dz</math> we obtain an infinite
triple Riemann sum
<math display="block">\sum_{E} \sum_{z} f(x, y, z) dx dy dz.</math>

<math display="block">\sum_{E} \sum f(x, y, z) dx dy dz</math>
is a finite hyperreal number and therefore has a standard part.
We are now ready to define the triple integral (see Figure 12.6.4).

DEFINITION
Given positive infinitesimal <math>dx</math>, <math>dy</math>, and <math>dz</math>, the <b>triple integral</b> of a continuous
function <math>f(x, y, z)</math> over E is
<math display="block">\iiint f(x, y, z) dx dy dz = st \left( \sum_{E} \sum_{E} f(x, y, z) dx dy dz \right).</math>
We shall now briefly state some basic theorems on triple integrals, which
are exactly like the corresponding theorems for double integrals.
INDEPENDENCE OF dx, dy, AND dz
The value of <math>\iiint_E f(x, y, z) dx dy dz</math> does not depend on <math>dx</math>, <math>dy</math>, or <math>dz</math>.
We shall usually use the notation <math>dV = dx dy dz</math> for the volume of an
infinitesimal <math>dx</math> by <math>dy</math> by <math>dz</math> rectangular box, and write
<math display="block">\iiint_E f(x, y, z) dV \qquad \text{for} \quad \iiint_E f(x, y, z) dx dy dz.</math>
<b>ADDITION PROPERTY</b>
If E is divided into two regions <math>E_1</math> and <math>E_2</math> which meet only on a common
boundary then
<math display="block">\iiint_E f(x, y, z) dV = \iiint_{E_1} f(x, y, z) dV + \iiint_{E_2} f(x, y, z) dV.</math>

ITERATED INTEGRAL THEOREM
If E is the region
<math>a_1 \le x \le a_2</math>, <math>b_1(x) \le y \le b_2(x)</math>, <math>c_1(x, y) \le z \le c_2(x, y)</math>,
<math display="block">\iiint f(x, y, z) \, dV = \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1(x)}^{b_2(x)} \int_{c_1(x, y)}^{c_2(x, y)} f(x, y, z) \, dz \, dy \, dx.</math>
then
If the region E is a rectangular box
<math>a_1 \le x \le a_2, \quad b_1 \le y \le b_2, \quad c_1 \le z \le c_2,</math>
there are six different iterated integrals over E, corresponding to six different orders
of integration. Here they are (in "alphabetical" order).
(1) <math display="block"> \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{b_1}^{b_2} \int_{c_1}^{c_2} f(x, y, z) \, dz \, dy \, dx </math> (2) <math display="block"> \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{c_1}^{c_2} \int_{b_1}^{b_2} f(x, y, z) \, dy \, dz \, dx </math>
(3) <math display="block"> \int_{b_1}^{b_2} \int_{a_1}^{a_2} \int_{c_1}^{c_2} f(x, y, z) \, dz \, dx \, dy </math> (4) <math display="block"> \int_{b_1}^{b_2} \int_{c_1}^{c_2} \int_{a_1}^{a_2} f(x, y, z) \, dx \, dz \, dy </math>
(5) <math display="block">\int_{a}^{c_2} \int_{a}^{a_2} \int_{b}^{b_2} f(x, y, z) \, dy \, dx \, dz \qquad (6) \quad \int_{c}^{c_2} \int_{b}^{b_2} \int_{a}^{a_2} f(x, y, z) \, dx \, dy \, dz.</math>
The Iterated Integral Theorem shows that each of these iterated integrals is equal to
the triple integral
<math display="block">\iiint f(x, y, z) \, dV.</math>
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> Evaluate <math>\iiint_E xy^2z^3 \, dV</math> where <math>E</math> is the rectangular box <math>0 \le x \le 2, \quad 0 \le y \le 1, \quad 0 \le z \le 4.</math>
There are six iterated integrals which all have the same value. We compute
one of them, and then another to check our answer.
FIRST SOLUTION <math display="block">\iiint_{z} xy^2 z^3 dV = \int_0^2 \int_0^1 \int_0^4 xy^2 z^3 dz dy dx.</math>
The inside integral is
<math display="block">\int_0^4 xy^2z^3 dz = \frac{xy^2z^4}{4} \bigg|_0^4 = 64xy^2.</math>
The second integral is
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{1} 64xy^{2} dy = \frac{64}{3}xy^{3} \bigg|_{0}^{1} = \frac{64}{3}x.</math>
The final answer is
<math display="block">\int_{0}^{2} \frac{64}{3} x \, dx = \frac{64}{6} x^{2} \bigg|_{0}^{2} = \frac{256}{6} = \frac{128}{3}.</math>

The inside integral is
<math display="block">\int_0^1 xy^2 z^3 \, dy = \frac{1}{3} xy^3 z^3 \bigg|_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} xz^3.</math>

Evaluate <math>\iiint_E y + z \, dV</math> where E is the region shown in Figure 12.6.5,
EXAMPLE 2
<math>0 \le x \le \pi/2</math>, <math>0 \le y \le \sin x</math>, <math>0 \le z \le y \cos x</math>.
Figure 12.6.5
<math display="block">\iiint y + z \, dV = \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^{\sin x} \int_0^{y \cos x} y + z \, dz \, dy \, dx.</math>
SOLUTION
We first evaluate the inside integral.
<math display="block">\int_0^{y\cos x} y + z \, dz = yz + \frac{1}{2}z^2 \bigg|_0^{y\cos x} = y^2 \cos x + \frac{1}{2}y^2 \cos^2 x.</math>
Now we evaluate the second integral.
<math display="block">\int_0^{\sin x} y^2 \cos x + \frac{1}{2} y^2 \cos^2 x \, dy = \frac{1}{3} y^3 (\cos x + \frac{1}{2} \cos^2 x) \bigg]_0^{-1}</math>
<math>=\frac{1}{3}\sin^3 x(\cos x + \frac{1}{2}\cos^2 x).</math>
Finally we evaluate the outside integral.

Here are some applications of the triple Infinite Sum Theorem. Perhaps
the simplest physical interpretation of the triple integral is mass as the triple integral
of density.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
The <b>mass</b> of an object filling a solid region E with continuous density <math>\rho(x, y, z)</math> is
<math display="block">m = \iiint_E \rho(x, y, z) \, dV.</math>
At every point of an element of volume <math>\Delta E</math> the density is infinitely
JUSTIFICATION

<math>\Delta m \approx \rho(x, y, z) \Delta V</math> (compared to <math>\Delta V</math>).
(See Figure 12.6.8.) By the Infinite Sum Theorem,
<math display="block">m = \iiint_{\mathbb{R}} \rho(x, y, z) \, \Delta V.</math>

An object in space has a moment about each coordinate plane.
DEFINITION
If an object in space fills a region E and has continuous density <math>\rho(x, y, z)</math>, its
moments about the coordinate planes are
<math display="block">M_{xy} = \iiint z \rho(x, y, z) \, dV.</math>
<math>M_{xz} = \iiint y \rho(x, y, z) dV.</math>
<math display="block">M_{yz} = \iiint_{\Gamma} x \rho(x, y, z) dV.</math>
The <b>center of mass</b> of the object is the point <math>(\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z})</math>, where m is mass and
<math>\bar{x} = \frac{M_{yz}}{m}, \quad \bar{y} = \frac{M_{xz}}{m}, \quad \bar{z} = \frac{M_{xy}}{m}.</math>
A point mass m has moment <math>M_{xy} = mz</math> about the <math>(x, y)</math> plane

An object in space has a moment of inertia about each coordinate axis.
Intuitively, the moment of inertia about an axis is the analogue of mass for rotations
about the axis.
DEFINITION
If an object in space fills a region E and has continuous density <math>\rho(x, y, z)</math>,
its moments of inertia about the coordinate axes are
<math display="block">I_x = \iiint_E (y^2 + z^2) \rho(x, y, z) dV,</math>
<math display="block">I_{y} = \iiint_{E} (x^2 + z^2) \rho(x, y, z) dV,</math>
<math display="block">I_z = \iiint_{\mathbb{R}} (x^2 + y^2) \rho(x, y, z) dV.</math>
JUSTIFICATION A point mass m has a moment of inertia about the x-axis of
<math display="block">I_x = (y^2 + z^2)m.</math>

12.7 CYLINDRICAL AND SPHERICAL COORDINATES
In evaluating triple integrals it is sometimes easier to use cylindrical or spherical
coordinates instead of rectangular coordinates.
A point <math>(x, y, z)</math> has cylindrical coordinates <math>(\theta, r, z)</math> if
<math>x = r \cos \theta</math>, <math>y = r \sin \theta</math>, <math>z = z</math>.
That is, as we see in Figure 12.7.1, <math>(\theta, r)</math> is a polar coordinate representation of <math>(x, y)</math>,
and z is the height above the <math>(x, y)</math> plane.
The name cylindrical coordinates is used because the graph of the cylindrical
coordinate equation <math>r = \text{constant}</math> is a circular cylinder as shown in Figure 12.7.2.

To get a formula for the triple integral over a cylindrical region E, we use
the Infinite Sum Theorem but take for <math>\Delta E</math> an infinitely small cylindrical box instead
of rectangular box.
CYLINDRICAL INTEGRATION FORMULA
Let E be the cylindrical region
<math>\alpha \le \theta \le \beta</math>, <math>a(\theta) \le r \le b(\theta)</math>, <math>c_1(\theta, r) \le z \le c_2(\theta, r)</math>.
The triple integral of <math>f(x, y, z)</math> over E is
<math display="block">\iiint_{\alpha} f(x, y, z) dV = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{a(\theta)}^{b(\theta)} \int_{c_1(\theta, r)}^{c_2(\theta, r)} f(x, y, z) r dz dr d\theta.</math>
To evaluate the triple integral we substitute
<math>f(x, y, z) = f(r \cos \theta, r \sin \theta, z).</math>
This is like the Polar Integration Formula but has an extra variable z.
In the iterated integral we do not integrate <math>f(x, y, z)</math> but the product of <math>f(x, y, z)</math> and <math>r</math>.
<b>PROOF</b> Let C be the region in the rectangular <math>(\theta, r, z)</math> space given by
<math>\alpha \le \theta \le \beta</math>, <math>a(\theta) \le r \le b(\theta)</math>, <math>c_1(\theta, r) \le z \le c_2(\theta, r)</math>.
The region C is shown in Figure 12.7.7.

radius b, and constant density 1, about its axis.

Step 2 The problem is greatly simplified by a wise choice of coordinate axes. Let
the z-axis be the axis of the cylinder and put the origin at the center of the
base. Then the region <math>E</math> in rectangular coordinates is
<math>-b \le x \le b</math>, <math>-\sqrt{b^2 - x^2} \le y \le \sqrt{b^2 - x^2}</math>, <math>0 \le z \le h</math>,
and in cylindrical coordinates is

Step 3 The problem looks easier in cylindrical coordinates.
<math display="block">x^2 + v^2 = r^2.</math>
<math display="block">I_z = \iiint (x^2 + y^2) \, dV = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^b \int_0^h r^2 r \, dz \, dr \, d\theta</math>

<math display="block">m = \iiint_{n} dV = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\theta} \int_{0}^{n-nr/\theta} r \, dz \, dr \, d\theta</math>

We see from Figure 12.7.12 that a point <math>(x, y, z)</math> has spherical coordinates <math>(\theta, \phi, \rho)</math> if

The graph of the equation <math>\rho = \text{constant}</math> is a sphere with center at the origin (hence
the name spherical coordinates). The graph of <math>\phi</math> = constant is a vertical cone with
vertex at the origin. The graph of <math>\theta</math> = constant is a half-plane through the z-axis.

The rectangular formula is really equivalent to the double integral for the
volume between two surfaces. Similarly, the cylindrical formula is equivalent to the
double integral in polar coordinates for the volume between two surfaces.

Here is the precise definition.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
Given a function <math>z = f(x, y)</math> and a unit vector <math>\mathbf{U} = \cos \alpha \mathbf{i} + \sin \alpha \mathbf{j}</math>, the
derivative of f in the U direction is the limit
<math display="block">f_{\mathbf{U}}(a,b) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{f(a+t\cos\alpha, b+t\sin\alpha) - f(a,b)}{t}.</math>
<math>f_{\mathbf{U}}(a,b)</math> is called a directional derivative of f at <math>(a,b)</math>.
The partial derivatives of <math>f(x, y)</math> are equal to the derivatives of <math>f(x, y)</math> in the
i and j directions:
<math>f_x(a,b) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{f(a + \Delta x, b) - f(a, b)}{\Delta x}</math>
<math display="block">= \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{f(a + t \cos 0, b + t \sin 0) - f(a, b)}{t} = f_{i}(a, b).</math>
<math>f_{y}(a,b) = \lim_{\Delta y \to 0} \frac{f(a,b + \Delta y) - f(a,b)}{\Delta y}</math>
<math display="block">= \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{f\left(a + t\cos\frac{\pi}{2}, b + t\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - f(a, b)}{t} = f_{j}(a, b).</math>

There is an easier way to find the directional derivatives of <math>f(x, y)</math> using the
partial derivatives. It is convenient to combine the partial derivatives into a vector
called the gradient of <math>f</math>.
DEFINITION
The gradient of a function <math>z = f(x, y)</math>, denoted by grad z or grad f, is defined by
<math display="block">\operatorname{grad} z = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \mathbf{j}.</math>
In functional notation,
grad <math>f = f_{\nu}(a,b)\mathbf{i} + f_{\nu}(a,b)\mathbf{j}</math>
Thus grad f is the vector valued function of two variables whose x and y
components are the partial derivatives <math>f_x</math> and <math>f_y</math> (Figure 13.1.3). Sometimes the
notation <math>\nabla f</math> or <math>\nabla z</math> is used for the gradient.

THEOREM 1
Suppose <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is smooth at <math>(a, b)</math>. Then for any unit vector <math>\mathbf{U} = \cos \alpha \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{i}</math>
<math>\sin \alpha \mathbf{j}</math>, the directional derivative <math>f_{\mathbf{U}}(a,b)</math> exists and
<math>f_{\mathbf{U}}(a,b) = \mathbf{U} \cdot \mathbf{grad} f = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \cos \alpha + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \sin \alpha.</math>

Then by the Chain Rule,

We can use Theorem 1 to give a geometric interpretation of the gradient
vector. Let us assume that <math>f(x, y)</math> is smooth at a point <math>(a, b)</math>, and see what happens
to the directional derivatives <math>f_{\mathbf{U}}(a,b)</math> as the unit vector <b>U</b> varies. If both partial
derivatives <math>f_x(a, b)</math> and <math>f_y(a, b)</math> are zero, then the gradient vector and hence all the
directional derivatives are zero. Suppose the partial derivatives are not both zero,
whence grad <math>f \neq 0</math>. Then
<math>f_{11} = \mathbf{U} \cdot \mathbf{grad} \ f = |\mathbf{grad} \ f| \cos \theta</math>
where <math>\theta</math> is the angle between U and grad f. Therefore <math>f_U</math> is a maximum when <math>\cos \theta = 1</math>
and <math>\theta = 0</math>, a minimum when <math>\cos \theta = -1</math> and <math>\theta = \pi</math>, and zero when <math>\cos \theta = 0</math> and
<math>\theta = \pi/2</math>. We have proved the following corollary.
<b>COROLLARY 1</b>
Suppose <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is smooth and grad <math>f \neq 0</math> at <math>(a, b)</math>. Then the length of
grad f is the largest directional derivative of f, and the direction of grad f
is the direction of the largest directional derivative of f.
On a surface <math>z = f(x, y)</math>, the direction of the gradient vector is called the
direction of steepest ascent, and the direction opposite the gradient vector is called
the direction of steepest descent (Figure 13.1.4).
<b>COROLLARY 2</b>
Suppose <math>z = f(x, y)</math> is smooth and <math>\partial z/\partial y \neq 0</math> at <math>(a, b)</math>. Then <b>grad</b> <math>f</math> is normal
(perpendicular) to the level curve at <math>(a, b)</math>. That is, <math>\operatorname{grad} f</math> is perpendicular
to the tangent line of the level curve (Figure 13.1.5).

PROOF By the Implicit Function Theorem, the level curve
<math display="block">f(x, y) - f(a, b) = 0</math>
has the tangent line
<math>\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}(x-a) + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}(y-b) = 0.</math>
<math>(a, b)</math> is on this line. Let <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> be any other point on the line. Then
<math display="block">\mathbf{D} = (x_0 - a)\mathbf{i} + (y_0 - b)\mathbf{j}</math>
is a direction vector of the line, and
<math display="block">\mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{grad} f = (x_0 - a) \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + (y_0 - b) \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 0.</math>
Thus grad <math>f</math> is perpendicular to the direction vector <b>D</b>.
Water always flows down a hill in the direction of steepest descent. Thus
on a topographic map, the course of a river must always be perpendicular to the
level curves, as in Figure 13.1.6.

13.2. LINE INTEGRALS
There are two ways to generalize the integral to functions of two or more variables.
One way is the line integral, which we shall study in this section. The other is the
multiple integral, which was studied in Chapter 12.
The line integral can be motivated by the notion of work in physics. The
work done by a constant force vector F acting along a directed line segment from
A to B is the inner product
<math>W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{S}</math>
where S is the vector from <math>A</math> to <math>B</math> (Figure 13.2.1).

DEFINITION
A smooth curve from A to B is a curve C given by parametric equations
<math>x = g(s), \quad y = h(s) \qquad 0 \le s \le L,</math>
<math>A = (g(0), h(0)), \qquad B = (g(L), h(L)),</math>
where:
<math>L = length of curve,</math>
<math>s = length of the curve from A to (x, y),</math>
<math>dx/ds</math> and <math>dy/ds</math> are continuous for <math>0 \le s \le L</math>.
We call A the initial point and B the terminal point of C. A smooth curve from
A to B is also called a directed curve, and is drawn with arrows.
Given s and an infinitesimal change <math>\Delta s = ds</math>, we let,
<math>\Delta x = g(s + \Delta s) - g(s), \qquad dx = g'(s) ds,</math>
<math>\Delta y = h(s + \Delta s) - h(s), \qquad dy = h'(s) ds,</math>
<math display="block">\Delta \mathbf{S} = \Delta x \mathbf{i} + \Delta y \mathbf{j}, \qquad d\mathbf{S} = dx \mathbf{i} + dy \mathbf{j}.</math>
Thus <math>\Delta S</math> is the vector from the point <math>(x, y)</math> to <math>(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y)</math> on C, and dS is an
infinitesimal vector tangent to <math>C</math> at <math>(x, y)</math> (Figure 13.2.4).

Notice that the inner product of <math>F</math> and <math>dS</math> is

This is why we use both notations <math>\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}</math> and <math>\int_C P \, dx + Q \, dy</math> for the line integral.
DEFINITION
The work done by a continuous force vector <math>\mathbf{F}(x, y)</math> along a smooth curve C
is given by the line integral
<math display="block">W = \int_{a} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}.</math>
JUSTIFICATION We can justify this definition by using the Infinite Sum Theorem
from Chapter 6. Let <math>W(u, v)</math> be the work done along C from <math>s = u</math> to <math>s = v</math>
(Figure 13.2.5). Then <math>W(u, v)</math> has the Addition Property, because the work
done from <math>u</math> to <math>v</math> plus the work done from <math>v</math> to <math>w</math> is the work done from <math>u</math> to <math>w</math>.
On an infinitesimal piece of C from s to <math>s + \Delta s</math>, the work done is
<math>\Delta W \approx \mathbf{F}(x, y) \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} \approx \mathbf{F}(x, y) \cdot d\mathbf{S}</math>
(compared to <math>\Delta s</math>).
<math display="block">\mathbf{F}(x, y) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = P \, dx + Q \, dy = \left( P \frac{dx}{ds} + Q \frac{dy}{ds} \right) \, ds.</math>

<b>THEOREM</b>
Let <math>\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}</math> be a line integral.
(i) If C is a horizontal directed line segment <math>x_0 \le x \le x_1</math>, <math>y = y_0</math>, then

(ii) If C is a vertical directed line segment <math>x=x_0,y_0\leq y\leq y_1,</math> then
<math display="block">\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_{y_0}^{y_1} Q(x_0, y) \, dy.</math>
(iii) If C is traced by a parametric curve
<math>x = g(t),</math> <math>y = h(t),</math> <math>c_0 \le t \le c_1</math>

A piecewise smooth curve is a curve C that can be broken into finitely many
smooth pieces <math>C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_n</math> where the terminal point of one piece is the initial
point of the next (Figure 13.2.9). For example, a curve formed by two or more sides
of a rectangle or a polygon is piecewise smooth. The line integral of <math>F(x, y)</math> over a
piecewise smooth curve <math>C</math> is defined as the sum
<math display="block">\int_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_{C_{1}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} + \int_{C_{2}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} + \dots + \int_{C_{n}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}.</math>

points are equal and that does not cross or retrace its path. Examples of simple
closed curves are the perimeters of a circle, a triangle, and a rectangle. The value
of a line integral around a simple closed curve C depends on whether the length s
is measured clockwise or counterclockwise, but does not depend on the initial point
(Figure 13.2.11). The clockwise and counterclockwise line integrals of F around a
simple closed curve C are denoted by

\oint_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}, \qquad \oint_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}.

Line integrals in space are developed in a similar way. Instead of an open
rectangle we work in an open rectangular solid. A smooth curve C in space has three
parametric equations with continuous derivatives,
<math>x = g(s),</math> <math>y = h(s),</math> <math>z = l(s),</math> <math>0 \le s \le L.</math>
Given a continuous vector valued function
<math>F(x, y, z) = P(x, y, z)i + O(x, y, z)j + R(x, y, z)k</math>
and a smooth curve C in space, we define the line integral of F along C, in symbols,

13.3 INDEPENDENCE OF PATH
13.3 INDEPENDENCE OF PATH
For functions of one variable, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus shows that
the integral is the opposite of the derivative. In this section we shall see that the line
integral is the opposite of the gradient.
By a vector field we mean a vector valued function
<math>\mathbf{F}(x, y) = P(x, y)\mathbf{i} + Q(x, y)\mathbf{j}</math>
where <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> are smooth functions on an open rectangle <math>D</math>.
For example, if <math>f(x, y)</math> has continuous second partials on D then its gradient
<b>grad</b> f is a vector field.
Many vector fields are found in physics. Examples are gravitational force
fields and magnetic force fields, in which a force vector <math>\mathbf{F}(x, y)</math> is associated with each
point <math>(x, y)</math>. Another example is the flow velocity <math>V(x, y)</math> of a fluid. A vector field in
economics is the demand vector
<math>\mathbf{D}(x, y) = D_1(x, y)\mathbf{i} + D_2(x, y)\mathbf{j}</math>
where <math>D_1(x, y)</math> is the demand for commodity one and <math>D_2(x, y)</math> is the demand for
commodity two at the prices x for commodity one and y for commodity two. All of
the examples above have analogues for three variables and three dimensions (and
the demand vector for <math>n</math> commodities has <math>n</math> variables and <math>n</math> dimensions).
DEFINITION
<math>f(x, y)</math> is a <b>potential function</b> of the vector field <math>Pi + Qj</math> if the gradient of f is
<math>Pi + Qj</math>.
Not every vector field has a potential function. Theorem 1 below shows
which vector fields have potential functions, and Theorem 2 tells how to find a
potential function when there is one.
Using the equality of mixed partials, we see that if the vector field <math>Pi + Qj</math>
has a potential function, then <math>\partial P/\partial y = \partial Q/\partial x</math>. If f is a potential function of <math>P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}</math>,
we have
grad <math>f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\partial P}{\partial v} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial v \partial x} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}.</math>
The vector field <math>-y\mathbf{i} + x\mathbf{j}</math> has no potential function, because
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b>
<math>\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial (-y)}{\partial y} = -1, \qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial x} = 1.</math>
THEOREM 1
A vector field <math>P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}</math> has a potential function if and only if <math>\frac{\partial P}{\partial v} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \mathbf{v}}</math>.

We have already proved one direction. We postpone the proof of the other
direction until later.
By definition, grad <math>f = Pi + Qj</math> if and only if <math>df = P dx + Q dy</math>. In general,
an expression <math>P dx + Q dy</math> is called a differential form. A differential form is called
an exact differential if it is equal to the total differential df of some function <math>f(x, y)</math>.
Using this terminology, Theorem 1 states that: <math>P dx + Q dy</math> is an exact
differential if and only if <math>\partial P/\partial y = \partial Q/\partial x</math>.

There is no potential function.
<b>EXAMPLE 3</b> Test for existence of a potential function:
