<math display="block">\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial (3x^2y^2)}{\partial y} = 6x^2y,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial (y^2 + 2x^3y)}{\partial y} = 6x^2y.</math>
There is a potential function.
THEOREM 2 (Path Independence Theorem)
Let <math>P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}</math> be a vector field such that <math>\partial P/\partial y = \partial Q/\partial x</math> and let A and B be
two points of D.
Let <math>f</math> be a potential function for <math>Pi + Qj</math>. For any piecewise smooth
(i)
curve C from A to B,
<math display="block">\int_C P \, dx + Q \, dy = f(B) - f(A).</math>
Since the line integral in this case depends only on the points A and B and
not on the curve C (Figure 13.3.1), we write
<math display="block">\int_{a}^{B} P \, dx + Q \, dy = \int_{C} P \, dx + Q \, dy.</math>
g is a potential function for <math>Pi + Qj</math> if and only if g has the form
(11)
<math display="block">g(x, y) = \int_{A}^{(x,y)} P dx + Q dy + K</math>
for some constant K.

Independence of path
Theorem 2 is important in physics. A vector field of forces which has a
potential function is called a conservative force field. The negative of a potential
function for a conservative force field is called a potential energy function. Gravity,
static electricity, and magnetism are conservative force fields. Part (i) of the theorem
shows that the work done by a conservative force field along a curve depends only
on the initial and terminal points of the curve and is equal to the decrease in potential
energy.
Mathematically, Theorem 2 is like the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
It shows that the line integral of grad f along any curve from A to B is equal to the
change in the value of f from A to B. When <math>A = B</math>, we have an interesting con-
sequence:
If <math>f(x, y)</math> has continuous second partials then the line integral of the gradient
of f around a simple closed curve is zero,
<math display="block">\oint_C \operatorname{grad} f \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0.</math>
Using part (ii), we can find a potential function <math>f(x, y)</math> for a vector field
<math>Pi + Qj</math> in three steps.
<math display="block">\frac{\partial P}{\partial v} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} \text{ on } D.</math>

We conclude this section with the proofs of Theorems 1 and 2. The proof
of Theorem 1 uses a lemma about derivatives of partial integrals.
<b>LEMMA</b>
Suppose <math>P(x, y)</math> is smooth on an open rectangle containing the point <math>(a, b)</math>. Then
<math display="block">\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \int_{a}^{x} P(t, y) dt = P(x, y),</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \int_{a}^{x} P(t, y) dt = \int_{a}^{x} \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}(t, y) dt.</math>
PROOF The first formula follows at once from the Fundamental Theorem of
Calculus. For the second formula, let <math>\Delta y</math> be a nonzero infinitesimal and let
<math display="block">z = \int_{a}^{x} P(t, y) dt.</math>

Taking standard parts, <math>\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{x} \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}(t, y) dt</math>.

<math>\operatorname{grad} g = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}</math>,

<math>\frac{\partial (g-f)}{\partial y} = 0</math> and <math>\frac{\partial (g-f)}{\partial y} = 0</math>,
<math>g - f</math> depends only on y and only on x,
<math>g(x, y) - f(x, y) = \text{constant},</math>
<math>g(x, y) = \int_{-1}^{x} P dx + Q dy + \text{constant.}</math>

13.4 GREEN'S THEOREM
Green's Theorem gives a relationship between double integrals and line integrals.
It is a two-dimensional analogue of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,
<math display="block">F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b F'(x) dx,</math>
and shows that the line integral of <math>F(x, y)</math> around the boundary of a plane region D
is equal to a certain double integral over D.
Let D be a plane region
<math>a_1 \le x \le a_2</math>, <math>b_1(x) \le y \le b_2(x)</math>.
The directed curve which goes around the boundary of D in the counterclockwise
direction is denoted by <math>\partial D</math> and is called the boundary of D (Figure 13.4.1).

As a corollary to Green's Theorem we get a formula for the area of D.
COROLLARY
If D has a piecewise smooth boundary, then the area of D is
<math display="block">A = \oint_{an} x \, dy = \oint_{an} -y \, dx.</math>
PROOF By Green's Theorem,

<math display="block">\oint_{\partial D} -y \, dx = \iint_{D} \frac{\partial 0}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial (-y)}{\partial y} \, dA = \iint_{D} dA = A.</math>

GREEN'S THEOREM (Vector Form)
Given a vector field <math>\mathbf{F}(x, y) = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}</math> on a region D with a piecewise smooth
boundary,
<math display="block">
\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{T} \, ds = \iint_{D} \operatorname{curl} \mathbf{F} \, dA,
</math>
<math display="block">
\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, ds = \iint_{D} \operatorname{div} \mathbf{F} \, dA.
</math>
The physical meaning of Green's theorem can be explained in terms of the
flow of a fluid (a liquid or gas). Let the vector field <math>F(x, y)</math> represent the rate and
direction of fluid flow at a point <math>(x, y)</math> in the plane. Consider a plane region D and
element of area <math>\Delta D</math> containing <math>(x, y)</math> (Figure 13.4.8).

We first explain the formula
<math display="block">\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{T} \, ds = \iint_{D} \operatorname{curl} \mathbf{F} \, dA.</math>
The line integral <math>\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{T} \, ds</math> of the flow component in the direction tangent to the
boundary is called the <i>circulation</i> of <b>F</b> around <math>\partial D</math>. Green's Theorem states that the
circulation of F around the boundary of D equals the integral of the curl of F over D
(Figure 13.4.9).

When we apply Green's theorem to an element of area <math>\Delta D</math> we get
<math display="block">\oint_{\partial \Delta D} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{T} \, ds \approx \text{curl } \mathbf{F} \, \Delta A \qquad \text{(compared to } \Delta A\text{)}.</math>
Thus the curl of <math>\mathbf{F}</math> at <math>(x, y)</math> is equal to the circulation per unit area at <math>(x, y)</math>.
If curl F is identically zero, the fluid flow F is called irrotational. By the
Exactness Criterion, F is irrotational if and only if <math>P dx + Q dy</math> is an exact differential.
The circulation of an irrotational field around any <math>\partial D</math> is zero.
Next we explain the formula
<math display="block">\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, ds = \iint_{D} \operatorname{div} \mathbf{F} \, dA.</math>
The line integral <math>\oint_{a} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, ds</math> of the flow component in the direction of the outward
normal vector is called the flux across <math>\partial D</math>. The flux is the net rate at which fluid is
flowing from inside D across the boundary and is therefore equal to the rate of
decrease of the mass inside D. Green's Theorem states that the flux of F across the
boundary of D equals the integral of the divergence of <math>\mathbf{F}</math> over D (Figure 13.4.10).

Therefore the divergence of F at <math>(x, y)</math> is the net rate of flow of fluid away from <math>(x, y)</math>.
and is equal to the rate of decrease in density at <math>(x, y)</math>. Positive divergence means that
the density is decreasing, and negative divergence means that the density is increasing.
If div F is identically zero, the fluid flow is called solenoidal, or incompressible.
By the Exactness Criterion, F is incompressible if and only if <math>-Q dx + P dy</math> is an
exact differential. The flux of an incompressible field across any <math>\partial D</math> is zero.

The line integral has an analogue for surfaces called the surface integral.
The form of the line integral which is most easily generalized to surfaces is the vector
form
<math display="block">\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, ds = \int_C -Q \, dx + P \, dy</math>
where N is the unit normal vector of C. This is convenient because surfaces also have
unit normal vectors.

Before stating the definition we motivate it with a fluid flow interpretation.
Remember that in the plane the line integral
<math display="block">\int_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, ds</math>
is equal to the flux, or net rate of fluid flow across the curve C in the direction of the
normal vector N.
Consider a fluid flow field
<math display="block">F(x, y, z) = Pi + Qj + Rk</math>
and a surface S in space. Call one side of S positive and the other side negative, and
at each point of S let N be the unit normal vector on the positive side of S. The surface
integral
<math display="block">\iint_{S} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, dS</math>
will be the flux, or net rate of fluid flow across the surface S from the negative to the
positive side (Figure 13.5.5).
With this interpretation in mind we shall define the surface integral and then
justify the definition. First we need the notion of an oriented surface.
DEFINITION
An oriented surface S is a smooth surface
<math>z = g(x, y)</math>
over a plane region D with a piecewise smooth boundary, together with an
orientation that designates one side of the surface as positive and the other
side as negative. (See Figure 13.5.6.)

13.6 THEOREMS OF STOKES AND GAUSS
Both Stokes' Theorem and Gauss' Theorem are three-dimensional generalizations
of Green's Theorem. To state these theorems we need the notions of curl and
divergence in three dimensions. The curl of a vector field in the plane is a scalar field,
while the curl of a vector field in space is another vector field. However, the divergence
in both cases is scalar.
<b>DEFINITION</b>
Given a vector field <math>\mathbf{F}(x, y, z) = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}</math>
in space. The curl of F is the new vector field
<math display="block">\operatorname{curl} \mathbf{F} = \left(\frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x}\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \mathbf{k}.</math>
This can be remembered by writing the curl as a "determinant"
<math display="block">\mathbf{curl}\,\mathbf{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{1} & \mathbf{J} & \mathbf{K} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ \mathbf{P} & \mathbf{O} & \mathbf{P} \end{vmatrix}.</math>

<math display="block">\operatorname{div} \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}.</math>
Find the curl and divergence of the vector field
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b>

<math display="block">= \left(\frac{\partial(zx)}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial(yz)}{\partial z}\right)\mathbf{i} + \left(\frac{\partial(xy)}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial(zx)}{\partial x}\right)\mathbf{j} + \left(\frac{\partial(yz)}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial(xy)}{\partial y}\right)\mathbf{k}</math>
<math>= -y\mathbf{i} - z\mathbf{j} - x\mathbf{k}</math>.
<math display="block">\operatorname{div} \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial(xy)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(yz)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(xz)}{\partial z} = y + z + x.</math>
Two interesting identities are given in the next theorem.
THEOREM 1
Assume the function <math>f(x, y, z)</math> and vector field <math>\mathbf{F}(x, y, z)</math> have continuous second
partials. Then
<math>\operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{grad} f) = 0, \quad \operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl} F) = 0.</math>
<b>PROOF</b> We use the equality of mixed partials.
grad <math>f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\mathbf{k}</math>.
<math display="block">\mathbf{curl}(\mathbf{grad}\,f) = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \end{vmatrix}</math>
<math display="block">= \left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial v \, \partial z} - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z \, \partial v}\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z \, \partial x} - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \, \partial z}\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \, \partial y} - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \, \partial x}\right) \mathbf{k}</math>
<math>= 0.</math>
The other proof is similar and is left as a problem.

<math display="block">\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{T} \, ds = \iint_{\mathcal{C}} \operatorname{curl} \mathbf{F} \, dA.</math>

13.6 THEOREMS OF STOKES AND GAUSS
Thus Stokes' Theorem has the scalar form
<math display="block">\oint_{\partial S} P \, dx + Q \, dy + R \, dz = \iint_{\partial S} \left( -H \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} - L \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} + M \right) dA.</math>
Stokes' Theorem has two corollaries which are analogous to the Path
Independence Theorem.
COROLLARY 1
If <math>f(x, y, z)</math> has continuous second partials, then the line integral of grad f
around the boundary of any oriented surface is zero,
<math display="block">\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{grad} \ f \cdot \mathbf{T} \ ds = 0.</math>
(See Figure 13.6.3.)
<i>PROOF</i> <math>\operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{grad} f) = 0</math>, so
<math display="block">\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{grad} \, f \cdot \mathbf{T} \, ds = \iiint \mathbf{curl}(\mathbf{grad} \, f) \cdot \mathbf{N} \, dS = \iiint 0 \, dS = 0.</math>
<b>COROLLARY 2</b>
The surface integral of curl F over an oriented surface depends only on the
boundary of the surface. That is, if <math>\partial S_1 = \partial S_2</math> then
<math display="block">\iint_{S} \operatorname{curl} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N}_{1} dS_{1} = \iint_{S} \operatorname{curl} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N}_{2} dS_{2}.</math>
(See Figure 13.6.4.)

Gauss' Theorem shows a relationship between a triple integral over a region
E in space and a surface integral over the boundary of E. It corresponds to Green's
Theorem in the form
<math display="block">\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, ds = \iint \operatorname{div} \mathbf{F} \, dA.</math>
Before stating Gauss' Theorem, we must explain what is meant by the surface
integral over the boundary of a solid region E. In general, the boundary of E is made
up of six surfaces corresponding to the six faces of a cube (Figure 13.6.7). Sometimes
one or more faces will degenerate to a line or a point.
y
Figure 13.6.7
The top and bottom faces of E are <math>(x, y)</math> surfaces, that is, they are given by equations
<math>z = c(x, y)</math>. However, the left and right faces of E are <math>(x, z)</math> surfaces <math>y = b(x, z)</math>, while
the front and back faces of E are <math>(y, z)</math> surfaces of the form <math>x = a(y, z)</math>. Surface integrals
over oriented <math>(x, z)</math> and <math>(y, z)</math> surfaces are defined exactly as for <math>(x, y)</math> surfaces except
that the variables are interchanged.
In the following discussion E is a solid region all of whose faces are smooth
surfaces.
DEFINITION
The <b>boundary</b> of E, <math>\partial E</math>, is the union of the six faces of E oriented so that
the outside surfaces are positive. The surface integral of a vector field <math>\mathbf{F}(x, y, z)</math>
over <math>\partial E</math>,
<math display="block">\iint \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, dS,</math>
is the sum of the surface integrals of F over the six faces of E. (See Figure
13.6.8.)

We are now ready to state Gauss' Theorem.
GAUSS' THEOREM
Given a vector field <math>F(x, y, z)</math> and a solid region <math>E</math>,
<math display="block">\iint_{SF} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, dS = \iiint_{S} \operatorname{div} \mathbf{F} \, dV.</math>
This equation may also be written in the form
<math display="block">\iint_{\partial F} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{N} \, dS = \iiint_{F} \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z} \, dV.</math>
Gauss' Theorem is sometimes called the Divergence Theorem.
For fluid flow, Gauss' Theorem states that the outward rate of flow across
the boundary of E is equal to the integral of the divergence over E (Figure 13.6.9).
As in the two-dimensional case, the divergence is the rate at which the density is
decreasing.

14.1 EQUATIONS WITH SEPARABLE VARIABLES
A first order differential equation is an equation involving an independent variable t,
a dependent variable y, and the derivative <math>dy/dt</math>. In many applications, the independent
variable t is time. A first order differential equation can be put in the following
form, where <math>f(t, y)</math> is continuous in both t and y.
FIRST ORDER DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION
<math>\frac{dy}{dt} = f(t, y).</math>
<b>(1)</b>
For instance, if <math>t</math> is time and <math>y</math> is the position of a particle at time <math>t</math>, the differential
equation (1) gives the velocity of the particle in terms of time and position. A
differential equation gives information about an unknown function <math>y(t)</math>. The general
solution of a first order differential equation is the family of all functions <math>y(t)</math> that
satisfy the equation. Each function in this family is called a particular solution of
the differential equation. In most cases, the family of functions will depend in some
way on a constant C, and the graphs of these functions will form a family of curves
that fill up the <math>(t, y)</math> plane but do not touch each other, as in Figure 14.1.1.
Some examples of first order differential equations were solved in Section 8.6.
For instance, it was shown that the general solution of the differential equation
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dt} = y(1 - y)</math>
<math>y(t) = \frac{1}{1 + Ce^{-t}}, \quad y(t) = 0.</math>
is
There is one particular solution for each value of the constant <math>C</math>, and one additional
particular solution <math>y(t) = 0</math>. The graph of this general solution is shown in Figure
14.1.2.

(3)
In an equation with separable variables, <math>dy/dt</math> is a product of a function of t and a
function of y. In particular, <math>dy/dt = g(t)</math> is a differential equation with separable
variables in which <math>h(y)</math> is the constant 1. Similarly, <math>dy/dt = h(y)</math> is a differential
equation with separable variables in which <math>g(t)</math> is the constant 1. An equation with
separable variables can be solved by separating the variables and integrating both
sides of the equation.

14.2 FIRST ORDER HOMOGENEOUS LINEAR EQUATIONS
In this section we study the following special type of differential equation.
FIRST ORDER HOMOGENEOUS LINEAR DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION
<math display="block">y' + p(t)y = 0.</math>
<b>(1)</b>
It is understood that t varies over some interval in the real line, and <math>p(t)</math> is a con-
tinuous function of t in the interval. The equation is called <i>linear</i> because y and y'
occur only linearly and homogeneous because the right side of the equation is zero.
The equation
<math>y' = ky</math>, or <math>y' - ky = 0</math>,
for exponential growth (see Section 8.6) is an example. The first order homogeneous
linear differential equation (1) has separable variables, because it can be written as
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dt} = -p(t)y.</math>
Its solution is given by the next formula.
METHOD FOR SOLVING FIRST ORDER HOMOGENEOUS LINEAR DIFFERENTIAL
<b>EQUATION (1)</b>
The general solution is
<math display="block">y(t) = Ce^{-P(t)},</math>
where <math>P(t)</math> is an antiderivative of <math>p(t)</math>. That is,
<math display="block">y(t) = Ce^{-\int p(t) dt}.</math>
This formula is obtained by the procedure described in Section 14.1 for differential
equations with separable variables, as follows. First write the equation in the form
<math display="block">\frac{dy}{dt} = -p(t)y.</math>
There is a constant solution <math>y(t) = 0</math>.
Step 1
Separate the variables and integrate:
Step 2
<math display="block">y^{-1} dy = -p(t) dt.</math>
<math display="block">
ln |y| = -\int p(t) dt + B.
</math>

14.3 FIRST ORDER LINEAR EQUATIONS
We shall now give a method for solving a differential equation of the following type.
FIRST ORDER LINEAR DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION
<math>v' + p(t)v = f(t)</math>.
<b>(1)</b>
Both <math>p(t)</math> and <math>f(t)</math> are continuous functions of t, where t varies over some interval I
in the real line. When <math>f(t)</math> is the constant function with value 0, the equation is a
homogeneous linear differential equation of the type studied in Section 14.2.
First order linear differential equations arise in models of population
growth with immigration. Suppose a population <math>y(t)</math> has a net birthrate of <math>b(t)</math> and
net immigration rate of <math>f(t)</math>. The net birthrate <math>b(t)</math> is the excess of births over deaths
per unit of population in one unit of time. In a small period of time of length <math>\Delta t</math>,
the difference of births and deaths is <math>b(t) \cdot y(t) \cdot \Delta t</math>, and the net immigration is
<math>f(t) \cdot \Delta t</math>. Then the population will be a solution of the differential equation
<math>y' = b(t)y + f(t)</math>, which is the same as equation (1) with <math>p(t) = -b(t)</math>.
The size of a bank account that earns interest and also changes due to
deposits and withdrawals can be described by a first order linear differential equation.
If the account earns interest at the rate of <math>r(t)</math> at time t, and the net deposit per unit
of time is <math>f(t)</math>, then the account size <math>y(t)</math> will be a solution of the differential equation
(1) with <math>p(t) = -r(t)</math>.
The next theorem will be helpful in solving an equation of the type (1).
THEOREM 1
Suppose that <math>y(t)</math> is a particular solution of the first order linear differential
equation
<math display="block">y' + p(t)y = f(t),</math>
<b>(1)</b>
and <math>x(t)</math> is a nonzero particular solution of the corresponding homogeneous
equation
<math display="block">x' + p(t)x = 0.</math>
<b>(2)</b>
Then the general solution of the original equation (1) is
<math>y(t) + Cx(t)</math>.
We already know from Section 14.2 how to solve the homogeneous linear
equation (2). So if we can find one particular solution of the linear equation (1), we
can use Theorem 1 to find the general solution. We postpone the proof of Theorem 1
to the end of this section.
A particular solution of a linear equation (1) can be found by the method
called variation of constants. Start with a particular solution <math>x(t)</math> of the corresponding

We conclude this section with a proof of Theorem 1. The proof uses the
Principle of Superposition.
PRINCIPLE OF SUPERPOSITION (First Order)
Suppose <math>x(t)</math> and <math>y(t)</math> are solutions of the two first order linear differential
equations
<math>x' + p(t)x = f(t),</math>
<math display="block">y' + p(t)y = g(t).</math>
Then for any constants A and B, the function
<math>u(t) = Ax(t) + By(t)</math>
is a solution of the linear differential equation
<math>u' + p(t)u = Af(t) + Bg(t)</math>.
Notice that all three differential equations have the same <math>p(t)</math>. The Principle
of Superposition follows from the Constant and Sum Rules for derivatives:
<math display="block">u' + p(t)u = (Ax + By)' + p(t)(Ax + By)</math>
<math>= Ax' + By' + Ap(t)x + Bp(t)y</math>
<math display="block">= A(x' + p(t)x) + B(y' + p(t)y)</math>
<math>= Af(t) + Bg(t).</math>
<b>PROOF OF THEOREM 1</b> We are given that y and x are solutions of
<math>y' + p(t)y = f(t)</math>
<b>(1)</b>
and
<math display="block">x' + p(t)x = 0.</math>
<b>(2)</b>
We must prove that a function <math>u(t)</math> is a solution of
<math>u' + p(t)u = f(t)</math>
<b>(3)</b>
if and only if <math>u = y + Cx</math> for some constant C.
Assume first that <math>u = y + Cx</math>. By the Principle of Superposition,
<math display="block">u' + p(t)u = f(t) + C \cdot 0 = f(t),</math>
so <math>u</math> is a solution of (3).

Now assume that <math>u</math> is a solution of (3). Using the Principle of Superposition
again,
<math>(u - v)' + p(t)(u - v) = f(t) - f(t) = 0.</math>
Thus <math>u - y</math> is a solution of the homogeneous linear equation (2). The
general solution of equation (2) is <math>Cx</math>. Therefore for some constant <math>C</math>,
<math>u - v = Cx</math> and <math>u = v + Cx</math>.

14.4 EXISTENCE AND APPROXIMATION OF SOLUTIONS
This section deals with arbitrary first order differential equations. It is optional and
therefore can be omitted if desired. Most first order differential equations cannot
be solved explicitly. However, it is possible to approximate a solution by a method
similar to the Riemann sum for the definite integral. The Euler approximation

## PDF page 875

865
14.4 EXISTENCE AND APPROXIMATION OF SOLUTIONS
starts by dividing the interval <math>[a, \infty)</math> into small subintervals of length <math>\Delta t</math>. When
<math>\Delta t</math> is real, it gives an approximate solution that can be computed numerically. When
<math>\Delta t</math> is infinitesimal, it leads to a precise solution and is useful because it shows that
a solution exists.
Throughout this section, we shall work with a first order differential equation
with an initial value
<math display="block">y' = f(t, y), \qquad y(a) = y_0.</math>
<b>(1)</b>
We assume once and for all that <math>f(t, y)</math> is continuous for all <math>t</math> and <math>y</math>.
DEFINITION
Let <math>\Delta t</math> be positive, and partition the interval <math>[a, \infty)</math> into subintervals of
length <math>\Delta t</math>. The Euler approximation for the initial value problem (1) is the
function <math>Y(t)</math>, <math>a \le t</math>, defined as follows. Start the graph of <math>Y(t)</math> at the point
<math>(a, y_0)</math>. Then move from <math>(a, y_0)</math> to <math>(a + \Delta t, Y(a + \Delta t))</math> along a straight line
with slope <math>f(a, Y(a))</math>. Once the value <math>Y(t)</math> is computed for a partition point
<math>t = a + k \Delta t</math>, move from <math>(t, Y(t))</math> to the next partition point <math>(t + \Delta t, Y(t + \Delta t))</math>
along a straight line with slope <math>f(t, Y(t))</math>.
The graph of <math>Y(t)</math> is the broken line shown in Figure 14.4.1. Each piece has
the slope required by the differential equation (1) at the beginning of the subinterval.
If <math>\Delta t</math> is small, then since <math>f(t, y)</math> is continuous, the slope of <math>Y(t)</math> should be close to
the correct slope. Thus we would expect <math>Y(t)</math> to be close to a solution of (1).
ŧ
Figure 14.4.1
The values of <math>Y(t)</math> at the partition points can be computed by an iteration
that can easily be carried out on a computer. The first three values are
<math>Y(a) = y_0</math>
<math display="block">Y(a + \Delta t) = y_0 + f(a, y_0) \Delta t,</math>
<math display="block">Y(a + 2 \Delta t) = Y(a + \Delta t) + f(a + \Delta t, Y(a + \Delta t)) \Delta t.</math>
Given the value <math>Y(t)</math> for a partition point <math>t = a + k \Delta t</math>, the next value <math>Y(t + \Delta t)</math> is

Using the sigma notation, the <math>(k + 1)^{st}</math> value of <math>Y(t)</math> can be written as
<math display="block">Y(a + k \Delta t) = y_0 + \sum_{n=0}^{k-1} f(a + n \Delta t, Y(a + n \Delta t)) \Delta t.</math>
This equation may also be written in the manner of a Riemann sum with <math>b = a + k \Delta t</math>:
<math display="block">Y(b) = y_0 + \sum_{a}^{b} f(t, Y(t)) \Delta t.</math>

which is approximately equal to <math>y_0</math> plus the integral
<math display="block">y(b) = y_0 + \int_0^b f(t) dt.</math>

We now consider Euler approximations with infinitesimal <math>\Delta t</math>. These approxi-
mations cannot be computed directly but are useful in showing that a differential
equation has a solution.
The Euler approximation <math>Y(t)</math> depends on both t and the increment size <math>\Delta t</math>.
Now let <math>\Delta t</math> be positive infinitesimal. By the Transfer Principle, <math>Y(t + \Delta t)</math> is still
given by the rule
<math>Y(t + \Delta t) - Y(t) = f(t, Y(t))\Delta t.</math>
Intuitively, the graph of <math>Y(t)</math> as a function of t is formed from infinitesimal line
segments, and the segment from t to <math>t + \Delta t</math> has slope <math>f(t, Y(t))</math>, as in Figure 14.4.3.
The next theorem shows that the Euler approximation for infinitesimal <math>\Delta t</math>
is infinitely close to a solution of the initial value problem.
<b>EXISTENCE THEOREM</b>
Let <math>\Delta t</math> be positive infinitesimal and let <math>Y(t)</math> be the Euler approximation of
the initial value problem
<math display="block">y' = f(t, y), \qquad y(a) = y_0</math>
<b>(1)</b>

The theorem shows that the initial value problem (1) has a solution
Discussion
as long as <math>Y(t)</math> remains finite. The solution is found by taking the standard
part of <math>Y(t)</math>. When <math>Y(t)</math> becomes infinite, we say that an explosion occurs
(see Example 2 in Section 14.1 and Example 3 in this section).
PROOF OF THE EXISTENCE THEOREM At <math>t = a</math>, <math>y(a) = st(Y(a)) = y_0</math>. Let M
be the largest value of <math>|f(t, Y(t))|</math> for t, a partition point between a and b.
Then M is finite. Since <math>Y(t)</math> never changes by more than <math>M \Delta t</math> from one
partition point to the next, we always have
<math display="block">|Y(t) - Y(s)| \le M|t - s|.</math>
Taking standard parts, we see that for real s and t in the interval <math>[a, b]</math>,
<math display="block">|y(t) - y(s)| \le M|t - s|.</math>
By the Transfer Principle, this also holds for all hyperreal s and t between
a and b. Then for any <math>a \le t \le b</math>,
<math>Y(t) \approx Y(st(t)) \approx y(st(t)) \approx y(t)</math>
and hence, because <math>f(t, z)</math> is continuous in z,
<math>f(t, Y(t)) \approx f(t, y(t)).</math>
Let <math>h(t)</math> be the real function
<math>h(t) = f(t, y(t)).</math>
Since Y is an Euler approximation,

<math display="block">Y(t) = y_0 + \sum_{s=a}^{t} f(s, Y(s)) \Delta t</math>
for each real point t between a and b. But <math>h(s) = f(s, y(s)) \approx f(s, Y(s))</math>, so
<math>Y(t) \approx y_0 + \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} h(s) \Delta t.</math>
This is just the Riemann sum of h. Taking standard parts, we get the integral
of <math>h</math>:
<math display="block">y(t) = y_0 + \int_{-1}^{t} h(s) \, ds.</math>
Finally, by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,
<math display="block">v'(t) = h(t) = f(t, v(t)).</math>
Thus <math>y(t)</math> is a solution of (1) as required.
To apply the Existence Theorem, we need a way of checking that <math>Y(t)</math> is
finite. Here is a convenient criterion.
LEMMA
Let <math>Y(t)</math> be an Euler approximation of the initial value problem (1) with
infinitesimal <math>\Delta t</math>, and let M and b be finite.
(i) If <math>|f(t,y)| \le M</math> for all <math>a \le t \le b</math> and all y, then <math>Y(t)</math> is finite for all
<math>a \leq t \leq b</math>.
(ii) If <math>|f(t, y)| \le M</math> for all <math>a \le t \le b</math> and all <math>y</math> within <math>M \cdot (t - a)</math> of <math>y_0</math>,
then <math>Y(t)</math> is finite for all <math>a \le t \le b</math>.
<b>PROOF</b> (i) Since <math>Y(t)</math> cannot change by more than <math>M \Delta t</math> from one partition point
to the next, we have
<math>|Y(t) - y_0| \le M \cdot (t - a) \le M \cdot (b - a).</math>
<math>M \cdot (b - a)</math> is finite, so <math>Y(t)</math> is finite.
The proof of (ii) is similar.
The lemma is illustrated in Figure 14.4.4. Choose a positive real number
Discussion
M. Part (i) of the lemma says that if <math>f(t, y)</math> is between <math>-M</math> and M, everywhere
in the vertical strip between <math>t = a</math> and <math>t = b</math>, then <math>Y(t)</math> is finite for <math>a \le t \le b</math>.
Part (ii) of the lemma says that if <math>f(t, y)</math> is between <math>-M</math> and <math>M</math>, everywhere
in the shaded triangle, then <math>Y(t)</math> is finite for <math>a \le t \le b</math>. Part (ii) is stronger
because the shaded triangle is a subset of the vertical strip. The proof shows
that <math>Y(t)</math> stays within the shaded rectangle for <math>a \le t \le b</math>.
The lemma and the Existence Theorem combined show that if we can find
an M such that <math>f(t, y)</math> is continuous and <math>f(t, y)</math> is between <math>-M</math> and M every-
where in the shaded triangle, then the initial value problem (1) has a solution
<math>y(t)</math> for <math>a \le t \le b</math>. The proof also shows that the solution <math>y(t)</math> is within the
shaded triangle for <math>a \le t \le b</math>.

Here is another theorem that shows that in most cases the solution is unique
and is close to the Euler approximations for small real increments <math>\Delta t</math>. In this theorem,
we shall write <math>Y_{\Delta t}(t)</math> instead of <math>Y(t)</math> to keep track of the fact that <math>Y(t)</math> depends on <math>\Delta t</math>
as well as on t.
UNIQUENESS THEOREM
Assume the hypotheses of the Existence Theorem and also that <math>f(t, y)</math> is
smooth; that is, the partial derivatives of f are continuous. Then the initial
value problem (1) has only one solution <math>y(t)</math> for <math>t</math> in <math>[a, b]</math>. Furthermore, the
Euler approximations <math>Y_{\Delta t}(t)</math> approach <math>y(t)</math> as the real number <math>\Delta t</math> approaches
zero; that is,
<math display="block">\lim_{\Delta t \to 0^+} Y_{\Delta t}(t) = y(t)</math>
for each <math>t</math> in <math>[a, b]</math>.

## PDF page 881

14.4 EXISTENCE AND APPROXIMATION OF SOLUTIONS
871
We shall not give the proof. The Uniqueness Theorem tells us two important
things about differential equations in which <math>f(t, y)</math> is smooth. First, it tells us that a
particular solution of such a differential equation will depend only on the initial
condition. Thus if an experiment is accurately described by a differential equation
with <math>f(t, y)</math> smooth, then repeated trials of the experiment with the same initial
condition will give the same outcome. Second, it tells us that the Euler approximations
will approach the solution of the differential equation as <math>\Delta t</math> approaches zero. Thus
we can get better and better approximations of the solution by taking <math>\Delta t</math> small.
<b>EXAMPLE 2 (Continued)</b> The function <math>f(t, y) = t - y^2</math> is smooth. The Uniqueness
Theorem shows that the initial value problem of Example 1 has just one
solution <math>y(t)</math> for <math>0 \le t \le 1</math>. Moreover, the Euler approximations <math>Y(t)</math> get
close to <math>y(t)</math> as the real increment <math>\Delta t</math> approaches zero. Thus the approxima-
tions computed in Example 1 really are approaching the solution.
We conclude with an example of an explosion and an example with more
than one solution.
<b>EXAMPLE 3 (An Explosion)</b> The initial value problem

<math display="block">\frac{-1}{y(t)} = t + C,</math>
<math display="block">y(t) = -(t+C)^{-1}</math>
(general solution),
<math display="block">1 = -(0 + C)^{-1}, 	 C = -1,</math><br> <math display="block">y(t) = (1 - t)^{-1}</math>
(particular solution).
The graph, shown in Figure 14.4.5, approaches infinity as t approaches 1
from the left. The function <math>y(t) = (1-t)^{-1}</math> is a solution for <math>0 \le t < 1</math>,
and the solution has an explosion at <math>t = 1</math>.

14.5 COMPLEX NUMBERS
This section begins with a review of the complex numbers. Complex numbers are
useful in the solution of second order differential equations. The starting point is
the imaginary number i, which is the square root of <math>-1</math>. The complex number system
is an extension of the real number system that is formed by adding the number i
and keeping the usual rules for sums and products. The set of complex numbers, or
complex plane, is the set of all numbers of the form
<math>z = x + iy</math>
where x and y are real numbers. The number x is called the real part of z, and y is
called the imaginary part of z. A complex number z can be represented by a point
in the plane, with the real part drawn on the horizontal axis and the imaginary part
on the vertical axis, as in Figure 14.5.1. The sum of two complex numbers is computed
in the same way as the sum of two vectors,
<math>(a + ib) + (c + id) = (a + c) + i(b + d).</math>
<math>x + iy</math>

14.5 COMPLEX NUMBERS
875
The product of two complex numbers is computed using the basic rule <math>i^2 = -1</math>
and the rules of algebra:
<math display="block">(a+ib) \cdot (c+id) = ac + ibc + iad + i^2bd = (ac - bd) + i(bc + ad).</math>
Compute the product of <math>3 + i6</math> and <math>7 - i</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b>
<math>(3+i6)\cdot(7-i)=(3\cdot7-6\cdot(-1))+i(6\cdot7+3\cdot(-1))=27+i39.</math>
The complex conjugate <math>\bar{z}</math> of z is formed by changing the sign of the imaginary part of z:
<math>\overline{a+ib}=a-ib</math>
The product of a complex number with its conjugate is always a nonnegative real
number, computed as follows.
<math>(a+ib)(a-ib) = a^2 - iab + iab + b^2 = a^2 + b^2</math>
<b>(1)</b>
The quotient of two complex numbers can be computed by multiplying the numerator
and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, as follows.
<math display="block">\frac{a+ib}{c+id} = \frac{(a+ib)(c-id)}{(c+id)(c-id)} = \frac{ac+bd}{c^2+d^2} + i\frac{-ad+bc}{c^2+d^2}.</math>
Compute the quotient <math>(1 + i)/(1 - i2)</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 2</b>
<math display="block">\frac{1+i}{1-i2} = \frac{(1+i)\cdot(1+i2)}{(1-i2)\cdot(1+i2)} = \frac{(1\cdot1-1\cdot2)+i(1\cdot2+1\cdot1)}{1+4}</math>
<math>=\frac{-1+i3}{5}=-\frac{1}{5}+i\frac{3}{5}</math>
In the real number system, a positive real number b has two square roots,
<math>\sqrt{b}</math> and <math>\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{b}</math>, and negative real numbers have no square roots. In the complex
number system, a negative real number <math>-b</math> has two imaginary square roots, <math>i\sqrt{b}</math>
and <math>-i\sqrt{b}</math>. The quadratic formula gives the roots of any second degree polynomial
in the complex number system.
QUADRATIC FORMULA
The roots of the polynomial
<math>az^2 + bz + c</math> where <math>a \neq 0</math>
in the complex number system are given by
<math display="block">z = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.</math>
The number <math>b^2 - 4ac</math> is called the discriminant. If a, b, and c are real, there
are three cases:
Case 1 If <math>b^2 - 4ac > 0</math>, there are two real roots.
Case 2 If <math>b^2 - 4ac = 0</math>, there is one real root.

It is often useful to represent a complex number in polar form. A point
<math>(x, y)</math> in the plane has polar coordinates <math>(r, \theta)</math> where <math>x = r \cos \theta</math>, <math>y = r \sin \theta</math>. The
complex number <math>x + iy</math> may be written in the polar form
<math>x + iy = r(\cos \theta + i \sin \theta).</math>
The coordinates r and <math>\theta</math> can always be chosen so that <math>r \ge 0</math> and <math>-\pi < \theta \le \pi</math>. The
number r, which is the distance of the point <math>(x, y)</math> from the origin, is the absolute value
of the complex number <math>x + iy</math>:
<math>r = |x + iy| = (x^2 + y^2)^{1/2}</math>.
The formula (1) for the product of a complex number and its conjugate may now
be written in the short form
<math>z\overline{z} = |z|^2</math>.
The real number <math>\theta</math> is an angle in radians and is called the argument of <math>x + iy</math>. The
argument can be computed by using the formula
<math>\tan \frac{y}{y} = \theta</math>,
and then choosing <math>\theta</math> in the correct quadrant. The polar form of a complex number
is illustrated in Figure 14.5.2. This figure is sometimes called the Argand diagram
of the complex number. The complex number with absolute value one and argument <math>\theta</math>
is sometimes called <math>cis \theta</math>:
<math>cis \theta = cos \theta + i sin \theta</math>.

<math>cis \theta</math> is helpful in computing products, quotients, and powers of complex
numbers. Using the addition formulas for sines and cosines, we can prove the product
formula
<math>(r \operatorname{cis} \theta) \cdot (s \operatorname{cis} \phi) = r \operatorname{s} \operatorname{cis} (\theta + \phi).</math>
<b>(2)</b>
In words, this formula states: To multiply two complex numbers, multiply the absolute
values and add the arguments. There is a similar formula for quotients:
<math display="block">\frac{r \operatorname{cis} \theta}{s \operatorname{cis} \phi} = \frac{r}{s} \operatorname{cis} (\theta - \phi).</math>
(3)
To divide two complex numbers, divide the absolute values and subtract the arguments.

<math display="block">=\cos\frac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=i.</math>

We now turn to complex exponents, which are useful in the study of differ-
ential equations. In order to give a meaning to an exponent <math>e^z</math>, we consider infinite
series of complex numbers. The sum of an infinite series of complex numbers is
defined by summing the real and imaginary parts separately. If <math>z_n = x_n + iy_n</math>, and
the series <math>\sum x_n</math> and <math>\sum y_n</math> both converge, the sum of the series <math>\sum z_n</math> is defined by the
formula
<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z_n = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x_n + i \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} y_n.</math>
In Chapter 9, we found that for real numbers z the exponent <math>e^z</math> is given by the power
series

## PDF page 889

14.5 COMPLEX NUMBERS
<math>e^z = 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2!} + \frac{z^3}{2!} + \frac{z^4}{4!} + \cdots</math>
When z is a complex number, this formula is taken as the definition of <math>e^z</math>. It can be
shown that the power series converges for every z and that the exponential rule
<math>e^{u+z} = e^u e^z</math> holds for complex exponents. In the case that z is a purely imaginary
number <math>z = iy</math>, the power series takes the form
<math>e^{iy} = 1 + iy - \frac{y^2}{2!} - i\frac{y^3}{2!} + \frac{y^4}{4!} + i\frac{y^5}{5!} - \cdots</math>
<math display="block">= \left[1 - \frac{y^2}{2!} + \frac{y^4}{4!} - \cdots\right] + i \left[y - \frac{y^3}{3!} + \frac{y^5}{5!} - \cdots\right].</math>
Using the power series for cos y and sin y, we obtain Euler's Formula:
<math>e^{iy} = \cos y + i \sin y = cis y</math>.
When z is a complex number <math>z = x + iy</math>, the exponent <math>e^z</math> is given by the formula
<math display="block">e^{x+iy} = e^x e^{iy} = e^x (\cos y + i \sin y).</math>

In Chapter 8, the hyperbolic cosine and hyperbolic sine were defined in
terms of <math>e^x</math> by the equations
<math>
cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}, \quad sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}.
</math>
Euler's Formula leads to similar equations for the cosine and sine.
<math>e^{iy} = \cos y + i \sin y,</math> <math>e^{-iy} = \cos y - i \sin y,</math>
<math>\cos y = \frac{e^{iy} + e^{-iy}}{2}, \quad \sin y = \frac{e^{iy} - e^{-iy}}{i2}.</math>
In the next section we will make use of complex valued functions, that is,
functions <math>f(t)</math> that assign a complex number <math>z = f(t)</math> to each real number t. The
derivative of a complex valued function is obtained by differentiating the real and
complex parts separately. Thus, if <math>h(t) = f(t) + ig(t)</math>, where g and h are real functions,
then <math>h'(t) = f'(t) + ig'(t)</math>.
For example, if <math>h(t) = e^{rt}</math>, where <math>r = a + ib</math> is a complex constant, then
<math display="block">h(t) = e^{at}(\cos bt + i\sin bt),</math>
<math display="block">h'(t) = ae^{at}(\cos bt + i\sin bt) + be^{at}(-\sin bt + i\cos bt)</math>
<math>=(a+ib)e^{at}(\cos bt+i\sin bt)=re^{rt}.</math>
Summing up, the usual rule <math>(e^{rt})' = re^{rt}</math> still holds when r is a complex
constant. We can also consider complex valued differential equations. The example
we shall need is the homogeneous linear differential equation
<math display="block">z'+rz=0,</math>

14.6 SECOND ORDER HOMOGENEOUS LINEAR EQUATIONS
A second order differential equation is an equation involving an independent variable t,
a dependent variable y, and the first two derivatives y' and y". The general solution
of a second order differential equation will usually involve two constants. Two initial
values are needed to determine a particular solution. A second order initial value
problem is a second order differential equation together with initial values for y and y'.
This section gives a solution method for second order equations of the following
very simple type.

## PDF page 892

882
14 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS
SECOND ORDER HOMOGENEOUS LINEAR DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION
WITH CONSTANT COEFFICIENTS
<math display="block">ay'' + by' + cy = 0,</math>
<b>(1)</b>
where a, b, and c are real constants and a, <math>c \neq 0</math>.
Discussion If <math>a = 0</math>, the equation is a first order differential equation <math>by' + cy = 0</math>.
If <math>c = 0</math>, the change of variables <math>u = y'</math> turns the given equation (1) into a
first order differential equation <math>au' + bu = 0</math>. In each of these cases, the
equation can be solved by the method of Section 14.1 or 14.2. (After finding
u, y can be found by integration because <math>y' = u</math>.)
In Section 14.2 we found that the first order homogeneous linear differential
equation with constant coefficients, <math>y' + cy = 0</math>, has the solution <math>y = e^{-ct}</math>. To get
an idea of what to expect in the second order case, let us try to find a solution of
equation (1) of the form <math>y = e^{rt}</math> where r is a constant. Differentiating and substituting
into equation (1), we see that
<math>a(e^{rt})'' + b(e^{rt})' + ce^{rt} = ar^2e^{rt} + bre^{rt} + ce^{rt}</math>
<math display="block">= (ar^2 + br + c)e^{rt}.</math>
This shows that <math>y(t) = e^{rt}</math> is a solution of equation (1) if and only if
<math display="block">ar^2 + br + c = 0.</math>
We should therefore expect that the solutions of the equation (1) will be built up
from the functions <math>y(t) = e^{rt}</math> where r is a root of the polynomial <math>az^2 + bz + c</math>. We
shall state the rule for finding the general solution of the equation (1) now and
prove the rule later on.

GRAPHS OF SOLUTIONS OF SECOND ORDER HOMOGENEOUS LINEAR EQUATIONS
Our next topic is graphs of solutions of second order homogeneous linear equations.
Several cases arise, including simple, damped, and overdamped oscillations.
Consider the second order homogeneous linear differential equation
<math display="block">ay'' + by' + c = 0.</math>
<b>(1)</b>

We shall concentrate on the case that
<math>a > 0</math>, <math>b \ge 0</math>, <math>c > 0</math>.
(We can always make <math>a</math> positive by changing all the signs if <math>a</math> is negative. The cases
with negative b or c are considered in the problem set at the end of the section.)
The equation has the characteristic polynomial
<math>az^2 + bz + c</math>
Let d be the discriminant of this polynomial,
<math>d = b^2 - 4ac</math>
Simple Oscillation This type of solution arises when <math>b = 0</math>. Since a and c are assumed
to be positive, the discriminant <math>d = -4ac</math> is negative, and the characteristic poly-
nomial has two purely imaginary roots, <math>\pm i\beta</math>. The general solution of equation (1) is
<math display="block">y(t) = A\cos(\beta t) + B\sin(\beta t).</math>
It is helpful to put this equation in a different form. The point <math>(A, B)</math> is on the circle
with center at the origin and radius <math>C = (A^2 + B^2)^{1/2}</math>. There is thus an angle <math>\theta</math>
for which
<math>A = C \cos \theta</math>, <math>B = C \sin \theta</math>,
as in Figure 14.6.4. The angle <math>\theta</math> can be computed as follows:
<math>\frac{B}{A} = \frac{C \sin \theta}{C \cos \theta} = \tan \theta, \qquad \theta = \arctan \left(\frac{B}{A}\right).</math>

Using the formula for the cosine of the difference of two angles, <math>\cos(\phi - \theta) =</math>
<math>\cos(\phi)\cos(\theta) + \sin(\phi)\sin(\theta)</math>, we find that
<math>y(t) = C\cos(\beta t)\cos(\theta) + C\sin(\beta t)\sin(\theta) = C\cos(\beta t - \theta),</math>
so that
<math>y(t) = C \cos(\beta t - \theta).</math>
The number C is called the <i>amplitude</i>, because the cosine curve oscillates between
C and <math>-C</math>. The number <math>\beta</math> is called the <i>frequency</i>, because the curve will complete
<math>\beta</math> cycles each <math>2\pi</math> units of time. The number <math>2\pi/\beta</math> is called the <i>period</i>, because each
cycle is <math>2\pi/\beta</math> units long. The angle <math>\theta</math> is called the <i>phase shift</i>. Thus the graph of each

The differential equations of this section provide simple models for a variety
of physical systems that oscillate, such as mass-spring systems and electrical networks.
When a horizontal spring of natural length <math>L</math> is compressed a distance <math>x</math>, it exerts a
force of approximately <math>F = -kx</math>. k is called the spring constant and depends on the
particular spring. The negative sign indicates that the force is in the opposite direction
from <math>x</math>, as in Figure 14.6.8. A mass <math>m</math> is attached to the end of the spring. From
Newton's Law,
<math>F = ma = mx''</math>
we obtain a second order differential equation for the position <math>x(t)</math>,
<math>mx'' = -kx</math>
<math display="block">mx'' + kx = 0.</math>

14.6 SECOND ORDER HOMOGENEOUS LINEAR EQUATIONS
Both constants k and m are positive, and the solution is the simple oscillation
<math>x(t) = A\cos(\beta t) + B\sin(\beta t)</math>
where <math>\beta = (k/m)^{1/2}</math>.
A mass-spring system immersed in oil (such as an automobile shock
absorber) is subject to a damping force <math>bx'(t)</math>, which is proportional to the velocity
<math>x'(t)</math> but in the opposite direction. This additional force will slow down the motion
of the spring and lead to a damped oscillation. The force is approximately
<math>F = -bx' - kx</math>
and thus satisfies the differential equation
<math display="block">mx'' + bx' + kx = 0.</math>
When the damping constant b is between 0 and <math>(4mk)^{1/2}</math>, the solution will be a damped
oscillation. The greater the value of b, the more quickly the oscillation will be damped
down. When b is equal to <math>(4mk)^{1/2}</math>, the solution will be critically damped; when b
is greater than <math>(4mk)^{1/2}</math>, the solution will be overdamped.
<b>EXAMPLE 5</b> Suppose a mass-spring system
<math>mx'' + bx' + kx</math>
has spring constant <math>k = 5</math>, damping constant <math>b = 4</math>, and mass <math>m = 1</math>. At
time <math>t = 0</math>, the position is <math>x(0) = 1</math> and the velocity is <math>x'(0) = 2</math>. Find the
position <math>x(t)</math> as a function of time.
The differential equation is
<math>x'' + 4x' + 5x = 0.</math>
The characteristic polynomial <math>z^2 + 4z + 5</math> has roots <math>-2 - i</math> and <math>-2 + i</math>.
Step 1
(These roots can be found using the quadratic equation.)
Step 2 The general solution is
<math display="block">x(t) = e^{-2t} [A\cos t + B\sin t].</math>
Find A and B using the given initial values.
Step 3
<math>1 = e^0 [A \cos 0 + B \sin 0], \quad A = 1.</math>
Compute <math>x'(t)</math> and substitute to find B.
<math>x'(t) = -2e^{-2t}[A\cos t + B\sin t] + e^{-2t}[-A\sin t + B\cos t],</math>
<math display="block">2 = -2e^{0}[\cos 0 + B\sin 0] + e^{0}[-\sin 0 + B\cos 0],</math>
<math>B=4</math>.
The particular solution is
<math display="block">x(t) = e^{-2t} [\cos t + 4 \sin t].</math>
This is a damped oscillation with period <math>2\pi</math>.

Let <math>r</math> and <math>s</math> be the roots of the characteristic polynomial, so that
<math>z^{2} + bz + c = (z - r)(z - s) = z^{2} - rz - sz + rs</math>
If <math>r</math> and <math>s</math> are distinct (either two different real numbers or complex conjugates), we
must show that the general solution is

If <math>r = s</math>, we must show that the general solution is

The plan is to break the second order equation (2) into a pair of first order differential
equations. It is useful to use the symbol <math>D</math> for the first derivative and <math>D^2</math> for the second
derivative with respect to t. Thus
<math>Dv = v', \qquad D^2v = v''.</math>
The differential equation (2) can then be written in the form
<math display="block">(D^2 + bD + c)v = 0.</math>
(3)
We now wish to "factor" the expression <math>D^2 + bD + c</math> as if it were a polynomial.
It is to be understood that <math>(D-r)(D-s)y</math> means <math>(D-r)u</math> where u is the function
<math>(D - s)y = y' - sy</math>. Thus, using the Sum and Product Rules for derivatives,
<math>(D-r)(D-s)v = (v'-sv)' - r(v'-sv) = v''-sv'-rv'+rsv</math>
<math>= v'' + bv' + cv = (D^2 + bD + c)v</math>
This shows that the second order equation (3) is equivalent to the pair of first order
equations
<math display="block">(D-r)u=0,</math>
<b>(4)</b>
<math>(D-s)y=u</math>
<b>(5)</b>
Equation (4) is a homogeneous linear equation whose general solution is
<math>u = Ke^{rt}</math>.
Equation (5) may now be put in the form
<math>v' - sv = Ke^{rt}</math>.
(6)
This first order linear equation was solved in Example 3 in Section 14.3. In the case
<math>r \neq s</math>, the general solution came out to be
<math display="block">y = \frac{K}{r - s}e^{rt} + Be^{st}.</math>
Putting <math>A = K/(r - s)</math>, we get the general solution
<math>y = Ae^{rt} + Be^{st}</math>.
In case <math>r = s</math>, the general solution is
<math>y = Ate^{st} + Be^{st}</math>.
where <math>A = K</math>. In each case we have the required formula for the general solution
of the original equation (2).

14.7 SECOND ORDER LINEAR EQUATIONS
This section contains a method for solving nonhomogeneous second order differential
equations. As in the previous section, we deal only with linear equations with constant
coefficients. We consider equations of the following type.
SECOND ORDER LINEAR DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION WITH CONSTANT
COEFFICIENTS
<math display="block">ay'' + by' + cy = f(t)</math>
<b>(1)</b>
where a, b, and c are real constants and a, <math>c \neq 0</math>.
A differential equation of this form describes a mass-spring system where an outside
force <math>f(t)</math> is applied to the mass. The function <math>f(t)</math> is called the <i>forcing term</i>.
As before, if <math>a = 0</math> the equation is a first order linear differential equation
in <math>y</math>, and if <math>c = 0</math> it is a first order linear differential equation in <math>y'</math>. In each of these
cases, the equation should be solved by the methods of Section 14.3. Hereafter we
assume <math>a, c \neq 0</math>.
To get started, let us review the first theorem on first order linear differential
equations. Theorem 1 in Section 14.3 states that the general solution of a first order
linear differential equation is the sum
<math>y(t) + Bx(t)</math>,
where <math>y(t)</math> is a particular solution of the given equation and <math>x(t)</math> is a particular
solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation. Here is a similar theorem
for second order equations.
THEOREM 1
Suppose that <math>y(t)</math> is a particular solution of the second order linear differential
equation
<math display="block">ay'' + by' + cy = f(t),</math>
<b>(1)</b>
and <math>Ax_1(t) + Bx_2(t)</math> is the general solution of the corresponding homo-
geneous linear differential equation
<math display="block">ax'' + bx' + cx = 0.</math>
<b>(2)</b>
Then the general solution of the original equation <math>(1)</math> is
<math>y(t) + Ax_1(t) + Bx_2(t)</math>.
As in the first order case, this theorem is proved using the Principle of
Superposition.
PRINCIPLE OF SUPERPOSITION (Second Order)
Suppose <math>x(t)</math> and <math>y(t)</math> are solutions of the two second order linear differential
equations
<math display="block">ax'' + bx' + cx = f(t),</math>
<math display="block">ay'' + by' + cy = g(t).</math>

## PDF page 903

893
14.7 SECOND ORDER LINEAR EQUATIONS
Then for any constants A and B, the function
<math>u = Ax + By</math>
is a solution of the linear differential equation
<math display="block">au'' + bu' + cu = Af(t) + Bg(t).</math>
Theorem 1 breaks the problem of finding the general solution of the equation
(1) into two simpler problems.
First problem: Find the general solution of the corresponding linear homogeneous
equation
<math display="block">ax'' + bx' + c = 0.</math>
Second problem: Find some particular solution of the given equation
<math>av'' + bv' + cv = f(t)</math>.
The first problem was solved in the preceding section. We now present a method for
solving the second problem. This method is sometimes called the method of judicious
guessing, or the method of undetermined coefficients. The method works only when
the forcing term <math>f(t)</math> is a fairly simple function, of the form
<math>p(t)e^{\alpha t}\cos(\beta t) + q(t)e^{\alpha t}\sin(\beta t)</math>
<b>(3)</b>
where <math>p(t)</math> and <math>q(t)</math> are polynomials. However, when it works it is a very efficient
method of solution. Often <math>f(t)</math> will be of an even simpler form, such as a polynomial
alone, or a single exponential or trigonometric function. In the case of a homogeneous
equation, where <math>f(t) = 0</math>, the zero function <math>y(t) = 0</math> is a particular solution. The
idea for solving a linear equation is to guess that the differential equation has a
particular solution, which looks like the forcing term <math>f(t)</math> but has different constant
coefficients. By working backwards, it is possible to find the unknown constants
and discover a particular solution. We illustrate the method with several examples.
<b>EXAMPLE 1</b> A mass of one gram is suspended from a vertical spring with spring
constant <math>k = 100</math>, as in Figure 14.7.1. At time <math>t = 0</math>, the mass is at position
<math>y(0) = 2</math> cm and has velocity <math>y'(0) = 50</math> cm/sec. Find the equation of motion
of the mass. It is understood that there is no damping, and the origin is at
the point where the spring is at its natural length.
Figure 14.7.1
In this problem there are two forces, the force of the spring and the force of
gravity. The force of gravity is a constant and is equal to mg dynes, always

## PDF page 904

894
14 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS
in the downward direction. The system is described by a second order linear
differential equation with a constant forcing term,
<math>my'' + ky = -mg</math>.
In this case <math>k = 100</math>, <math>m = 1</math>, and <math>g = 980</math>, so the differential equation is
<math>y'' + 100y = -980.</math>
<b>(4)</b>
To solve the problem, we first find some particular solution of the differential
equation (4), then use Theorem 1 to find the general solution, and finally
substitute to find the particular solution for the given initial values <math>y(0) = 2</math>
and <math>y'(0) = 50</math>.
Since the forcing term is a constant <math>f(t) = -980</math>, we guess that the differ-
ential equation (4) has a particular solution, which is a constant. In this
example it is easy to see by inspection that the constant function
<math display="block">u(t) = \frac{980}{100} = -9.8</math>
is a particular solution of the differential equation (4). By the method of
the preceding section, the characteristic polynomial <math>z^2 + 100</math> has roots
<math>\pm i10</math>, and the corresponding homogeneous differential equation <math>x'' + 100x</math>
= 0 has the general solution
<math>A \cos (10t) + B \sin (10t)</math>.
According to Theorem 1, the general solution of the original differential
equation (4) is the sum of the particular solution of the original equation
and the general solution of the homogeneous equation. Thus the general
solution of equation (4) is
<math>y(t) = A\cos(10t) + B\sin(10t) - 9.8.</math>
Use the initial value <math>y(0) = 2</math> to find A.
<math>2 = A\cos(0) + B\sin(0) - 9.8 = A - 9.8, \quad A = 11.8</math>
Now compute <math>y'(t)</math>, and substitute the given initial value <math>y'(0) = 50</math> to
find B.
<math display="block">y'(t) = -10A\sin(10t) + 10B\cos(10t).</math>
<math>50 = -10A \sin(0) + 10B \cos(0) = 10B</math>, <math>B = 5.0</math>.
The required particular solution is thus
<math>y(t) = 11.8 \cos(10t) + 5.0 \sin(10t) - 9.8</math>
shown in Figure 14.7.2.
In the remaining examples we shall concentrate on the first part of the
problem, finding some particular solution of the given differential equation. In
each case we could then find the general solution by solving the corresponding
homogeneous equation and applying Theorem 1 as we did in Example 1.
<b>EXAMPLE 2</b> Find a particular solution of the differential equation
<math display="block">v'' - v' - 6v = 5 + 18t^2.</math>

Figure 14.7.2 Example 1
Since <math>f(t)</math> is a polynomial of degree two, we guess that some particular
solution <math>y(t)</math> is a polynomial of degree two,
<math display="block">y(t) = K + Lt + Mt^2.</math>
First we find the first and second derivatives of <math>y(t)</math>.
<math display="block">y' = L + 2Mt, \qquad y'' = 2M.</math>
Next we substitute these derivatives into the given differential equation.
<math display="block">y'' - y' - 6y = 2M - (L + 2Mt) - 6(K + Lt + Mt^{2})</math>
<math display="block">= (2M - L - 6K) + (-2M - 6L)t - 6Mt^{2}</math>
<math>= 5 + 18t^2</math>.
In the last equation the coefficients for each power of <math>t</math> must be equal. There
are three equations, for units, <math>t</math>, and <math>t^2</math>.
units: <math>2M - L - 6K = 5</math>
<math>t: -2M - 6L = 0</math>
<math>t^2</math>: <math>-6M = 18</math>.
We can now solve the three equations for the three unknowns <math>K</math>, <math>L</math>, and <math>M</math>.
<math>K = -2</math>, <math>L = 1</math>, <math>M = -3</math>.
The required particular solution is then
<math display="block">y(t) = -2 + t - 3t^2.</math>
It can be shown that whenever the forcing term <math>f(t)</math> is a polynomial of
degree <math>n</math>, the differential equation (1) will have a particular solution that is a poly-
nomial of degree n. When <math>f(t)</math> is a polynomial of degree n, the guess <math>y(t)</math> should be a
polynomial of degree n with unknown coefficients,
<math display="block">y(t) = A_0 + A_1 t + \dots + A_n t^n.</math>

<b>EXAMPLE 3</b> Find a particular solution of the differential equation
<math display="block">v'' + 7v' + 10v = e^{3t}.</math>
We guess that there is a particular solution that is a constant times <math>e^{3t}</math>,
<math>v(t) = Me^{3t}</math>.
The first two derivatives of <math>y(t)</math> are
<math>y'(t) = 3Me^{3t}, 	 y''t = 9Me^{3t}.</math>
Substitute these into the original differential equation.
<math>9Me^{3t} + 21Me^{3t} + 10Me^{3t} = e^{3t}</math>.
Cancel the <math>e^{3t}</math>, and solve for the unknown constant M.
<math>9M + 21M + 10M = 1</math>, <math>M = \frac{1}{40} = 0.025</math>.
The required particular solution is
<math>v(t) = 0.025e^{3t}</math>
Here is the rule for guessing a particular solution of the differential equation
of the form (1) when the forcing term <math>f(t)</math> is an exponential function <math>f(t) = e^{kt}</math>. We
first should find the roots of the characteristic polynomial <math>az^2 + bz + c</math>. If k is not
a root of the characteristic polynomial, there is a particular solution of the form
<math>y(t) = Me^{kt}</math> (as in Example 3 above). If k is a single root of the characteristic poly-
nomial, there is a particular solution of the form <math>y(t) = Mte^{kt}</math>. If k is a double root of
the characteristic polynomial, there is a particular solution of the form <math>y(t) = Mt^2e^{kt}</math>.
Find a particular solution of the differential equation
EXAMPLE 4
<math display="block">y'' + 7y' + 10y = e^{-2t}</math>
The characteristic polynomial <math>z^2 + 7z + 10</math> has roots <math>-2</math> and <math>-5</math>. Since
<math>-2</math> is a single root of the characteristic polynomial, our guess at a particular
solution should be
<math>y(t) = Mte^{-2t}</math>.
The first two derivatives of <math>y(t)</math> are
<math>v'(t) = Me^{-2t} - 2Mte^{-2t}</math>
<math>v''(t) = -4Me^{-2t} + 4Mte^{-2t}</math>
Now substitute into the original differential equation.
<math>e^{-2t} = v'' + 7v' + 10v</math>
<math>= -4Me^{-2t} + 4Mte^{-2t} + 7Me^{-2t} - 14Mte^{-2t} + 10Mte^{-2t}</math>
<math>= 3Me^{-2i}</math>.
Then <math>M = 1/3</math>, and the required particular solution is
<math display="block">y(t) = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right) t e^{-2t}.</math>

14.7 SECOND ORDER LINEAR EQUATIONS
In this example the simpler guess <math>Le^{-2t}</math> would not have worked. The trouble
is that <math>Le^{-2t}</math> is a solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, so it cannot
also be a solution of the original differential equation. To see what happens, let us
try to use the method with the guess <math>u(t) = Le^{-2t}</math>. Computing the first two derivatives
and substituting, we get
<math>u'(t) = -2Le^{-2t}, \qquad u''(t) = 4Le^{-2t},</math>
<math>e^{-2t} = u'' + 7u' + 10u = 4Le^{-2t} - 14Le^{-2t} + 10Le^{-2t}</math>
The right side of the above equation adds up to zero, so we cannot solve for the
unknown constant L.
In a physical system, the forcing term is often a simple oscillation that can
be represented by a function of the form <math>f(t) = G\cos(\omega t) + H\sin(\omega t)</math>. Here is the
rule for guessing a particular solution of the differential equation (1) when the
forcing term is <math>f(t) = G\cos(\omega t) + H\sin(\omega t)</math>. If <math>z = i\omega</math> is not a root of the charac-
teristic polynomial, then the differential equation will have a particular solution of the
form <math>y(t) = K \cos(\omega t) + L \sin(\omega t)</math>. On the other hand, if <math>z = i\omega</math> is a root of the
characteristic polynomial, then there is a particular solution of the form <math>y(t) = Kt \cos(\omega t)</math>
<math>+ Lt \sin(\omega t)</math>.
<b>EXAMPLE 5</b> Find a particular solution of the differential equation
<math>y'' + 16y = -\sin(4t)</math>.
The characteristic polynomial has roots <math>\pm i4</math>. Then <math>\cos(4t)</math> and <math>\sin(4t)</math> are
already solutions of the homogeneous equation, so our guess must have an
extra factor of <math>t</math>. The guess for a solution is then
<math display="block">y(t) = Kt\cos(4t) + Lt\sin(4t).</math>
Compute the first two derivatives of <math>y(t)</math>.
<math>y'(t) = K[-4t\sin(4t) + \cos(4t)] + L[4t\cos(4t) + \sin(4t)],</math>
<math display="block">y''(t) = K[-16t\cos(4t) - 8\sin(4t)] + L[-16t\sin(4t) + 8\cos(4t)].</math>
Now substitute into the original differential equation.
<math>K[(-16t + 16t)\cos(4t) - 8\sin(4t)]</math>
<math display="block">+ L[(-16t + 16t)\sin(4t) + 8\cos(4t)] = -\sin(4t).</math>
<math>-8K\sin(4t) + 8L\cos(4t) = -\sin(4t).</math>
From the sine terms we get <math>-8K = -1</math>, so <math>K = \frac{1}{8}</math>. From the cosine terms we
get <math>8L = 0</math>, so <math>L = 0</math>. The particular solution is therefore
<math>y(t) = 0.125t \cos(4t)</math>.
In Example 5, the particular solution oscillates more and more wildly as
t approaches infinity, as shown in Figure 14.7.3. This happens because the forcing
term <math>\cos(4t)</math> has the same frequency as the solutions of the homogeneous equation,
<math>A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t)</math>. In this case the forcing term causes the oscillation to build up.
This phenomenon is called <i>resonance</i>.
If, instead, the forcing term in Example 5 had a different frequency, <math>-\sin(\omega t)</math>
where <math>\omega</math> is not equal to 4, then the particular solution of the differential equation
would be a simple oscillation of the form <math>K \cos(\omega t) + L \sin(\omega t)</math>, whose amplitude
does not change with time.

Exercise 5
Find a particular solution of the differential equation
<b>EXAMPLE 6</b>
<math display="block">y'' + 6y' + 25y = \cos{(4t)}.</math>
The characteristic polynomial <math>z^2 + 6z + 25</math> has roots <math>-3 \pm i4</math>. Since i4
itself is not a root, the proper guess is
<math display="block">y(t) = K \cos(4t) + L \sin(4t).</math>
Both a cosine term and a sine term are required, because the derivative of
a sine is a cosine. Compute the first two derivatives of <math>y(t)</math>.
<math>y'(t) = -4K \sin(4t) + 4L \cos(4t),</math>
<math display="block">y''(t) = -16K\cos(4t) - 16L\sin(4t).</math>
Now substitute into the original differential equation.
<math display="block">\cos(4t) = [-16K\cos(4t) - 16L\sin(4t)] + 6[-4K\sin(4t) + 4L\cos(4t)]</math>
<math>+ 25[K\cos(4t) + L\sin(4t)]</math>
<math display="block">= (-16K + 24L + 25K)\cos(4t) + (-16L - 24K + 25L)\sin(4t).</math>
Both the <math>\sin(4t)</math> coefficients and the <math>\cos(4t)</math> coefficients must be the same
on both sides of the equation. Thus we have two equations in the two un-
knowns <math>K</math> and <math>L</math>.
<math>\sin (4t) \text{ terms}: 0 = -24K + 9L.</math>
<math>\cos{(4t)}</math> terms: <math>1 = 9K + 24L</math>.
Solve for <math>K</math> and <math>L</math>.
<math>K = \frac{1}{73}, \qquad L = \frac{8}{219}.</math>
The required particular solution is
<math>y(t) = \left(\frac{1}{73}\right)\cos(4t) + \left(\frac{8}{219}\right)\sin(4t).</math>

## PDF page 909

14.7 SECOND ORDER LINEAR EQUATIONS
In Example 6, the particular solution is a simple oscillation, while the
general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation is a damped oscillation.
The general solution is their sum:
<math display="block">y(t) = e^{-3t} [A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t)] + \left[ \left( \frac{1}{73} \right) \cos(4t) + \left( \frac{8}{219} \right) \sin(4t) \right].</math>
The first term, <math>e^{-3t}[A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t)]</math>, approaches zero as <math>t \to \infty</math> and is called
the transient part of the solution. The second term, <math>[(1/73)\cos(4t) + (8/219)\sin(4t)]</math>,
is called the steady part of the solution. The constants A and B, which depend on
the initial conditions, appear only in the transient part and not in the steady state
part of the solution. No matter what the initial conditions are, every particular
solution will approach the steady state part of the solution as <math>t \to \infty</math>. The effect of
the initial conditions dies out as <math>t \to \infty</math>.
The same thing happens in any mass-spring system with damping where
the forcing term is a simple oscillation. Let us consider a mass-spring system
<math>my'' + by' + ky = \cos(\omega t)</math>
<b>(5)</b>
where m, b, and k are positive and the forcing term <math>\cos(\omega t)</math> has frequency <math>\omega</math>. A
particular solution can be found of the form
<math>K\cos(\omega t) + L\sin(\omega t)</math>.
The constants K and L can be computed as in Example 6. The general solution of
equation (5) is
<math display="block">y(t) = e^{-\alpha t} [A\cos(\beta t) + B\sin(\beta t)] + [K\cos(\omega t) + L\sin(\omega t)].</math>
As in Example 6, the first term approaches 0 as <math>t \to \infty</math> and is called the transient part
of the solution, and the second term is called the steady state part of the solution.
Again, every particular solution of the mass-spring system will approach the steady
state part of the solution as <math>t \to \infty</math>.

How does the infinitesimal calculus as developed in this book relate to the traditional
(or <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math>) calculus? To get the proper perspective we shall sketch the history of the
calculus.
Many problems involving slopes, areas, and volumes, which we would today
call calculus problems, were solved by the ancient Greek mathematicians. The
greatest of them was Archimedes (287-212 B.C.). Archimedes anticipated both the
infinitesimal and the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> approach to calculus. He sometimes discovered his results
by reasoning with infinitesimals, but always published his proofs using the "method of
exhaustion," which is similar to the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> approach.
Calculus problems became important in the early 1600's with the develop-
ment of physics and astronomy. The basic rules for differentiation and integration
were discovered in that period by informal reasoning with infinitesimals. Kepler,
Galileo, Fermat, and Barrow were among the contributors.
In the 1660's and 1670's Sir Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
independently "invented" the calculus. They took the major step of recognizing the
importance of a collection of isolated results and organizing them into a whole.
Newton, at different times, described the derivative of y (which he called the
"fluxion" of y) in three different ways, roughly
The ratio of an infinitesimal change in <math>y</math> to an infinitesimal change in <math>x</math>.
(1)
(The infinitesimal method.)
The limit of the ratio of the change in y to the change in <math>x</math>, <math>\Delta y/\Delta x</math>, as <math>\Delta x</math>
(2)
approaches zero. (The limit method.)
The velocity of y where x denotes time. (The velocity method.)
(3)
In his later writings Newton sought to avoid infinitesimals and emphasized the
methods (2) and (3).
Leibniz rather consistently favored the infinitesimal method but believed
(correctly) that the same results could be obtained using only real numbers. He
regarded the infinitesimals as "ideal" numbers like the imaginary numbers. To justify
them he proposed his law of continuity: "In any supposed transition, ending in any
terminus, it is permissible to institute a general reasoning, in which the terminus may
902

## PDF page 913

<b>EPILOGUE</b>
903
also be included." This "law" is far too imprecise by present standards. But it was a
remarkable forerunner of the Transfer Principle on which modern infinitesimal
calculus is based. Leibniz was on the right track, but 300 years too soon!
The notation developed by Leibniz is still in general use today, even though
it was meant to suggest the infinitesimal method: <math>dy/dx</math> for the derivative (to suggest
an infinitesimal change in y divided by an infinitesimal change in x), and <math>\int_{h}^{a} f(x) dx</math>
for the integral (to suggest the sum of infinitely many infinitesimal quantities <math>f(x) dx</math>).
All three approaches had serious inconsistencies which were criticized most
effectively by Bishop Berkeley in 1734. However, a precise treatment of the calculus
was beyond the state of the art at the time, and the three intuitive descriptions (1)–(3)
of the derivative competed with each other for the next two hundred years. Until
sometime after 1820, the infinitesimal method (1) of Leibniz was dominant on the
European continent, because of its intuitive appeal and the convenience of the
Leibniz notation. In England the velocity method (3) predominated; it also has in-
tuitive appeal but cannot be made rigorous.
In 1821 A. L. Cauchy published a forerunner of the modern treatment of
the calculus based on the limit method (2). He defined the integral as well as the deriva-
tive in terms of limits, namely
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) dx = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0^+} \sum_{a=0}^b f(x) \Delta x.</math>
He still used infinitesimals, regarding them as variables which approach zero. From
that time on, the limit method gradually became the dominant approach to calculus,
while infinitesimals and appeals to velocity survived only as a manner of speaking.
There were two important points which still had to be cleared up in Cauchy's work,
however. First, Cauchy's definition of limit was not sufficiently clear; it still relied on
the intuitive use of infinitesimals. Second, a precise definition of the real number system
was not yet available. Such a definition required a better understanding of the
concepts of set and function which were then evolving.
A completely rigorous treatment of the calculus was finally formulated by
Karl Weierstrass in the 1870's. He introduced the <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition as the definition of
limit. At about the same time a number of mathematicians, including Weierstrass,
succeeded in constructing the real number system from the positive integers. The
problem of constructing the real number system also led to development of set theory
by Georg Cantor in the 1870's. Weierstrass' approach has become the traditional or
"standard" treatment of calculus as it is usually presented today. It begins with the
<math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\delta</math> condition as the definition of limit and goes on to develop the calculus entirely in
terms of the real number system (with no mention of infinitesimals). However, even
when calculus is presented in the standard way, it is customary to argue informally in
terms of infinitesimals, and to use the Leibniz notation which suggests infinitesimals.
From the time of Weierstrass until very recently, it appeared that the limit
method (2) had finally won out and the history of elementary calculus was closed.
But in 1934, Thoralf Skolem constructed what we here call the hyperintegers and
proved that the analogue of the Transfer Principle holds for them. Skolem's construc-
tion (now called the ultraproduct construction) was later extended to a wide class of
structures, including the construction of the hyperreal numbers from the real numbers.
